ARTHUR PAULSEN
Grand Master

ARTHUR PAULSEN

Grand Master
19'50 - 1951

In 1885 Grand Lodge, in selecting its Grand Master, chose Brother
Wiley James Tinnin from the little town of Weaverville in Trinity
County. It could not be foreseen at that time that sixty-five years would
elapse before another member of Trinity Lodge No. 27 was chosen to
occupy the highest office within the gift .of the Masons of California.
Such, however, was the case, and on October 13, 1950, Right Worshipful Arthur Paulsen, Deputy Grand Master, was elected Grand Master
of the Grand Lodge and for the succeeding twelve months was received
throughout the jurisdiction as Most Worshipful Arthur Paulsen, Grand
Master of Masons in California. If the delay of sixty-five years was to
be sure of having a distinguished brother from Trinity Lodge of whom
the entire state could be proud, the time spent in waiting was well spent.
Arthur Paulsen was born in Weaverville May 4, 1890, the son of
Peter M. and Barbara Paulsen, California pioneers of Gold Rush days.
Peter Paulsen engaged not only in mining, the common pursuit of the
day, but also in the hotel business in Weaverville.
Arthur Paulsen and Jennie Skinner were married in Sacramento
October 21, 1919 and to them was born a daughter, Gloria Evelyn, now
Mrs. Gloria Yarbrough. Gloria made the Grand Lodge Week an exciting and anxious one for her father and mother with the expectation of
their first grandchild and almost simultaneously with the closing of
Grand Lodge on Friday, October 12, came the news of the birth of a
grandson, Michael Lee.
Arthur Paulsen received his early education in Weaverville, and
was admitted to the practice of law in California March 12, 191 7.
Elected to the office of District Attorney of Trinity County in.January
1923, he filled the post with distinction. He became a judge of the
Superior Court of Trinity County in January 1933, a position in which
he has distinguished himself. Judge Paulsen is recognized by his colleagues as being possessed of a very fine legal mind, and much of his'
time is spent away from w eaverville holding court in various parts of
the state at the request and direction of the State Judicial Council.
Responding to the call of his country in 1917, he enlisted in World
War I, and served in the 1Hth Field Artillery in France.
His Masonic career has been one of service to Trinity Lodge No. 27,
where he was raised August 2, 1913, and to the Grand Lodge of California. His first position in Trinity Lodge No. 27 was that of Senior
Deacon and he became Master in 1924. He was appointed Junior Grand
Deacon of the Grand Lodge in 1941 and in 1943 very capably filled the

office of Grand Orator. He served as a member of the Committee on
Charters, the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Special Committee on
the Masonic Homes, and the Special Committee on Masonic Homes
Admissions. In 1947 he was elected the Junior Grand Warden of Grand
Lodge, and served successively as Senior Grand Warden, and Deputy
Grand Master until his election as Grand Master in 1950.
Judge Paulsen is a member of Royal Arch Masons, serving as High
Priest of Trinity Chapter, later consolidat ed with Shasta Chapter .
No. 19.
As might be expected of a judge and an outstandin g citizen of his
own county, Arthur Paulsen has been identified with all worthwhi le
public services including the Red Cross, Tuberculo sis Association, the
Boy Scouts, and crippled children's organizati ons. Hfa other member.ships include the American Legion, Veterans of Foreign Wars, the
Order of Odd Fellows, and the Native Sons of the Golden West. With
all his activity, he still found the time to serve on the Board of Trustees
of Trinity Congrega tional Church in Weavervi lle.
It has been well said that "It is the lot of many to rule: to rule well
is the fortune of but few" and no better single descriptive phrase could
be chosen for the term of Grand Master Paulsen. When it was necessary
to rule, he ruled well, with firmness and impartiality. Perhaps it was the
fact that he lived in a remote, mountainous county, far removed from the
stress and strain of city life, that gave him such clear objective thinking
on the problems of the Grand Lodge, but whatever it was, the depth of
his understan ding was matched only by his sincerity in applying the
principles of Freemaso nry to the situations which confronted him. He
will long be respected for meeting and talking with the brethren "on the
level" and he will likewise be well remembered for his intense interest in
a new program of Masonic education.
As time adds luster to the names of men who build well in organizations, the name of Arthur Paulsen will stand out in the long list of men
who have served the Grand Lodge of California during the past one
hundred years.

DEVOTIONAL SERVICES
That We May Live Effectively
Very Reverend C. B. SYLVESTER, Grand Chaplain
For the sake of a good beginning, may I refer you to a directive
handed down by Jehovah to Jeremiah-the greatest of the Hebrew
prophets:
"Run ye to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, and ... seek
in the broad places thereof, if ye can find a man" (v.l ).
Since history began there has never been a dearth of men. They
have swarmed forth over the face of the earth, fighting their battles and
winning their wars; building their cities and civilizations; developing
their commerce on land and sea; and multiplying their numbers at a prodigious pace.
At the very hour in which God summoned the prophet to his important quest, there were more men on the earth than at any other previous time in history. Why, then, was this behest wrapped up in terms
so tense and urgent? Men were everywhere-help yourself!
The irony of it all is that there has never been enough men amply
equipped with moral power to do the world's finest work. Great ideals
do not march to their consummation with only a token support. "Too
Uttle and too late" is the sorry spawn of incompetency and unconcern.
However, the scarcity of men does not dispose of their necessity.
Society. after all, is but the extension of individual life, and every institution "is but the lengthened shadow of a man." It is not possible to
build a golden state out of leaden statesmen. When society pays its
homage to the cult of mediocrity, and our institutions fall into the hands
of second and third rate men, the nation heads in toward moral paralysis.
Out of a long list of traditional moral qualities, I have selected three
--old as Eden and as up-to-date as this morning's sunrise-for our consideration at this hour.

One day when Heine was standing in front of the cathedral of
Amiens, a young man standing near ventured to ask him why such
cathedrals are no longer built. The great one replied, "It takes convictions to build cathedrals like that." By that same token convictions must
be mixed with the rising walls of any temple where the soul of man
makes its home.

There are certain popular substitut es which we may as well ~isl:'°se
of once for all. Being short on convictions we are long on prejudices.
But a prejudice is not a conviction. Prejudic e has ~o eyes-it ~annot see.
It has on ears-it cannot hear. It has no brain-it cannot think. It has
no heart-it cannot love.
Our scorn of men because they are white, black. brown, or .yello:v';
because they are Christian . Jew or Turk, may not be the kind of insanity
that drives us to the mad-house; but it is an irrationa lity that breaks the
bonds of universal brotherh ood. and condemn s great. sectors o.f the
human family to live in ostracism and loneliness. Certainl y. that is not
conviction.
Our fortunes are not improved by the substitution of opinions for
convictions. Our America n "long suit" is the forming of judgmen ts without the facts-pr obably .the most unscientific thing we do. And we a.re
usually as far from the truth as the teach~r who insist.ed that the artist
who shaped the faces of the Egyptian Sphinxe s took his model from the
picture of George Washing ton.
But, somewhere, on a dateless day, in an hour of which many o~ us
are sometimes aware, groping amid alternati ves and asking question s
no one has ever answere d, a Star fell from the skies and lighte~ our
way to certainty and decision. Since then we have made no concession or
compromise. Right has been right and wrong ~as been wron.~. Some
things may be true in San Francisc o and false m New York. But the
rightness of right and the wrongne ss of wrong" are true in San Francisco, New York, Calcutta and Bombay. Wrong would be wro~g thou~h
it appear in Paradise . Right would be right though it make its bed i~
Perdition . A lie is the black thing that God has always hated, though .it
fall from the lips of an angel. Truth, though spoken by the devil.
still wears the livery of ineffable splendor .
Prejudic e is poison ivy.
Opinions are autumn leaves that flutter before every wind.
Convictions are the bloom of the Century plant - rare, regal in
beauty, and self-cont ained.
Of course you are intereste d to know just how far this thing I have
been emphasizing will carry one. My answer to the query may be found
in a bit of biograph y.
The Rev. R. B. Palmore achieved a place of distinction as a ~eader in
a great religious denomination of America, and closed his ~u?hc career
as editor of a powerfu l religious journal. Long after the Civil yY ar he
found among his father's papers, a deed to 5,883 acres of ~and. m West
· Virgini a-the only heir to the property . Putting the deed m his pocket,
young Palmore drove out from Charlest own, West Virginia , lo~a.ted thde
estate traced its boundari es and found that hundred s of families ha
moved in, built their humble homes, and were living serenely in a sense

of security. Flowers were planted, trees were growing, gardens were
cultivated, and home life was orderly and frugal. Great lawyers were
ready to inaugura te proceedi ngs which would have dispossessed the
settlers and made the legal owner a millionaire. In reporting this episode the New York Sun said that after prayer and sleepless hours, a
great "conviction" laid hold of young Palmore to the effect that social
concern was vastly more importan t than his personal fortune, and obedient to "the heavenly vision" he consumm ated his decision to leave the
settlers in quiet possession of his estate by executing deeds of conveyance to every family on the plantatio n.
How far will Convicti on carry one? Well, all the way to destiny and that may be as far as any of us wish to go.

And unless we set ourselve s to search diligently for such men, as•
sign them to great public trusts when we have found them, and support
them when the minions of indecenc y attack them, we may expect social
corruption to spread until the underwo rld advance s to the seats of
power.
The sorry circumstance of our day is that public characte r, from the
administration of governm ent down to the smallest political unit, has
progressively deteriora ted to the lowest level since the Civil War.
Men in high places have given and taken bribes, officials have loot~
the public treasury, gangster ism has enjoyed political hospitality, the
multitudes pass by unconcerned, and the looters are still out of jail.
Accordin g to Senator Fulbrigh t, this corrosion has swept beyond
the boundar y line of politics and has begun its work in our- areas of
education. In a speech before the Senate in April of this year, Senator
Fulbrigh t said, among other things, "let us consider what has developed
in our colleges where characte rs of our young men and women are
being molded. Our colleges, under extreme pressure from the alumni.
have become so intent upon winning football and basketba ll games that
they use any means to gain their ends. They make a mockery of the
whole concept of amateur sport. They corrupt not only the hired players,
but also the entire student body who learn from their elders, the cynical,
immoral doctrine that one must win at all costs!"
The great controve rsy in our America is not "Commu nism vs. Capi·
talism;" it is "Moral Rearmam ent vs. Immoral Decay."

from the presiden cy of Rutherfo rd B. Hayes. By 1903 he had indicted,

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND MASTER
ARTHUR PAULSEN, Grand Master
My Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Once again it becomes the d~ty of one who has been signally honored by the fraternity to give an account of his stewardship.
Fqr the world at large the year last past has been one of great uncertainty. Men have longed for peace while they prepared for war.
Years of struggle and deprivation have brought some to that state of
desperation that destroys even their will to resist enslavement. While
our own country and our state have enjoyed a sense of security not
possessed by the world at large, the constant threat of war and the demands of the preparedness program have directly or indirectly affected
our growth and the plans of many of our lodges.
On the whole, however, the past twelve months have been marked
by substantial numerical growth and real achievement. In spite of building restrictions and other limitations upon the normal activities of our
lodges and building assodations, new temples have been completed and
new lodges have been formed, and our membership has increased to well
over two hundred thousand. How well we have builded may be a matter
that only the future can determine, but we may be sure that if we remain
true to the guiding principles of this great institution and have the vision
and devotion to apply them to the problems of today and of the days to
come, ·we need not fear for the Masonry of tomorrow.
The past year has been an unusually busy one for the ceremonial
officers of thfs Grand Lodge. In fact, so many demands were made upon
our time and upon the expense allowances of all officers that it became
necessary to curtail attendance at many special ceremonies in order that
we might stay within our ·budget. Whether or not it is desirable that all
officers attend all special communications of Grand Lodge, we have felt
that the budget should govern and have regulated our travel accordingly.
At the last Annual Communication the Centennial Spirit found expression in a liberal attitude toward applicants for Charters and nine
were issued, more than had been expected. It was our pleasure, therefore,
to constitute the following lodges:
Lake Tahoe Lodge No. 707, October 20, 1950
Westchester Lodge No. 703, November 3, 1950
Seafaring Lodge No. 708, November 4, 1950
Orinda Lodge No. 704, November 10, 1950
El Cerrito Lodge No. 705, November 11, 1950
Hunters Point Naval Lodge No. 706, November 17, 1950
Lorenzo Lodge No. 709, November 18, 1950
Rim of the World Lodge No. 711, November 24, 1950
Anacapa Lodge No. 710, November 25, 1950
As we look back upon these ceremonies and view the accomplish-

16

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ments of these new lodges and observe the boundless enthusiasm of
their officers, we need have no fear for their future. Without exception,
they will stand as enduring blocks in the temple of California Masonry.
Last October the Grand Master reported that he had been privileged
to lay an unusual number of cornerstones of Masonic Temples. At that
time it appeared that we were destined to start construction of a large
number of new temples. The demands of the preparedness program,
with the consequent restriction of building of this kind, made this impossible. But notwithstandin g the great difficulties encountered by our
brethren in matters of finance, in securing proper materials and in obtaining skilled labor, your Grand Officers were called upon to dedicate
the following temples:
Garden Grove Temple, January 6, 1951
Temple City Temple, March 24, 1951
San Gabriel Temple, June 23, 1951
Foothill Temple, July 28, 1951
Northeast Temple, August 11, 1951
North Hollywood Temple, September 8, 1951
Colusa Temple, September 22, 1951
One of the most delightful ceremonies of the year was that in which
we re-dedicated the old temple at Benicia. This was the first Masonic
Hall ever constructed in California.You will recall that this had been lost
to the craft and had been used for many years for C'!mmercial purposes.
A movement was started to re-purchase it and failing in an effort to
secure the aid of Grand Lodge, the brethren of the Benicia area raised
the fund themselves, purchased and rehabilitated the old structure and
restored it to its original form, where it now stands as one of our most
important Masonic shrines.
In this connection you may be interested in knowing that our brethren
of Western Star Lodge No. 2 at Shasta are busily engaged in their plans
for the future. The old lodge building which was constructed in 1853
and which has a vault provided by Grand Lodge, must remain and be
preserved as a shrine to pioneer Masonry, but it is now too small for
present day demands. About fifteen hundred dollars has been raised to
purchase the lot adjacent to the old site and it is hoped that before too .
long additional quarters will be available.
These building programs will always stand out in my memory .as
among the most inspiring achievements of modern Masonry. In most mstances, nearly all the construction work of these new temples has been
performed by the brethren of the lodge and stand as perpetual monuments to their skill as both operative and speculative members of the
craft. In some instances, costly equipment and materials have been donated not only by members of the lodges, but as well by sojourners,
relatives of deceased Masons, and even by persons not connected with
the fraternity-a tribute to the splendid public relations that exist in
such localities.

NEW LODGES

Recognizing the great need in certain parts of the state for new
lodges, I announced at the beginning of the year that if the proper
groups were formed in such localities, upon a proper showing dispensations would not be too difficult to secure. Yet only four such lodges have
been instituted this year, as follows:
Los Altos Lodge, February 28th
Castro Valley Lodge, May 19th
Blue Lakes Lodge, June 16th
Magnolia Park Lodge, July 2nd
The fact that there were no more requests for such dispensations
was due largely to the great difficulty of securing accommodations. Due
to the great demands now being made by our lodges and other groups
sponsored by Masons or members of their family upon our temple
facilities, it is almost impossible for a new lodge to secure quarters unless
it is adequately financed in advance or can build its own temple immediately. While our Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Financing has
been most helpful in trying to solve this perplexing problem, there can
be no question but that scarcity of accommodations is delaying the
formation of many much needed new lodges.

GRAND LODGE RECORDS

Shortly after the close of the last communication of Grand Lodge,
we were advised by our military authorities that there was a strong
probability of war at any time, and particular ly during the spring and
summer months of this year. We. like all others, were urged to make all
necessary preparatio ns for the protection of our people and our property.
The valuable and irreplaceable records of our Grand Lodge are
admittedly in a target area highly vulnerable to assault by bombing.
With a view to placing these records or microfilms thereof in a place of
safety, I called together the heads of the principal committees concerned
and the members of the emergency group created by legislation last
October. to get their views on the steps that could ·b e taken. It was
unanimously agreed by that group that certain records and microfilms of
others should be deposited in a place which would be safe from bombing and I therefore approved a sufficient appropria tion from Grand
Lodge funds to construct a suitable vault in the basement of the new
Columbia Temple in Tuolumne County. The Temple, as all know, is the
property of this Grand Lodge, is newly constructe d and offered unusual
facilities for constructi on of such a vault. In addition, it was in an area
of the state having unusual factors of safety.
NEBRASKA RECORD

Each day many problems come across the desk of a Grand Master,
and many of them, though important in themselves, do not loom large
as a matter of precedent . However, one matter apparently trivial on its
face, has come to my desk this year which deserves the most earnest and
serious considerat ion of this Grand Lodge, and which in due time will
be reported upon by our Committee on Grievance s.
Several months ago a complaint was received from the Grand Lodge
of Nebraska, stating that a member of a California lodge residing in
that state, had violated the law thereof and was subject to trial. In
accordanc e with their establishe d trial procedure, they tried the California brother, found him guilty and ordered him expelled.
If this were a case of a serious and aggravate d offense. one which
was clearly a violation of the law of this Grand Jurisdiction, it would
present no particular problem. But this is not the facl The offense of
which the California brother stands convicted is one which is not, if I
"1nderstand the record correctly, in contraven tion of our own laws.
When the record of conviction from the Grand Jurisdiction of
Nebraska came to me, I ordered it transmitte d to the Grand Lodge
Committee on Grievance s for review, for the solution of the problem

Mason." The question immediately arose whether or not the amendment
was retroactive. I held that it was prospective only in operation.
There is nothing in our law which prohibits a Master Mason from
seeking the memberships mentioned in said question prior to the expiration of the period of twelve months. The obligation to wait that length
of time arises solely out of the promise given by the applicant at the time
of filing his application for degrees. Inasmuch as no such promise was
signed or made by any applicant prior to the expiration of the annual
communication of Grand Lodge last year, there was no obligation resting upon such Master Masons to comply with the rule.
Under Section 315 of our Ordinances, the amendment became
effective immediately upon the close of the last annual communication
of Grand Lodge. I instructed all Secretaries to make the necessary
changes in the application form , and to require all applicants to answer
the question as amended before it was received by the lodge.
DECISION NO. 11

Following the decision of the Grand Master made last year and
approved by Grand Lodge to the effect that Section 151 of our Ordinances which authorizes the deposit of lodge funds in a bank or banks,
did not permit the deposit of such funds in a building and loan association, I was besieged with inquiries concerning the interpretation of Section 152 of the Ordinances, and the legality of investments in building
and loan associations.
I advised all lodges that Section 151 related solely to the deposit of
lodge funds, 'While Section 152 related to the investment of such funds,
and that the decision of the Grand Master last year did not apply in any
way to the interpretation of Section 152.
Any doubt that may have heretofore existed regarding the legality
of investment of lodge funds in building and loan association certificates
has been removed by the action of the California Legislature, Statutes
1949, Chapter 202, which now provides that savings banks may invest
in certificates of building and loan associations. Under our law this automatically makes such investments legal for Masonic Lodges.
DECISION NO. Ill

Another question of more than passing importance in the ·management of the funds of constituent lodges was presented to me for decision
by King Solomon's Lodge. A resolution was passed by that lodge, providing "that no officer or member will have the authority to incur any
Indebtedness against King Solomon's Lodge of more than two hundred
dollars for any single activity excepting relief of the lodge, unless approved by a majority vote of the membership prior to such activity, and
that this motion shall remain in effect and not be changed unless the

27

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNiA

membership have thirty days' notice thereof."
After the passage of the above resolution by majority vote, and at
the next stated meeting, the Master ruled that the resolution was out of
order and directed that the record thereof be deleted from the minutes of
the previous meeting. The proponents of the resolution therefore requested a ruling from the Grand Master. The be~ief i.s commonly held
that with the adoption of uniform by-laws, the legislative power of constituent lodges in matters of this kind have been practically destroyed.
Standing resolutions have been disapproved many times, but so far as I
am advised, the disapproval has always been based upon the ground
that the resolution in question was in conflict with by-laws or some
higher authority.
The funds of a constituent lodge are under the control of the lodge,
subject to such rights as are specifically conferred on officers ~uch as the
Charity Committee, or can reasonably be inferred. Our Ordinances repeatedly refer to "the lodge" in connection with the use of lodge fun?s·
While Section 115 of the Ordinances recognizes the "primary executive
authority" of the Master, it also recognizes the legislative power ~f the
lodge "relative to its internal concerns" in cases where the exercise of
such authority does not conflict with some higher law.
I ruled that a standing resolution, placing a limitation in advance
upon the power of officers to incur indebtedness. would b.e le~al and
binding, provided always that it is so drawn as not to conflict with any
statutory delegation of power to the officers or members of the lodge as
provided by other provisions of our law.

decision. It might be argued with great force that the rejection of the
proposed legislation was based upon the ground that it was not necessary in the light of the prior decision. However, this was not the case.
The matter was debated solely upon its merits, and as a matter of policy
the majority of the members of the Grand Lodge held that this should
not be a part of our law, at least in statutory form.
It must be admitted as a matter of law, that the failure to enact the
proposed ordinance did not change the force and effect of the former
decision, and that under our law as it now stands, one who has been
convicted of a felony, or at least who has served a term in a state prison,
is not entitled to apply for the degrees. Because of the confusion which
has gro'Wn out of the conflicting actions heretofore mentioned, and because, like practically all members of my profession I feel that the decision of 1875 is unsound in the light of modern conditions, I again present
the matter to Grand Lodge that all doubt as to our policy in such an important matter be removed. At the time of the rendition of the old decision in 1875, it was the policy of our criminal law generally .to exact
"an eye for an eye.'' At that time courts were not authorized to grant
probation to offenders where there were extenuating circumstances and
a likelihood that the offender might be reformed. Small children were
sent to jail for long periods of confinement and society was reluctant to
show consideration or leniency of any kind for one who had once transgressed our statutes or violated our moral law, regardless of the circumstances or what atonement had been made in later life.
Those of us who spend our lives in trial courts realize that there are
cases occasionally where justice may miscarry,' or where men may be
found guilty•on technical grounds even in the absence of moral turpitude
or intent to commit a crime. One of the cases reported to me by the
Master of a lodge recently, involves a question where the prospective
applicant was convicted many years ago, in his early youth, of manslaughter growing out of the reckless driving of an automobile.
The second case involves a question where a man was convicted in
his early youth under circumstances which have caused many people
to question the justice of the decision.
I am of the opinion that the instances where lodges in this Grand
Jurisdiction would elect an applicant who had once been convicted of a
felony would be rare indeed. There are cases, however, familiar to all
those engaged in law enforcement, where the circumstances are such that
it can not be said at the present time as a matter of practical experience
that the applicant is not under the tongue of good report in the communiy where he has since spent his life and where he is best known to
those about him. Not only are there cases where a serious doubt exists
as to the moral guilt of the defendant in the first instance, but it is firmly
established through the many succeeding years that such defendant
has demonstrated his worth and character to those who are best qualified to act.

26

DECISION NO. IV

Within the past month I have received inquiries from two diff~rent
lodges which again raised the question whether or ~~t an applicant
who admittedly has been convicted of a felony may petition for degrees.
In 1875 this Grand Lodge decided that one who had se~ved a term
in a state prison was not "under the tongue of good report and could
not petition for the degrees.
·
.
No doubt the questions have again arisen because of the. acti~n of
Grand Lodge at the Annual Communication of 1948, at which time a
resolution was offered for the purpose of amending Section 208 of the
Ordinances. to provide specifically that one convicted of a .felony c~uld
not apply for the degrees. After considerable debate on this resolution,
.
it was rejected.
In the light of the record as thus shown, it appears that since 1875,
by decision of Grand Lodge, such a person is not under the tongue of

A NEW PROJECT

d k
I have devoted the major part of my
As most of you alrea y now, f
f one great project. In recent
time and effort this year to the promo ion ~t in some way to create an
years several Grand ~~sters ha::~o~p Masonic information. All but
efficient and more amb1t10u_s :~o.y
That one resulted in the appointone of the propos~ls met w~as:~i~r~~formation. In its early years the
ment of a Comm1t~ee on
t exclusively to matters of symbolism,
committee directed its eff~rts alfosh. 6. Id the work was most excellent.
allegory and kindred subiects. n t is e

29

In later years a more practical turn was taken and a number of worthwhile and most commendable pamphlets were issued for the enlightenment of candidates and newly made members. Since the creation of that
committee, we have expended on this project a large sum of money, but
excellent as the work has been, we have not approached a proper goal.
This is recognized by the present committee, which has realized from .
the beginning that the limits set for its activities are too narrow.
Long before I reached this office, I became convinced from my
observations and conversations with members of the craft in all parts of
the state that the time had come for us to undertake a well-thought-out
and more ambitious plan for the dissemination of practical information
and the education of all Masons---especially those who have just joined
our ranks-in the principles and purposes of this institution. Perhaps
there has never been a time prior to this when the craft would have been
interested in such a plan, but I sincere~y believe that it is now at hand.
Many other Grand Jurisdictions have recognized this need, and a number have already made great progress in their plans. To be effective,
any program adopted must enlist the talent of the best students, teachers
and speakers among us. This talent must be sufficiently well distributed
through the state to give service of some kind to all lodges: and the cost
to Grand Lodge must not be excessive.
To explore the "possibilities of such a program and to bring to this
communication a report of the activities of other Grand Jurisdictions,
I appointed a committee to investigate and analyze their work and in
due time this committee will give you its findings and recommendations.
It has formulated legislation which I shall submit to you with the hope
that it will be adopted.
The legislation proposed will probably not meet with approval in
every minor detail, even by those who believe in the proposed program.
Such matters are of necessity subject to compromise. In undertakings of
this kind we must to some extent experiment and make such changes as
seem advisable in the light of future experience: but the value of such a
project is far too great to be delayed and the need ~oo pressing to be
blocked by minor differences of opinion.
Briefly stated, the proposed legislation would authorize the Grand
Master to form by warrant a sufficient number of Research Lodges to
meet our needs. Such lodges would be organized solely for this purpose
and would not confer degrees or perform many duties of ordinary lodges.
They would be under the supervision of Grand Lodge at all times and
would be designed to serve in such manner as it directs.
Research Lodges should not--and I can not emphasize this too
strongly-seek to occupy the field now · covered by other Masonic
bodies: and they should not compete with the activities of constituent
lodges. They should confine their activities to such work as lies legiti.mately within the field of Craft Masonry. Their members should not
become Masonic Monks but should devote their time and their talents to

Tc All Lodges:
Brethren:

August 27. 1951

Chain Letters
My attention hc.s recently been called several ti~es to the .fact that
certain brethren in this Grand Jurisdiction are sending out cham letters
which are strictly in violation of law.
It is my direction that this matter be called to the attention of the
brethren at the next stated meeting, and if the names of such pers.ons ~re
known, it is my direction that the Inspector be informed of the identity
of the senders of such letters, and that he report those na~es to me as
soon as possible.
Furnishing Mailing Lists
My attention has also been called to the fact that a number of. requests have been circulated for the names of Masons for use for various
purposes not connected with activities approved by Grand Lodge or by
Masonic Law.
·
d
This is contrary to our ordinance s and all Masons are directe
not to
furnish such lists.
Masonic Clubhouses
The attention of the Craft is again directed to the fact that Grand
Lodge of California supports two splendid Masonic Clubhouse s at two
of our great Universities, and that a large number of students who would
be eligible to enjoy the benefits of such clubhouses, apparentl y are unaware of such facilities.
It is my sincere hope that this matter be again brou~ht t~ the atte~tion of our brethren who are sending children to the Um:ersi~y o~ California or the University of California at Los Angeles with the vie': to
making these splendid facilities available to as many students as possible.
Fraternall y yours,
Attest:

ARTHUR PAULSEN.

SPECIAL FUNERA L SERVICE
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of California:
The undersign ed hereby proposes the following resolution for adoption by Grand Lodge:
RESOLV ED, that the following is hereby adopted as a funeral service to be used by lodges at Masonic funerals following the service by a
clergyman :
Brethren and Friends:
From time immemorial. it has been the custom among Free and
Accepted Masons, at the request of a brother, to accompany his remains
to the place of interment and there deposit them with the brief formalities of the Craft.
In conformit y with this usage, and in testimony of our love and esteem for our departed brother, we have assembled here in the character
of Freemaso ns to offer up to his memory, the last sad tribute of our
affection: thereby demonstra ting the sincerity of our Brotherly love and
our steady attachmen t to the principles of our Institution.
As no man should enter upon any important affair without first invoking the blessing of God, we bow our heads in prayer.
.
Chaplain Most Glorious God! Author of all good, and Giver of all mercy! Pour
:lown Thy blessing upon us, we beseech Thee, and strengthen our solemn

34

engagements with the ties of sincere affection! Endow us with fortitude
and resignation in this hour of our sorrow, and grant that this dispensation from Thy hands may comfort those who now meet here to mourn.
May the present example of mortality remind us of our approaching dissolution, and draw our attention to Thee, our only refuge in time of need.
Endow us with the vision of faith to see that realm beyond the skies
where the veil of sorrow never hides the light: and when the contests of
our transitory life on Earth are ended, may we be received into Thy
Everlasting Kingdom. Amen.
Response: So mote it be.
(Master reads the Sacred Roll and deposits it on the casket.)
(The apron is taken from the casket by the S. W. and handed to the ,
·
Master.)
This lamb-skin apron is an emblem of innocence and the peculiar
badge of a Mason. It is more ancient than the Golden Fleece or the
Roman Eagle, and, when worthily worn, more honorable than the Star
or Garter, or any other Order which earthly power can confer. By it
we are admonished of that purity of life and rectitude of conduct by
which alone we may hope to gain admission into that Celestial Lodge
above where the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe forever presides.
( Deposits a pron on casket)
(Taking sprig of Acacia)
This Acacia, which once marked the temporary resting place of one
illustrious in Masonic legend, is an emblem of immortality. By it we are
reminded that we have an imperishable spirit in us which will never,
never die.
(Deposits Acacia)
Our brother has reached the end of his earthly toils. The brittle
thread which bound him to earth has been severed. The silver cord is
loosed: the golden bowl is broken; the pitcher is broken at the fountain;
the wheel is broken at the cistern. The dust has returned to the Earth
as it was and the spirit has returned to God who gave it.
"Man that is born of woman is of few days and full of trouble.
He cometh forth as a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a
shadow and continueth not."
This is the state of man: today he puts forth the tender leaves of
hope: tomorrow blossoms,
And bears his blushing honors thick upon him,
The third day comes a frost.
The Almighty Fiat ~as made at the foundation of the World,
"Dust thou art, and unto dust shall thou return."
Unto its final resting place we consign his body, earth to earth;
ashes to ashes: dust to dust.

MEETINGS AT BENICIA TEMPLE

in s~ch dispensation, at a place other than the regular place of

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREAS, during the year 1950, the members of Benicia Lodge
No. 5, F. & A. M., acquired and reconditioned the First Masonic Temple
built in the State of California, located in the City of Benicia and,
WHEREAS, this project cost the treasury of Benicia Lodge $4,450.00 and many hours of labor and,
WHEREAS, this First Temple was dedicated to Masonic purposes
by the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California on January 27,
1951 and,
WHEREAS, it now stands as a Masonic Shrine of great interest to
alJ regular Masons,
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: that this Grand
Lodge take proper action to authorize all regular Lodges within i~s
jurisdiction to confer Degrees in the First Masonic Temple under their
own charters as is now the case with the Masonic Home at Decoto and
the Masonic Temple at Columbia.
Attest:
DwlGHT E. WooD, Secretary
Benicia Lodge No. 5, F. & A. M.
By Special Resolution of Benicia Lodge
No. 5, F. & A. M., At their Stated
Meeting of October 3, 1951-A. L. 5951.
Referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes, and on
Jurisprudence.

At our Stated Meeting of August 13th, 1951, the following resolution
was presented and unanimously adopted with the request that it be
presented to Grand Lodge in October 1951, for their consideration and,
if favorably received, be adopted by that Grand Body:
RESOLVED, that, inasmuch as a member receiving a 50 year
button for continuous membership for that length of time, must be
at least seventy one years of age, and in most cases, unable. to continue in a legitimate occupation for a livelihood, that Grand Lodge
cause to have printed a Life Membership Certificate the same to
be furnished with the 50 year button to be presented to the Brother
entitled to that Honor.
The lodge does not consider that we are giving enough honors
to 50 year members who have served the Fraternity for that length
of time, nor are the constituent lodges furnished with a service for
the memory and respect for their Brethren who have passed into
the Great Beyond, except in Grand Lodge, where very few of the
membership are present from each lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
CARL C. MIKESELL, Secretary
Needles Lodge No. 326, F.&A.M.
Referred to the Committees on Finance and on Policy and General
Purposes

ADDITION OF SECTION 332Yz
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California, F. & A. M.:
I offer the following resolution:
Be It Resolved: That a new section be added to the Ordinances to
be numbered 332Yi, to read as follows:
Whenever the Junior Warden of any lodge in this jurisdiction
learns, or it is called to his attention, that a member of his lodge is a
barkeeper or is engaged either as principal, agent or employee, in the
saloon business (except in connection with and as part of the operation
of a bona fide hotel or restaurant) he shall send by registered mail, with
request for return card signed by addressee only, a notice to such member stating that he has been informed that such member is a barkeeper
or is engaged in the saloon business as above stated, and reciting a copy
of Section 210 of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge in full, and stating
unless such member notifies him or the Master in writing within sixty
days stating whether he is or is not a barkeeper or in the saloon business,
and adding such explanations as he may desire, he will automatically be
expelled from the lodge at the stated meeting next after the expiration
of such sixty days, and at said stated meeting the master will announce

ADVA NCE NOTIC E OF PROPO SED LEGISL ATION
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
It is apparen t that many of the resolutions introduc ed and much of
the legislation proposed at Grand Lodge Commun ications is contemplated for some period of time prior to the actual opening of the Communications. Under the present system, Grand Lodge members are called
upon to act on such proposal s with at best a few days for consideration
and discussion and frequent ly with only a few hours for such consideration.
In an attempt to provide more time for discussion of proposed measures among Grand Lodge members and where desirable within constituent lodges the following resolution is presente d:
Resolved:
( I ) That members of Grand Lodge who wish to introduc e resolutions or propose legislation or initiate other action by Grand
Lodge are encourag ed to submit a copy of such proposal s to the
office of the Grand Secretar y in time to permit distribution of
these proposal s to the constitue nt lodges of the jurisdiction before the start of the Grand Lodge Communications.

AMEN DMEN T OF SECTIO N 163
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge of California:
Wherea s Section 163 of the ordinanc es of Grand Lodge prohibits
membership in more than one Lodge in this jurisdiction at the same time,
and
Whereas , groups of Masons seeking a dispensa tion for the formation of a new Lodge often need the guidance of Past Masters as officers
but such Past Masters are unwilling to dimit from the Lodge they served
as Master, and
Whereas , Past Masters and members of this Grand Lodge have
sufficient experience as Masons to be trusted not to abuse the privilege
of belonging to more than one Lodge in this jurisdiction at the same time,
Now, therefore ,
Be It Resolved: That Section 163 of the Ordinan ce be amended to
·
read as follows:
"Sec. 163. No Mason shall be a member of more than one Lodge in
this jurisdiction at the same time, except as members of this Grand Lodge
acquire membership in a new Lodge by being named as an officer in a
dispensation or resulting charter."
Respectf ully submitted,
JoHN H. FERGUSON, P. M.
Long Beach Lodge No. 327
. ARTHUR J. S1SSONS, P. M.
Los Cerritos Lodge No. 674
Referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on
Jurisprudence.

AMENDMENT OF SECTION 152
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
At the request of the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Financing
I respectfully recommend that Section 152 be amended by adding the
"Words "or Lodges" immediately following the word "Lodge" in the
second line of paragraph 2 ( b) as it appears in Ross Digest. The Committee has interpreted the law to mean that a Lodge or Lodges shall hold
a controlling interest in any such corporation. The basis for such interpretation may be found in Section 151 which provides that "a Lodge or
Lodges may hold shares of stock in a corporation organized for the purpose of purchasing, erecting or maintaining and holding title to real
estate for a Temple for Lodge uses," etc. Nevertheless, it is believed
that the suggested amendment is necessary to clarify a section of the law
which has caused a great deal of controversy.
Respectfully ~ubmitted,
E. J. BucKFELDT, Past Master, Alexander Hamilton Lodge No. 535
Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

INCLUDING PRAYERS IN SHORT FORM
GRAND LODGE OPENING
Whereas: The simplified form for opening and closing Grand Lodge
in special communication as already adopted omits any mention of the
Grand Chaplain; and
Whereas: Masonic meetings of every character are traditionally
opened and closed with prayer and as it is believed the religious nature
of a Masonic Lodge and our dependence upon Divine Providence are
neglected by the newly adopted legislation, the Grand Lodge Communications for which the new ritual is designed contain important passages for use by the Grand Chaplain; now therefore be it
Resolved: That the Special Committee on Grand Lodge ceremonies
be instructed and is hereby ordered to revise the simplified opening and
closing ceremonies to include appropriate references to the Grand
Chaplain and the prayers which he customarily gives.
Respectfully submitted,
JosEPH C. Cox, Master
Signal Lodge No. 543
FRED B. GRAY, Master

R. E. Dolley Lodge No. 616
Referred to Special Committee on Grand Lodge Ceremonies for
report next year.

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
For Fiscal Year Ending July 31, 1951
To the Brethren of Grand Lodge:
In the Auditor's reports for the year ending July 31, 1951, will be
found Consolidated Statement of Assets Owned or Under Control of
Grand Lodge. and Liabilities. and Consolidated Statement of Cash
Receipts and Disbursements from Funds of or Controlled by Grand
Lodge for the same period. In the cash consolidated statement appears
an itemized statement of funds in custody of Grand Lodge and held in
operating funds. In exhibits pertinent to the consolidated statement of
assets and liabilities appear detailed listings of securities owned. It is
suggested to such members of Grand Ledge as are interested in reviewing the several listings ·o f securities that they will notice the different
types of securities that now are a part of the portfolio pursuant to the
new investment policy. Also in the exhibits will be found more detail of
receipts and disbursements and cash items: the increase in the endowment fund and how accounted for: securities purchased and otherwise

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

acquired and securities redeemed and sold: and the following ,pertinent
to Masonic Homes, balance sheet, statements of cash receipts and disbursements, revenue and expense, and direct and detailed operating
expenses of Decoto and Covina.
· It will be remembered that, at the Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge in 1950, a special committee on Investment of Funds, appointed
to consider the recommendation of the Grand Treasurer that Grand
Lodge adopt the "Prudent Man Rule" as an investment policy for its
various funds, submitted a favorable report which was adopted as to
policy. (Proceedings 1950, pages 105-109.) The report was referred
to the Committee' on Jurisprudence for legislation, which was formulated,
reported to Grand Lodge and unanimously adopted. (Proceedings 1950,
pages 246-247.)
Pursuant to that legislation the Investment Committee embarked
upon the responsibility of authorizing investments in consonance therewith. The committee, as of July 31, 1951, has consisted of the Grand
Treasurer, the Assistant Grand Treasurer, the Chairman of, the Committee on Finance, the President of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes, and the Chairman of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board
or a member of that board designated by him, and in this capacity
Brother Charles E. Moore was designated by the Chairman. Chairman
Bashor of the Endowment Board has also attended meetings.
This Committee duly organized and adopted a plan for conferences
at meetings to be held at stated intervals in San Francisco. Also, the
Grand Secretary was requested to act as Secretary of the Committee
and he has faithfully discharged that responsibility. After careful review
of the investment management service field, Moody's having been also
favorably recommended by the Assistant Grand Treasurer and having
submitted a statement of services contemplated for the guidance of the
Committee and compensation therefor, were selected as financial advisors for the Committee.
Moody's personal management service was organized in 1900 and
therefore has had fifty years of service business. Investment counseling
evolved in time to its present status about twenty years ago and now
accounts for approximately half the total business. At the time of inves- ·
tigation it had employed m investment advisor service, full time, 118
persons, and 17 part time. Al1 principals had had twenty years or more
experience. This is but a partial summary of the detail studied on a
current report on Moody's. A contract engaging Moody's Investors
Service was approved and the Chairman authorized to execute the same
November 16, 1950, for a term of one year from and after November
16, 1950.
Committee meetings were held November 16, 1950, and adjourned
to meet November 30, 1950, February 8, 1951, and May 24, 1951. The
foregoing are meetings during the fiscal year July 31st, 1950-51. Tht:te

has been a subsequent meeting, August 24, 1951. These meetings were
well attended and approved representatives of Moody's were present.
These were Messrs. Richard T. Langan. Pacific Coast Manaqer. resident in Los Angeles, and Frank H. Weyeneth. San Francisco Manager.
The Committee in its deliberations was guided by an agenda previously
prepared by the Assistant Grand Treasurer in conference with the
Grand Treasurer and the Grand Secretary, and included recommendations made by Investment Counsel a reasonable time in advance of the
meetings. Such counsel also has the entire investment portfolio of
Grand Lodge under continuous review and intermediate suggestions of
purchases and sales are recommended.
Thus far the Committee has determined to follow a defensive purchase program, which still continues. From December 1, 1950 through
July 31. 1951, the cost of securities purchased under the Grand Lodge
plan amounted to $1,032,701, and the market value of these securities
as of July 31, 1951, amounted to $1.086,871.
To date the permissible percentages of investments in securities have
not been reached. This is indicative of precautionary policy. The percentages in total are as follows:
Group I-Cash and Governments...............- .................... · 74.3%
Group II-Other Bonds and Preferred Stocks................ 6.4%
Group III-Common Stocks .............................................. 19.3%
The percentage return on total investments on November 30, 1950,
was 1.97%. As of July 31, 1951 the perecntage was 2.61 %.
Stated in dollars. the dollar income as of November 30, \ 950, was at
the rate of $120.597 per year. On July 31, 1951 it was at the rate of
$158.566.
The foregoing is submitted merely as informative with respect to
the results of the program to the end of the fiscal year.
In accordance with Grand Lodge regulations, all securities are at
present in the custody of the Anglo California National Bank of San
Francisco.
At the meeting on February 8, 1951, at the suggestion of the Grand
Treasurer, it was moved, seconded and carried that the auditor employed
by Grand Lodge be authorized to conduct a current audit of sales and
purchases of securities authorized by the Investment Committee, or
otherwise.
At the meeting -on August 24, 1951. subsequent to the fiscal year, it
was concluded to present a resolution to Grand Lodge to amend Section
~6, Subsection 4 by adding the words "or gift" following the word
bequest."
In accordance with the request of the Committee, the Grand Treasurer recommends adoption of the proposed amendment.

At the same meeting it was concluded that when "not fully listed
securities" received by bequest or gift are to be held longer than one .
year, they then become a part of the total for purposes of percentages
invested in each category. This requires no amendment, but is mentioned
herein for the record.
There was an additional amendment recommended by the Committee, namely, that Section 86, Subsection 2 ( b) be amended by adding
the words '"or will be" following the word '"must." The purpose is to
confer the same authority on the Investment Committee with respect
to the purchase of preferred stocks as it has with respect to the purchase
of evidences of indebtedness, as related to listing. In accqrdance with
the request of the Committee, the Grand Treasurer recommends such
amendment to Grand Lodge.
One other interesting item relates to the sale of Treasury bonds in
1950. Fram the several portfolios marketable government bonds totaling
$1,559,000 at cost were sold on September 8, 1950 (which was before
the formation of the Investment Committee) for $1.5n,l l 6.05, which
resulted in a profit of $18,116.05. On July 31, 1951. our' year-end, the
market had dropped to $1.520,285.17, which would have entailed a loss
of $38,714.83, or a net difference of $56,830.88. ·
The accounting plan presently in operation is centered in the office
of the Grand Secretary, and, as a result. the contacts between the offices
of Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer are numerous. It is my privileqe
and pleasure to compliment the Grand Secretary and his hard-workiiig
and faithful assistant, Henry Oliphant, and the office on the diligence
and efficiency exhibited. This is emphasized by the current audit of
Walter Parker, whose services also warrant special mention. It is not a
simple task and he cooperates courteously. It is my recommendation that
every member of Grand Lodge should make an effort to analyze the
Auditor's reports. The set up has been simplified from time to time so
that reports may be readily reconciled. In addition to informing themselves it is well that those who have any knowledge at all of investments
should afford the responsibile officers the beneflt of any suggestion.
See "Special Report-Trusts Turn to Stocks" U.S. News & World
Report. 9-28-51, page 50. copy of which is flied with original of this
report in the Grand Lodge office.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my Tenth Annual Report
as your Grand Secretary.
This has been an interesting decade of Masonic service, and I take
this occasion to thank Grand Lodge for the opportunity to serve and,
also, to thank the Grand Masters who have made all of this service so
pleasant.
The splendid cooperation of the Secretaries and the Inspectors continues: and it is because of this, and the excellent work of the Office Staff,
that we are able to handle the large volume of work which necessarily
flows through the office of a Grand Lodge as large as California.

SAN SIMEON LoDGE No. 196

On August 24, 1951, the hall of San Simeon Lodge No. 196 was deA
•troyed by fire with the loss of all furnishings and equipment and, also,
the loss of the charter. Perhaps lightning does not strike twice in the
Bame place but fires do, because it is the second time this has happened
to San Simeon Lodge. At the direction of the Grand Master I issued a

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

duplicate charter to this lodge with, of course, the proper endorsement.
In spite of all our urging many Lodges still have not had their
charters photostated for which a simple procedure is set up in the Grand
Lodge Office. Unfortunately San Simeon Lodge was one of these, although, as heretofore stated, they had previously lost a charter by fire.
We again urge all Lodges which have not done so to send their
charters to us to be photostated.

A~ENDMENT TO SECTION 101
It is my opinion that we work a hardship on members of Lodges from
other jurisdictions who desire to join in a petition for a dispensation to
form a new Lodge by requiring them to first dimit from the Lodge of
which they are a member. If the dispensation is not granted, they are
then without affiliation in any Lodge. I. therefore, recommend that Section 101 be amended to correct this requirement. .
AMENDMENT TO SECTIONS 176-250-251
The present regulations gover~ing the issuing and recording of dimits
and the completion of affiliation frequently create circumstances in which
continuous membership is impossible, thus breaking a member's record
of active membership in good standing. I, therefore, recommend revision
of Section 176. Section 250-1 st and 250-2nd.

MEMBERSHIP
In presenting the membership totals I have taken the years 1940,
1941, 1945, 1950 and 1951. These years have been selected to indicate
the period immediately preceding World War II, the end of World War
II and the end of the ten year period of my incumbency as Grand Secretary.
A study of these figures will indicate the comparative growth, and
they do present some very interesting facts. The growth from 125,843
to the all time high of 202.500 indicates a net gain of 76,657. This is
j>robably not in proportion to the total gain in population in the state, but
is entirely in keeping with the traditional viewpoint of Masonry in general, and the Grand Lodge of California in particular, on the matter of
growth.

REPOR T OF THE GRAN D LECTU RER
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge
Free and Accepte d Masons of California:
With this, the first year of the second century of Masonry in California rapidly drawing to a close. it is again afforded me the pleasure
and the privilege of submittin g to this Grand Lodge the Annual Report
of the Grand Lecturer , as required by Section 50 of the Constitu tion. I
am reminded that, if this year merits no other distinctio n, your Grand
Lecturer can at least boast of having been accorded the honor to serve
the last year of the first century and the first year of the second century
of the existence of Masonry in Californ ia. And to you, my Brethren , I
am indeed grateful for the opportun ity to serve.
Condition of Lodges
Reports received from Inspecto rs of the Masonic Districts throughout the jurisdicti on indicate lodges are generally in a good condition , and
while applicati ons for the degrees of Masonry are not as plentiful as they
have been in recent years, there are still sufficient candidat es to permit
officers of lodges to maintain a fair degree of proficiency and an abundance of enthusia sm. This, in my opinion. is a healthy condition , as it
gives opportun ity to plan program s for the spiritual and intellectu al improveme nt of our members and allows time for social and fraternal intercourse. The successfu l Master is one who. not burdened with too much
degree work, has arranged his program so as to attract the maximum
attendan ce of his members througho ut his year, and who is not discouraged because his initial attempts may not have been successfu l. The
so-called "Degree Mill" is attractiv e to none but the officers in line, and,
to them, only because of the opportun ity afforded to succeed to higher
stations. As attendan ce at meetings and active interest in all lodge functions are of vital importan ce to the well-bein g of a Masonic lodge. we
should therefore discoura ge as much as possible the conferrin g of multiple degrees. and with patience and persever ence endeavo r to arrange
program s sufficiently interestin g to encourag e participa tion by our members. The officers, however , should be as letter-pe rfect in their work as
possible and thorough ly intereste d in their duties, for there is nothing
more importan t than the ritual of our Order when degrees are being
i;:onferred.

Visitations Made
During the past year I have had the pleasure to be present at, and to
participa te in. many Grand Lodge ceremoni es througho ut the State.
Without exceptio n the attendan ce of the Masons in the immedia te
vicinity was excellen t and the little courtesie s extended your Grand
Officers were many. In addition to my regular duties it was my pleasure

72

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to attend numerous schools of instruction in the Sacramento and San
Joaquin Valleys, and I was, on each occasion, thoroughly impressed by
the excellence of the work exemplified. I wish to commend the Inspectors
of these Districts on the results of their labors. Many invitations received
by me were impossible to accept because of conflicting commitments or
distance involved.

Inspectors' Spring Conferences
Too much emphasis cannot be placed upon the value of the Inspectors' Spring Conferences, conducted by the Assistant Grand Lecturers of the six Divisions in the early part of the year. Coming as they do
when the Inspectors are schooling their newly installed officers in their
ritualistic work. these meetings serve to eliminate error and at the same
time to establish confidence. I attended all five of the Spring Conferences
(I mention five because two of the six Divisions in the State combined
for their meeting). and was deeply impressed by the thoroughness with
which the work was performed. At each of these meetings we were
favored by an informal address of approximately two hours in length by
our Grand Secretary, Lloyd E. Wilson, who, at the direction of the
Grand Master. was present to give enlightenment on some of the questions which are frequently asked of the Inspector. Brother Wilson's
contribution to the success of these meetings was acclaimed by the Inspectors throughout the State. and it is generally hoped that future
Grand Masters will issue similar directives . .

Conference Meeting Dates
Division 1and2 (combined): June 8, 9 and 10 at Lake Tahoe: conducted by Assistant Grand Lecturers Gilbert C. De Forest, P.G.M .• and
Mervyn E. Hanshaw.
Division 3: May 11. 12 and 13 at Guerneville. conducted by Assistant Grand Lecturer Elbert W. Davis.
Division 4: June 1, 2 and 3 at Yosemite Valley: conducted by Assistant Grand Lecturer Raymond G. Taylor.
Division 5: May 25. 26 and 27 at Santa Barbara; conducted by Assistant Grand Lecturer Guy B. Mize.
Division 6: May 4. 5 and 6 at Del Mar, San Diego County: conducted by Assistant Grand Lecturer Augustus H. Allen.
There is no greater reward to be achieved from a job well done than
the personal satisfaction resulting from accomplishment. The Assistant
Grand Lecturers ask no words of commendation, but I would be remiss
were I not to call attention to the excellent work they have done and to
personally thank them for their co-operation.

An Increase in Appropriation Requested
At the last Commu nication of the Grand Lodge addition al funds
were appropr iated for the use of the Ritual Committee and for the necessary travelin g expense s of the Inspect ors. It has been found that the
amount request ed by the Grand Lecture r and approve d by the Grand
Lodge has been insufficient to take care of increase d costs and the addition of two new Assista nt Grand Lecture rs to the Ritual Committee,
and the appoint ment of an addition al number of Inspectors. Rigid economy has been exercised during the last year, even to the extent of combining our Ritual Committee meetings with the Spring Confere nces in
order to keep expense s down. Notwith standin g, our appropr iation has
been exhaust ed without meeting all importa nt needs. I therefor e respectfully request that the sum of $9500.00 be set aside for use of the Ritual
Committee during the ensuing year.

friendship. To the Grand Secreta ry. Lloyd E. Wilson . for his splendi d
contribu tion to the success of our Spring Confere nces. And to Henry D.
Oliphan t, Assista nt Grand Setreta ry, and the personn el of the Grand
Lodge office. go my hearty thanks for the many little favors and courtesies extende d me during the last year.
And to you, my Brethre n, my especial thanks for the opportu nity to
serve.

Most Worshipful. distinguished Past Grand Masters. Officers.
Members. and Guests of this Grand Lodge- Brethre n all:
Several weeks ago during the progres s of the trans-Pa cific yacht race
one of the occasional but dramati c incidents of the sea occurred. A crew
member from one of the competing yachts was lost overboa rd. Before
speed could be slackened so that the yacht could turn around and effect
his recovery, he was lost in the vastnes s of the great Pacific. For more
than thirty hours there was no trace of him, and the feeling grew that
further search would be futile. Just fifteen minutes before the order came
to abando n the search, crewme n of a navy rescue craft sighted and saved
the solitary figure bobbing on the sea. Truly a miracle had been realized.
In the interviews that followed, this question was inevitab ly asked
o_f the man who h~d ~~en lost-"W hat did you think about during the
tlDle you were adrift? Natural ly, the immediate hope and expecta tion
had been of rescue since his fall into the sea had been observed. But as
the yacht sailed beyond his view and the hours slowly passed without
sight of help, decreas ing hope must have been followed by increasing
fear. During these hours he reporte d he thought of all the things he had
ever done, and even more of the things which should have been but
were not done'. Certain ly no circumstances could produce a situatio n
more conducive to great soul searchin g and critical self appraisa l.
You and I will probabl y never have an experience of just this kind.
But this man's experience should make crystal clear to all of us the
necessi ty of so living from day to day that in our respective hours of
crisis, and such experiences come to all, we shall in our own hearts and
minds not be found wanting . If we practice diligently the tenets of
Freema sonry that we know so well, we can and will achieve a pattern
of living equal to all occasions. With this thought in mind I'd like to
have you join with me in exploring some of the aspects of living which
ought to charact erize the Master Mason.
Some years ago there was published a book entitled. "'!'he Marks of
an Educate d Man", which became a best seller of that day. It was
extreme ly popular because the author sought to do what is always intriguing but what is not always simple- namely , to analyze the qualities
of persona lity and charact er which make for successful living. People
being what they are, there is within the heart and mind of every person
the continu ing desire. sometimes weak and sometimes strong. but everpresent. to discover ways and means of living more richly and more
fully than he has before. It is this spirit which account s for whatev er

76

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

progress man has made and may make. Let us think together, therefore,
of what are, or perhaps should be, the marks of a Master Mason.
As a major premise of our present consideration no statement could
be more significant than these brief words of a fellow Californian, Edwin
Markham.
We are all blind until we see
That in the human plan
Nothing is worth the making
Unless it makes the man.
Why build these cities glorious
If man unbuilded goes 7
In vain we ·build a world
Unless the builder also grows.
Free Masons are in the finest sense of the word, and in accordance
with their rich traditions, builders-builders today of huqi.an character
even as their operative forebears were builders of stately cathedrals. In
both kinds of endeavor certain common qualities are essential. These
are the marks of a Master Mason to which we shall devote our thought
and our attention.
The Master Mason, more so than other men, must possess an inquiring mind. Our great ritual is nothing but meaningless words and
empty forms unless we probe ·beyond the symbols to discover the ideas
and the ideals which they represent. Back of every material thing, there
was first a plan; back of the plan, there was first the inspiration born of
and from an inquiring mind. Today there is a great tendency for people
to be superficial in many ways. We are prone to take for granted the
comforts of life, the achievements of science, and the human liberties
wihch have made them possible. We cannot, we dare not fall into such
ways, without placing in jeopardy the values which free men have always cherished. The key to our survival, the key to our progress, is to
be found in the cultivation of an inquiring mind. This is one mark of a
Master Mason.
The Master Mason, more so than other men, must be a skilled
craftsman. Whatever his work, whether it be in business or on the farm,
trade or profession, he should take pride in doing a superior job. The
very word "Master" suggests competence of a high order. We must not
be satisfied with less. What would this nation be today if the men and
women of yesteryears had assumed an attitude of "good enough" What I have done is not my best, but it will get by? History is full of
examples of primitive societies where basically this attitude dominated
and was responsible for their elemental mode of existence. History is
also full of examples of great civilizations, which having risen to new
heights of cultural achievement, decayed and fell when the spirit of the .

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

77

people became one of "good enough." It is not the lot of every man to
be a leader, but it can be the lot of every man to make his contribution.
Let us always remember what the historian Green has told us, that the
world is moved not only by the mighty shoves of the heroes, but also by
the aggregate of the tiny pushes of each honest worker. This quality
is also the mark of a Master Mason.
The Master Mason, more so than other men, must be an understanding friend. An American patriot once stated during the critical
years of our nation's birth, "These are times that try men's souls." The
same sentiment can be repeated today with equal fervor and with equal
justification. We are again engaged in a great human conflict, the contributing factors to which are many and varied; and yet which in the
final analysis stem from the fact that we have not yet learned how to
live together as friends and brothers. Obviously, there is no simple
answer to the present complication. However, of this I am very sure, a
spirit of sincere friendship, based on mutual respect for our fellow men
because of their dignity and worth as human beings, will provide the
only satisfactory climate in which differences can be resolved. This is
easy to say; it is difficult to achieve. To have a friend, one must be a
friend. This too is the mark of a Master Mason.
The Master Mason, more so than other men, must be an exemplary
citizen. The teachings of our fraternity are the same principles which
undergird real democracy. No matter what its form or name may be, any
government whose sovereignty is vested in its people can be only as
strong as they are intelligent and responsible in meeting the demands
imposed on free people. America today has the novel and diffcult role,
whether she wants it or not, of being a world leader. Her success, as well
as the fate of millions throughout this world, will be conditioned in
large measure by the maturity, the courage and the devotion we display
in the discharge of our civic obligations. Do you vote at each election for
which you are eligible, first having studied the relative merits of the
issues and candidates which may be under consideration? How well do
you support your duly elected officers as they seek to do their duty,
sometimes in the face of strong pressures not in the public interest? Is
law observance a good thing only so long as it applys to the other fellow? These and other tests will provide simple answers to the question
of how well we are meeting our acknowledged responsibilities. Good
citizenship is an essential mark of a Master Mason.
The Master Mason, more so than other men, must be a person of
ICrupulous integrity. The legend of the third degree, one of the landmarks of Freemasonry, is an impressive illustration of this important
Virtue. The significant human freedoms which have been won over the
ages at so great a price-the right to worship God according to the
dictates of one's own conscience; the right to peaceably assemble, such
as in a Masonic Lodge; the right to speak one's thoughts, so long as they

79

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

are free from slander: these and all of the other cherished rights of free
people--can continue to exist only where a nation's citizens manifest
a high order of personal integrity. All social institutions--our governments, our schools, our churches, our businesses-will be strong and
effective in direct ratio to the integrity of their members, and especially
of their leaders. As we evaluate the life of our times, feeling deep concern
about the precarious state of national and world conditions, is it not
probable that one reason for our present plight is the light regard among
too many people for this quality of personal integrity? Constancy of
character, based on righteousness and morality, is a clear mark of a
Master Mason.

ancient Institution.
A year ago the Grand Orator of California Masonry's centennial
year, in an extremely able address before this Grand Lodge, presented a
challenge for the Master Masons of this jurisdiction to continue building
well the Unfinished Temple. A strong foundation was laid and a fine
superstructure erected in the first hundred years. It becomes our task
now to provide the detail and ornamentation which will make this Temple not merely functional but truly beautiful. We can accomplish our
mission only if we are strong in those qualities which we have discussed
this morning. Are they in a significant measure characteristic of you?
Do you have an inquiring mind, a probing spirit, always seeking to
extend your intellectual horizons?
Are you a skilled craftsman, ever proud of the contribution you can
make to the world of work?
Are you accepted as an understanding friend, interested in and able
to see in all men their true potential as members of the human family?
Do you exemplify the attributes of a good citizen, being one who
knows and accepts the responsibilities attendant to your community's
welfare?
Are you one whose integrity is such that your word is regarded as
good as your bond?
Do your decisions reflect a high level of values in which considerations of prime import always come first?
Is yours a faith which gives to all life meaningful purpose and intelligent direction?
If these things are true, you are indeed proceeding in the ways of a
Master Mason.
May this hour be one of solemn rededication to the task that should
consume us all-that of building finer and nobler personality and character. To the end that all who know us may see in the work we do and
in the lives we lead the true marks of a Master Mason, let us be guided
by the thought of John Ruskin who once said-"When we build, Jet us
think that we build forever. Let it not be for the present delight nor for
present use alone. Let it be such work as our descendants will thank us
for, and let us think as we Jay stone on stone, that a time is to come when
those stones will be held sacred because our hands have touched them,
and that men will say as they look upon the labor and wrought substance
of them-'See! This our Fathers did for us.'" .

78

The Master Mason, more so than other men, must have a substantial
capacity for weighing values. Life in one respect may be regarded as a
continuous experience of making choices. The decisions men accept
materially shape not only their own lives, but may profoundly influence
the future of all those associated with them. The real measure of any
man is to be found not in what he professes, but in how he lives. As the
well-known American essayist, Ralph W a]do Emersor{, has put it
"What you do speaks so loudly I cannot hear what you say." You and I
daily condition the future of ourselves and of our families by the alternatives we select in any given situation requiring deliberation and decision.
Fortunately, as Freemasons we are in possession of criteria by which we
can :make intelligent, ethical judgments. To the extent that we do so, we
are demonstrating a quality which is still another distinguishing mark
of a Master Mason.
The Master Mason, more so than other men, must have a vital faith,
a faith that transcends mere worldly knowledge, a faith born of the
experience that when human strength and wisdom fail, divine assistance
is a real and present resource. The life of any individual is immature
until he comes to recognize and accept his own inadequacies and his own
]imitations. In some high moment of genuine humility he may discover
the truth of that seeming paradox, to save one's life he first must lose it.
Out of apparent defeat can come great victory. God is good. We must
know Him and be His if our lives are to reflect the divine destiny inherent
within each human spirit. Dynamic faith of this kind is a basic mark of a
Master Mason.
It will already have been noted by many the repetition of the phrase,
"The Master Mason, more so than other men, ..." The meaning of this
should be readily evident. The fraternity of Freemasonry accepts for
membership only good men of high purpose. Let me say at this point,
parenthetically but with emphasis, that if we fail in this respect we have
failed in our obligations. The charge you know so well might properly
be recalled to mind-namely, that you will refuse to recommend anyone
to a participation in our privileges unless you have strong reasons to
believe that by a similar fidelity he will ultimately reflect honor on our
