Mounting costs for the operation of business generally in the country and the ever-increasing cost of living likewise make themselves felt
in the operation of both our Homes.
The Board is of the opinion that the brethren of this state, while
not approving extravagances or unnecessary expenditures, do not desire
the service in these two Homes to be any less than that which should
reasonably be provided and it is inevitable that costs will increase
generally in proportion to other similar costs elsewhere.
During the year the Board has had the advantage of studying the
report prepared by the State Department of Social Welfare following
their survey and study prior to renewing the state license at Covina.
Tmis report covers thirty-nine typewritten pages and contains much
information both by direct statement and by analysis, that is both
interesting and helpful to the Board.
It is not possible or desirable to reproduce the report here in full,
but a few excerpts are interesting. Referring to Superintendent Henry,
the report states, on Page 5, .. He is an indefatigable worker, who does
not spare himself in his earnestness to maintain the highest standards
in every unit of operation."
Referring generally to the increasing cost of maintenance, the report
states: "The per capita cost for food, which includes food for twentyfive staff members, averages approximately $32.00 per month. This
should be ample for a well-balanced and nutritious dietary."
Concerning the declin·e in admission and population over a period
of years, the report, in advancing reasons therefor, states, .. Another less
obvious cause for decrease in population may be found in the increased
public interest in services to children, which is reflected in Social Security benefits, Veterans' benefits, family service agencies, extended day
centers, family counselling, etc."
These few quotations merely serve to point the way toward some of
the problems which confront the Trustees and to which they have been
giving attention over a period of years. The Board's own study, analysis
and charting of population trends and causes, recently completed, is
undoubtedly the best study of its kind ever made of the Home at Covina.

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: I herewith present for your consideration my eleventh
annual report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Decoto, for
the year ending July 31, 1951, and the 53rd Superintendent's report of
the Home.
In reporting the activities of the Home for the past year I find there
have been few changes in the general routine of the affairs at the Home
to report, however, the ranks of the staff has suffered a very severe loss.
Miss Ester G. Payne, who was head of our hospital department for 30
years, terminated her services with the Home last October, and Mrs.
Virginia M. Lord, who was for 15 years assistant in the hospital, and
for the past 10 years Matron of the Home, found it nee'.essary to resign
in December.
Miss Bess Payne, who had been assistant, took civei; the responsibilities of the hospital, and Mrs. Mildred Harris, who was associated
with the University Mound in San Francisco for a number of years,
was appointed Matron.
Our endeavors to maintain a social atmosphere among the members
of the Home, which would be in keeping with the high ideals of our noble
fraternity, has met with satisfactory results. A large majority of the
Home family seem to be very happy and contented, and are enjoying to
the fullest the many comforts the Home has to offer. The members of
the Home are showing a greater interest in the general routine work
and a larger number are contributing, willingly, their part according to
their strength to the well-being of the Home.
The general health condition of the members of the Home has been
very good during the past year. Those who are infirm and feeble.. 64 in
number, are being cared for in our hospital where they receive night
and day attention and service.
There were on August 1, 1950, the beginning of our fiscal year,
being cared for in the Home, 176 women and 118 men. During the year
22 women were admitted, average age 77.95 and 25 men at an average of
76.2. During the sa,me period we lost by death 22 women, average ago
82.2 and 22 men, average age 82.95. There were withdrawn during
the year 4 women and 5 men, leaving at the end of the year 116 men
and 172 women, the average age for men 78.9, and for women, 79.42.
Included in this number are 9 married couples.

Report of the Superintendent - Covina Ho~e
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is my privilege and pleasure to present to you my third annual
report of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina for the year ending
July 31, 1951.
HOME MEMBERSHIP

The population of our Home Family, as of July 31, 1951, numbered
sixty children. Thirty-four boys and twenty-six girls. An increase of
three children over the preceding year. Twelve children have left us
during the year - eleven boys and one girl. Of this number five were by
graduation from Covina Union High School and six went to re-established homes. One girl entered Chaffey Junior College in February and
four ·boys plan to attend various colleges this fall. Eight boys and seven
girls, ranging in age from five to fifteen years, were admitted to the
Home during the year.

LODGE VISITATIONS

ENTERTAINM ENT

The deep interest in our Home and in the welfare of our children,
as shown by the Masonic Lodges and affiliated organization s, has been
very gratifying. We are indeed sincerely grateful for the ~upport of our
friends, not only in visiting the Home, but in their untiring interest and
loyalty as expressed by generous donations of every description, a record
of which will be found in another section of this report. Our children and
staff were happy to welcome to the Covina Home a total of three thousand, five hundred and fifty-eight visitors during the year, including
fifty-four Masonic Lodges and affiliated organization s as group visitations. It is worthy of note that the policy of visitations on the first and
third Sunday of each month has been of immeasurab le assistance in
guaranteein g and protecting the children that they might enjoy the
benefits of relaxation and diversion from routine programs.

It was again the pleasure of the children and staff to begin the year

cians and sponsored by Beverly Hills Lodge No. 528. At the Masonic
Temple in Monrovia the children were guests of Monrovia Lodge No.

Christmas Party. This was followed by Christmas parties given by
Carmelita Lodge No. 599 and Hollywood Lodge No. 355. At our big
"family" Christmas party we were honored to have as our special guests
the southern members of the Board of Trustees and their families and
Mr. and Mrs. John M. Downen. Weekend "snow trips" were enjoyed
by all the children, thus enabling them to enjoy this season of the year
so many Californians miss. The San Bernardino Santa Fe Masonic
Club was host to the boys and girls at the National Orange Show at
San Bernardino; children attended the Al Malaikah Shrine Circus in
Los Angeles and witnessed on the Home grounds a mammoth display
of fireworks through the courtesy of friends in the various Bureaus of
Fire Prevention. We continue to enjoy, through the kindness of six
major motion picture studios, the best of feature and comedy pictures

pictures for our children's weekly movie, we are deeply grateful. Elsewhere in this report will be found a more complete record of entertainment activities.

SUMMER PROGRAM

A complete and rather extensive program was planned and carried
out for the summer of 1951, whereby every boy and girl received the
benefit of a vacation in a locale entirely different from their daily surroundings. On July 1, under the supervision of the Superintend ent and
a qualified staff, the Senior and Intermediat e girls started on a three
thousand mile camping tour of northern California, visiting National
and State Forests and Parks, as well as many cities and points of interest,
eg. Sequoia, Bass Lake, Yosemite, Lake Tahoe, Virginia and Carson
City, Nevada, Mount Lassen, Mount Shasta, Shasta Dam, Sacramento
(where the group was received by Governor Warren). Next they visited the Masonic Home for the Aged at Decato, where they enjoyed the
hospitality of Superintend ent and Mrs. Eubanks; then to Grand Lodge
and San Francisco; stopping at Big Sur on the way home to Covina.
The Senior and Intermediat e boys enjoyed approximate ly the same trip,
leaving Covina, July 22, and returning home August 7. Over fifteen
thousand miles were covered by our three camping vehicles on the two

Armed Services overseas. As a parable to the adage that the proof of
the pudding is in the tasting, certainly the yardstick by which the success of any institutional program might well be measured is by the
achievements and accomplishments of its Alumni. Such a measurement
applied to the Masonic Home for Children would impress every individual and leave, beyond a shadow of a doubt, pride and personal satisfaction in contributing and making possible the achievements of our Home
Alumni.
This year of association with the children, staff. and friends of our
Home Family has been personally very gratifying. The continuing
friendly guidance and counsel. tendered with warm understanding of the
various matters encountered in the administration of a program of child
care, by the Board of Trustees has indeed been ~n inspir~tion; that ~11
may work together in serving the best interests of our children and tn
the true exemplification of Masonic charity.

FARM AND GROUNDS

Of the many activities engaged in by the children in our program
directed toward increasing and developing individuality, interest, poise,
and other qualities so necessary for success, the highlight may well have
been the accomplishments of our Masonic Pioneers' 4-H Club. Awards,
recognition and individual achievement have been the result of the efforts
expended by the children. Sueh recognition included swine production,
beef feeder projects and sheep production, as well as sewing and the
field of home-making. Under the direction of our farm supervisor, the
Masonic Pioneers' 4-H Club has contributed much toward alleviating
the high cost of living for our Home Family. During this past year we
have produced, butehered and consumed approximately four thousand
and fifty-six pounds of beef (live weight): seven thousand, five h~ndred
and eighteen pounds of pork (live weight); ftve hundred and twentyseven pounds of dressed rabbit; seven hundred and fifteen pounds of
chicken (live weight); one hundred and sixty pounds of geese and ducks
(live weight); two hundred and ten pounds of lamb (live weight). Six
hundred and thirty-two pounds of pork was converted into hams and
bacon.
MASONIC HOME ALUMNI

their childhood took place on Sunday, September 24, 1950. Each class
was well represented. There was also an especially good attendance at

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Perhaps there is no more certain way to present this report than
under the above caption. It has been only a few years since the original
start of the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund Program. We should all be
most appreciative of the vision shown by the devoted Masons who conceived of such an idea. We can add our thanks to those who labored to
put in concrete and constructive form a program where all could share
in the over-all picture in accordance with his ability and the dictates of
his own conscience. True-blooded Americans abhor the idea of dole,
and this is particularly true of our Craft. Yet the opportunity to assist,
even in a small way, those less fortunate than ourselves, and above all
to take steps to provide for the security of such brethren, their widows
and orphans, is one of the wisest motives of the Fraternity. Such has
been our opportuntiy for the past few years in building the Endowment
Fund, as we have marched along together.
FOUR MILLION DOLLARS PLUS
From the small yet fertile seed of those first few dollars, we can now
look with pride to the sizable sum of our Endowment of over four
million dollars. More important, perhaps, is the substantial increase of
individual contributors during the past fiscal year. This number has
reached an all-time high of 60,801. This is approximately 8,000 more
individual contributors than any previous year. The income from bequests was likewise substantial. aggregating well over $100,000.00.
Along with the high total contributed through Lodges of almost $242,000.00, this made our aggregate increase above $364,000.00, or a total
Endowment Fund as of August 1st of $4,244,715.81
OPERATIVE PROCEDURE
Your Board is more or less limited in its working procedure by its
legislative setup. It is charged "to study, devise and carry out plans for
the securing of adequate endowment for the Masonic Homes of California." Such an educational program has been followed. In an effort to
make this procedure more effective, the jurisdiction has been divided
into Districts, and servicing certain of these is the responsibility of individual Board members. This has made it possible to have such a
member responsible for contacts, and as the liaison person to work with
Inspectors and individual Lodges in that area. We believe this has

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

96

proven more effective in giving a personal touch in operation of our
work. There has been evident increase and demand for more information about our Homes. Visitations have grown, and we have experienced
the widest distribution of pamphlets in our history, totalling approximately one hundred thousand. Our Honor Certificates were perfected
and issued to ninety-two Lodges last year. The reactions to this innovation have been most gratifying. We believe it is not only a stimulus
for continued activities, but a well-deserved citation that in general is
much appreciated by the individual Lodges.

APPRECIATION

If we were permitted to paraphrase, we would say, "As the Master
goes, so goes the Endowment Fund." The Most Worshipful Grand
Master has been invaluable in "spreading the gospel" about our two
splendid Homes. We realize that the successful year has been in a great
measure due to his efforts. Never have we had more and better cooperation from the Inspectors. This, plus the increase of interest on the part
of the Masters, Officers and those assigned for special duties; those
individual members of the Craft who, for some special reason, have
developed a particular interest and have made it their business to carry
the message whenever possible; the sum total of such cooperation has
made it possible for your Board to give this splendid report.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

relief of strangers and sojourners from abroad. In this connection we
had the curiosity to inquire of the secretary of that Board as to the
amount expended for Masons hailing from subordinates of the Grand
Lodge of England and Scotland and the amounts refunded. His report
to us shows that since 1881 his Board has expended for Masons from the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of England $19,435, of which $1,231 has
been reimbursed: for Masons from the Grand Lodge of Scotland $4,076,
of which only $69.35 has been reimbursed: and that of the $205,707 so
expended for relief of sojourners and strangers from abroad much less
than one-fourth has been paid back."
In the report of the same Board of Relief, representing the Masonic
year just completed, we find that they expended $11,609.25 for relief
during the year and of this amount the Board of Relief has been reimbursed in full for all of its Masonic charity.
The reports of the Boards of Relief show that during the past year
they have conducted 893 funerals, have made 18,913 service calls upon
the sick, for investigation, relief and all other matters ;equiring their
personal attention.
They also report that they have advanced a total of $46,258.00 for
relief. Of this amount the Boards of Relief have been reimbursed in all
but $125, representing only one case from all of those handled by the
various offices.

We concur in the comments of Past Grand Master Gaylord and are
proud to report that the Boards of Relief continue to carry out these
·
principles.

In recent years, several of our Boards of Relief have developed and
are now maintaining blood banks for the benefit of Masons and their
families. During the past year these Boards report that there has been
donated 1605 units of blood and that 1539 units have been withdrawn
for the use of our brothers. This represents a saving to them of $40, l 35.
Past Grand Master Gaylord in his message to Grand Lsdge in 1932
said, "We must not forget that Masonic charity is neither mechanical
nor mercenary. Our charity funds are a trust and must not be carelessly
or extravagantly disbursed, conversely, no worthy brother or his dependents should suffer by reason of technicalities, nor should worthy
applicants to a board of relief he made to feel that our charity is mechanical or grudgingly bestowed, or that our sole purpose is to avoid the disbursement of charity funds. The Board of Control in .its activities necessarily emphasizes the necessity for economy and business-like methods,
particularly at a time when demands are numerous. Because of this function Boards of Relief and other executive officers should not misconstrue
the purpose of the Board of Control or the extent of Masonic charity.
Necessarily, cases will arise where immediate assistance in reasonable
amounts is essential to adequate relief of the situation, and good
judgment must be exercised as well as business methods: this does not
mean extravagance or carelessness, but it does mean the exemplification
of brotherhood: our charity is brotherhood and not fraternal insurance."

EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

We now maintain seven employment bureaus in this jurisdiction.
During the past year, at the request of the Honolulu Board of Relief.
the Board of Control approved the dissolution of that employment
.
bureau.
The primary purpose of our employment bureaus is to assist worthy
Master Masons, their widows and orphans, in securing employment,
thereby assisting in maintaining their morale and avoiding the necessity
of direct relief.
During the past year our employment bureaus registered 6,989 for
employment: of these 4,975 were male and 2,014 were female. Of the
total registered, 2,913 were actually placed in jobs. We had 10,406 positions offered through our offices by employer inquiry. No fees are
charged in our employment bureaus either to the employee or the employer. Were we to make such a charge and were we to use the State of
California's prescribed maximum rates, which commercial agencies may
charge, we would have earned $1 77, l 07 .00. This we like to consider as
the amount saved our unemployed brothers.
APPROPRIATIONS

Employment offices receive their financial support from their Boards
of Relief together with aid from Grand Lodge. The Board of Control
has developed a formula to determine the maximum amount which we
will ask Grand Lodge to appropriate to any employment office. After
several years of use, we believe that this formula has proved itself to be
equitable and just, not only to Grand Lodge but also to our Boards of
Relief. This year the Board of Control has approved the following listed
appropriations for the seven employment offices and has filed them, as
required, with the Finance Committee with our recommendation for
approval.

REIMBURSEMENTS

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON THIRTY-SECOND
ANNUAL OBSERVANCE OF PUBUC SCHOOLS WEEK

A Board of Relief, having assisted a needy sojourning brother, may
find that it is unable, for some reason, to make itself whole by being
reimbursed ei~her by the brother's lodge or his Grand Lodge. Such board
may then turn to Grand Lodge and request reimbursement from Grand
Lodge funds. This plan is a well considered portion of our Masonic
charity program. Knowing that the strength of Grand Lodge is behind
our Boards of Relief. permits our secretaries to have the proper mental
attitude in dealing with relief cases, thus permitting each case its full
measure of needed relief.
During the past year only one case required our attention. The Board
of Relief of Bakersfield was called upon to bury a brother, a life member ·
of Peace and Harmony Lodge No. 834 A. F. and A. M. of Rangoon
Burma, of the Grand Jurisdiction of Scotland. This brother and his wife
left Burma in December 1948, but were permitted to bring only a limited
amount of funds with them, nor has any money since been released to
them. The brother's wife works as a waitress in order to make a living.
On March 9, 1951, the brother died in extreme poverty. He was buried
with Masonic honors. His lodge was contacted by registered air mail
regarding the expense of his funeral. To date there has been no response.
The Board of Control has, therefore, recommended to the Finance Committee that the Masonic Board of Relief of Bakersfield be reimbursed in
the amount of $125.
BOARD OF CONTROL

The Board of Control held three meetings during the past Masonic year. In February it met for three days in Santa Monica with all
of the Southern California Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus.
In June there was a three day session in Stockton with the Northern
California Boards and Bureaus. The Board of Control is meeting during
this session of Grand Lodge, having started work last Saturday and will
continue through the balance of this week.
Representatives of the Board of Control attended all of the Masonic
Breakfasts throughout the State. Reports on the Board's activities were
made at the Los An~eles, Lon,g Beach, Sacramento, East Bay and Fresno
Breakfasts and the· second annual dinner of the Board of Relief of San
Francisco.
Our Boards of Relief are operating efficiently, economically, and
harmoniously and all credit should be given to the brothers who are now
serving the craft as secretaries and managers.
Respectfully submitted,
JACK C. BUTLER
JOHN T. MARTIN .

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
It is impossible for this General Committee, in rendering its annual
report on 1951 Public Schools Week Observance, to sufficiently express
its thanks to local committees for their fine cooperation in the 32nd
Annual Observance.
This statement will be understood when our brethren examine the
splendidly organized reports which again, for the second time, will be
on display during Grand Lodge.
This committee carefully studied the reports from each Lodge
throughout the jurisdiction. Our report attempts to present a digest of
the inspiring evidence of one of the finest Observances on our records
under the following topics:

PROCLAMATIONS
"The Public School -

An American Heritage"

The more general use of the 1951 State slogan and scroll symbol
throughout the jurisdiction decidedly strengthened publicity impact.
The apt themes contained in the proclamations of the Grand Master
Most Worshipful Arthur Paulsen and Governor Earl Warren were
also widely quoted. ·
Grand Master Paulsen proclaimed in part:
"Never in history have so many people throughout the world
been denied access to authentic sources of information. Never before were the forces of thought~control more powerful, and never
was the need for a public schools system greater . • ."
Governor Warren's annual proclamation likewise stressed the importance of the Observance which originated with our Grand Lodge.
He said in part:
"History teaches, and many recent examples in various parts of
the world have demonstrated with startling clarity, that freedom such
as we cherish cannot long exist without popular understanding and
appreciation of individual responsibility.
"One of the basic institutions upon which we rely for the furtherance
of our American ideals is the public school system. Public schools, by
enabling every child to gain a liberal education regardless of station in
life, promote recognition of the responsibilities of citizenship and constitute a major bulwark against subversive doctrines.

106

107

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"We in California are proud of the school system that has been
developed in our State. Its success has been due to many factors-the
interest of mothers and fathers in their children, the cooperative efforts
of state and local officials, and the energy and determination of those
public spirited men and women who are devoting their lives to the teaching of our children.
"The continued progress of our school system requires increased
public understanding of the importance of education and the greatest
possible encouragement and support of our teachers . . ."
To these proclamations were added countless numbers issued by
the Mayors of cities and towns throughout the state. Industries and
organizations with statewide membership added formal resolutions and
comments.
The three heads of the York Rite Bodies sent proclamations to their
members urging the support of Public Schools Week and requiring that
no meeting be held during the week that would conflict.
The California Legislature formally recognized the Observance with
Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 30, adopted in Assembly March
15, 1951, and in the Senate March 22, 1951 as follows: .
Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 30-Relative to Participation in
the events of the Thirty-second Annual Public Schools Week.
WHEREAS, The Thirty-second Annual Public Schools Week will
be observed in California during the week of April 23d to April 27th by
an open house in all public schools: and
WHEREAS, Countless citizens throughout the State have formed
committees to cooperate with school officials and students to enliven our
interest in the function of our public schools in guarding and strengthening the concepts of our democracy: and
WHEREAS, The slogan of the Thirty-second Annual Public Schools
Week is "The Public School-An American Heritage": and
WHEREAS, The object is to encourage public attendance at the
school programs to insure a wider knowledge of the importance of public
schools in our social progress: now, therefore be it
Resolved by the Assembly of the State of California, the Senate
thereof concurring, That all citizens of the State of California are hereby
urged to attend the events of Public Schools Week, as a demonstration
of the importance of public education in the effort to preserve and make
stronger the American way of life.

INFORMATION PLEASE!

What's the Date?
The constantly recurring question!
As pointed out in last year's report-subject to the Grand Master's
approval and proclamation-Public Schools Week date is traditionally
set starting the FOURTH MONDAY IN APRIL. Not the fourth week
as has been assumed by some.
For instance, the fourth Monday in April, 1952 falls on April 28.
The erroneous fourth Week in April would be the 21st.

Start Earlier!
The committee is inspired by overall enthusiastic requests for it to
send material and information as sent last year to each lodge-earlier.
We are making every effort to do so. But, there are time factors over
which the Committee has no control:
1. Timing of the Grand Master's proclamation.
2. Appointments or delegations of new Lodge chairmen and committee members.
3. The above factor explains why several new committee chairmen
did not receive General Committee material elaborated this year.

FUTURE SUGGESTIONS

Composite Amplification of 11W by Don't You?"
. . . Recommend that Lodges be encouraged to have schools put on
program, preferably the 6.rst day of the Observance in Lodge rooms.
This would act as springboard for Public Schools Week and create
greater interest among the brethren and their families.
. . . (Five Lodge Combination.) . . . Suggest Public Schools Week
should commence on Sunday. Thus various churches or church groups
could be incorporated, as for instance meetings in the Congregational
Church. Combined or concerted action of Lodges in large centers of
population is more conducive for large attendance than individual
efforts of single Lodges.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF MASONIC CLUB HOUSE,
BERKELEY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University,
Berkeley, California, presents this report covering the past Masonic
year. We believe that the general appearance of the building and
grounds at our Berkeley Clubhouse, and the facilities available there,
are better than they have been during the past ten years. This is a result
of the generosity of yourselves and the Finance Committee, particularly
in the past three or four years. We appreciate the confidence you have
reposed in us and the students, and assure you that it has been a pleasure
for each of the trustees to serve you and these young people.
The budget for the new year adopted by the Board of Trustees at its
meeting on September 25, 1951 calls for the expenditure of $16,200.00
in ordinary operation, and in addition, depreciation in the same amount
as fixed last year, viz., $4,010.00, plus the regular $3,000.00 reimbursement by Grand Lodge for the kitchen and building improvements installed several years ago, making a total of $23,210.00.
This budget, which was carefuly prepared by the Board, sitting as a
committee of the whole, has been verified at their request by our architect, Brother A. Lewis Koue, as to the items making up the total of
$3,370.00 for equipment and property improvements included in the
above $16,200.00 for said ordinary operation. The budget is included
herein as Exhibit "A" to this report; you will find in it a separate detail
in a footnote, and you will also observe on examining the latter that the
bulk of the items and costs comprising this special item for improvements,
etc., are requirements for the promotion of the health and safety of the
students and guests of the Clubhouse. We respectfully request the approval of our current budget covering the twelve months ending August
31, 1952, our fiscal year.
While the report of the auditors, F . W. LaFrentz & Company,
Certified Public Accountants, for the past fiscal year shows "Budgeted
Income in Excess of Expenditures ... $2,337.58," we respectfully invite
your attention to the fact that in the previous fiscal year we overexpended our budget by an even larger sum, namely, the sum of
$2,808.68, and to the further fact that we did not request one year ago
that this over-expenditure be made up by Grand Lodge, which means
that our reserves were called upon to supply the difference.
The Club has continued to supply the social needs of the University
of California students at Berkeley who have Masonic affiliations, serving an average group of some 300 members, the decrease being largely
attributable to the decreased enrollment at the University. However, the
students appear to have greatly appreciated your benefactions and ad-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

123

vise that the club spirit is increasingly good as you will note from the
report of Robert V. Airhart, President of the student group. Because of
its succinctness and clarity it follows herewith as part of our report :
"The Board of Trustees
University Masonic Club
Berkeley, California
Dear Sirs:
The University Masonic Club has just completed a most successful year. We had an average membership of over three
hundred despite the decrease of students attending the University, the scarcity of money, and the uncertain world conditions.
The success of the Masonic Club this year has been due largely
to the increasing club spirit of its members. This fact, coupled
with the very excellent social calendar, allowed us to use the
facilities of the club house most advantageously.
Two new systems were tried this year for the first time. By
constitutional amendment, the term of office of council members
was extended to one full year. Dues were increased to ten dollars
a year, and could be paid for a year at the start of the fall term.
The combination of these two new systems gave us an excellent
chance to budget our money for the full year from the very beginning.
This year marked the revival of two events which the club
has not seen in many years. I am referring to the float in the Big
Game Parade, and the Variety show. Both were big hits, and I
am sure they will become annual events at the club.
The most memorable event of the year wa; the reception,
dinner and dance honoring The Most Worshipful Arthur Paulsen, Grand Master of Masons in California. A speech by the
Grand Master on the basic ideals of Masonry highlighted the
evening.
Many years ago, a very far sighted council reserved one
hundred dollars toward the purchase of a motion picture projector. No money was taken from or added to this fund for several years. Many times council came close to spending the money
for something else, but never did. This year by sticking to our
budget, we were able to add enough to the fund to buy a Bell &
Howell sound projector.
We now have a bulletin board in front of the club. The board
is of redwood construction, and will be illuminated for night display. I would like to thank the board, the Grand Lodge, and
Henry Morse Stephens Lodge for helping us to obtain this very
welcome addition to the club.
Special thanks go to you the Board of Trustees, and to our
Hostess Mrs. Edna Morton for the very welcome suggestions

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and cooperation you have given me in the past year. Many thanks
also go to my two unofficial assistants, Past Vice-President,
Helen Blake, and President Elect, Bob Keldgord. They will never
know how much help they were.

the absence of proper plans and details showing these facilities as altered
through the years. As a result of this effort, the office of the hostess for
the first time since the building was built is now receiving proper heat
from the main furnace. With this kind of help and the assistance of a
good Building Committee, which last year was headed by Brother Rus. sell C. Horstmann, we have been able to obtain greatly increased efficiency from the equipment and furnishings in the building.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF THE
MASONIC CLUB HOUSE, LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The activities and uses at the Masonic Club House adjacent to the
campus of the University of California at Los Angeles have been so
varied and numerous.during the past year that your Board of Directors
can only hope to summarize them in this report.
During the past year the University has completed additional facilities for undergraduate and graduate students. Notable among these
new buildings is the unique and specially designed building housing the
School of Law, which was opened last month. Much progress has been
made ·also in connection with the School of Medicine and teaching hospital which are to rise on the campus. Our club house remains, however,
as one of the ornaments of Westwood Village, which definitely is no
longer a village.
The major value and chief use of the club house remains the day by
day, hour by hour coming and going of a large group of students. As a
place to study, its Thompson Hall, library and three conference rooms
are not surpassed on the campus; for relaxation, its spacious lounge,
televi~on room and radio corner are greatly prized. The dining room
and snack bar cater to the requirements of the inner man, while the
billiard room and auditorium-ballroom provide ample space and facilities for the more active and larger events.
During the academic year which closed in June sixty-six group
meetings and social gatherings were held. The attendance record made
by the Director of Activities shows that over 7,400 students attended
these affairs with several drawing more than five hundred students to a
single affair. The calendar discloses a variety of programs ranging from
vocational discussion groups to formal balls.
Mention should be made that the students have not confined their
activites to their own welfare and pleasure, however. During the
Thanksgiving recess the students had as their guests at the club house
forty-five boys and girls chosen by the All Nations Club who otherwise
would not have had a turkey dinner .at that season. Each week five students, in rotation, made the twenty mile trip across to the east side of the
city to serve as recreational assistants at the All Nations Club. The student group also held several benefit affairs for the summer camp for
underprivileged children which the university student body sponsors.
Our report last year mentions that a large department store was
under construction immediately to the east and also fronting on Le Conte

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

129

Avenue. It has now been completed and opened. Anticipating s~me such
development. your Board of Directors acquired, ten years ago, twentytw~ feet .additional frontage as a buffer between our building and any
which might be erected to the east. We might as well confess that we
permitted the general contractor to use this parcel during construction
and in return exacted, without cost to us, the reenforcement of our rear
foundations, landscaping of the buffer area and the paving of a larger
out door patio area. The unique architecture of this widely spread commercial neighbor is such that the two block frontage of it and our club
house is pleasing and similar.
Ten days ago we received the resignation of Brother Oscar Lawler,
P.G.M., as a member of the Board and accepted it with regrets. His
association with the Board during the past six years had been most
pleasing and beneficial and we shall miss his genial personality and
valuable counsel. His successor has not been elected yet.
The new university semester is less than a month under way and
official registration figures have not been announced. Unofficial tabulations indicate that, as with collegiate institutions across the nation, enrollment has dropped. The student registration will. however, exceed
14,000. Early returns indicate that the membership at the club house
will equal that of last year.
Your Board has adopted a proposed budget for the coming year and
respectfully requests an appropriation therefor. Despite increases for
our employees' salaries and property taxes, again this year, as in 1948,
we have adopted a budget which is less than that for the precediDg year,
less by $1.335.00. The items of the budget are as follows:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLICATIONS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee which was appointed by the Grand Master on
February 5, 1951, reports as follows:
This Committee has inspected many of the so-called Masonic publications published in this jurisdiction; has made extensive inquiries and investigation and has held two formal hearings at which owners of such
publications by invitation appeared and voluntarily responded to questions propounded by members of this Committee. The questions, answers and comment were taken by official Court Reporters, members of
our fraternity, and reduced to transcript form. One hearing was held in
Los Angeles on April 7, 1951, and the other in San Francisco on June
23, 1951.
At the Los Angeles hearing the following appeared:
Calvin Jesse Carey, Publisher of Bay Area Mason and Eastern Star.
His father, Ernest Regan Carey, voluntarily appeared and testified
but he had no financial interest in the publication.
Marguerite Pray, Publisher of The Masonic News of Huntington
Park.
Ben Morrison, Publisher of Masonic Review Digest.
Norman Ives Stewart, Publisher of Masonic Directory and Eastern
Star News.
Cecil Loomis, Publisher of The Channel Counties Mason and Eastern Star.
.
Mike S. Oldershaw, Publisher of Kern County Masonry and Eastern
Star.
The following were invited but did not attend:
J. H. Hovick, Publisher of Hiram's Masonic Journal.
F. A. Barman, Publisher of Hiram's Masonic Herald.
Frank Thomas, Publisher of The Masonic Magazine and Eastern
Star News.
At the San Francisco hearing the following appeared:
Glenn Martin Whitfield. Publisher of The Masonic Star. His attorney, Alfred Breslauer, was present. His wife, Mrs. Whitfield, a part
owner, was present and testified.

132

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Sidney M. Brown, Publisher of The Masonic Trestle Board and East
Bay Masonic News.
James Adam, Publisher of The Masonic World.
The following were invited but did not attend:
Sidney H. Foster, Editor of Fellowship. a Magazine for Masons.
Cecil F. Neely, Scribe Vallejo Pyramid of Sciots, Publisher of The
Masonic News.
Marcus L. Waltz, Publisher of San Luis Obispo County Mason &

Ted Staatz. Publisher of Sciots Booster.
From the . inspections, inquiries, investigations and hearings this
Committee finds concerning said so-called Masonic Publications as
follows:
1~ All persons who appeared at the hearings were members of our
fraternity except two: all members belong to Lodges in this jurisdiction except two who belong to Lodges in Chicago. All publications published by non-Masons which came to our attention
sprang from publications started by Masons.
2. The owners who appeared at the hearings and others operate
their publications for their own personal gain and private profit
and advertising is their major source of revenue.
3. There are more than twenty such publications, using in their titles
the words Mason, Masons or Masonic, published in this jurisdiction, sixteen of which have been examined by one or more members of this Committee. None of said publications has official sanction, which was admitted by all owners who testified. None rises
to the dignity of a creditable Masonic publication. From a news
standpoint none possesses originality and all except one or two
would contain no news but for the "scissors and the paste pot".
4. Few of said publications have a worthy subscription list and some
have none. Distribution is effected partially by some and wholly
by others by placing bundles of publications in lodge halls, temples and other meeting .places.
5. One of the publications has members of Job's Daughters and of
Eastern Star solicit subscriptions in several localities upon a
commission basis.
·
6. Some of the publications use or have used lodge rosters and the
Grand Lodge roster to obtain subscriptions and advertising. One
publication carries a feature called "Lodge of the Month", in
which is printed the history of a particular Lodge and the Secretary or a member of that Lodge makes up and delivers a mailing
list to the publisher so that a copy of the issue may go to the members of the Lodge. This contravenes Masonic law. ( 732 Ross Digest.)

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

133

7. Some of the publications solicit and obtain trestle boards and news
items for publication purposes from various Lodges and some
Lodges even pay some of the publications five cents per member
per issue for such publishing. This violates Masonic law. ( 732
Ross Digest. )
8. Some of the publications solicit, obtain and publish special article~
written by Grand Lodge Officers.
9. One publication maintains its business office in a Masonic Temple.
10. Some of the publications obtain and publish pictures of Grand
Lodge Officers without their consent. One such publication published the picture of our Grand Master on the front page without
his permission. This perversity was obviously calculated to capture pecuniary advantage on the ·avenue of official significance.
11. One publication carries a printed list of advisers consisting of
members of Grand Lodge and even Past Grand Masters. This
tends to lend official sanction.
·
12. Some of these publications have been constituted official publications of bodies whose membership requires Masonic affiliation.
This tends to confer official sanction because some people believe
that members of such bodies are Masons of first rank. One publication carried a statement that it was the official publication of
two particular Masonic District Officers Associations but the
statement has been withdrawn since this Committee started work.
13. At least two of said publications are incorporated possibly as a
shield ~gainst liability to the true owners.
14. Some years ago a Masonic Periodicals Corporation was formed
under the guise of making a publication to disseminate Masonic
light. Some $80,000.00 worth of stock was sold to members in this
state. It failed miserably-approaching a Masonic scandal.
15. A publisher of one of the publications using "Masonic" in its
title was sued for slander in the courts of this state but the case
was dismissed.
16. All owners, except two, who appeared at the hearings stated that
they would discontinue the use of Masonic words in their titles
if Grand Lodge so decreed.
17. Some publications publish political advertising and liquor ads
which cast discredit upon our fraternity. It is not lawful for our
rosters to be used for political purposes by candidates. So the publications which use our rosters and publish political ads indirectly
thwart our law. ( 732 Ross Digest.)
18. At least one publication has published the name of an applicant
for the degrees. This is transgression of our law.

From its investigation and the above findings your Committee has
reached the following conclusions:
I. All Masons have declared upon their honor that they were
uninfluenced by mercenary motives in seeking admission to
our fraternity.
II. These so-called Masonic publications by their very names,
nature and method of operation, however extensive the publishers' denial. convey to the general public official Masonic
status. ·
III. Advertising or solicitation thereof by a Lodge or by a Mason
in or for any publication or medium which purports to be
. Masonic in name or character achieves exploitation of the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

137

great name of our fraternity and is repugnant to the fundamental traditions and unwritten law of Masonry.
IV. Advertising practices by so-called Masonic publications in
this jurisdiction have in numerous cases reached the level of
a racket which must not be tolerated by this Grand Lodge.
V. Masonry abhors the use of its good name for commercial
purposes.
VI. That a copy of this report including the resolution which follows be sent by the Grand Secretary to the Master of every
Lodge in this jurisdiction with directions to read the same at
three stated meetings and that a copy thereof be sent by the
Grand Secretary to every Inspector in this jurisdiction who
shall be required to report every infraction of the resolution
to the Grand Master.
VII. That a copy of the resolution which follows be mailed by the
Grand Secretary to every so-called Masonic publication in
this state with a statement that it is now the law of this
jurisdiction.
VIII. That a copy of the resolution which follows be sent by mail in
a sealed envelope by every Lodge in this jurisdiction to all
members thereof with a statement that it is now the law of
this jurisdiction.
IX. That this Committee, but not necessarily its present members,
be continued for the purpose of giving further consideration
to tb.e promiscuous use of our name, symbols, emblems and
insignia.
On the morning of October 18, 1873, in this Grand Lodge assembled
our brothers spoke as follows:
"If Masons, being about to engage, or already engaged, in a
private enterprise, seek by any means whatever to induce the public to believe that their enterprise is, or is to be, conducted under the
auspices, or under the control and management, or upon the credit
and responsibility of the frate~ity of Masons, they are guilty of
a fraud upon the public and an outrage upon Masonry, and should
be dealt with accordingly. As to the public, they are seeking its
confidence under false pretenses and are unworthy to be trusted:
and as to Masonry, they regard not its good name among men, but,
for their own private gain, would expose it to the risk of bearing all
the odium necessarily attendant upon possible mismanagement and
failure."
"Its (Masonry's) symbols and emblems, its signs and tokens, its
name and fame, its rank and honorable titles, belong not to an
individual for his own use and benefit, but are talents entrusted to

138

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

him to be used for special and exclusive purposes. These purposes
are purely Masonic, and there is no reasonable excuse for misap·
prehension of their true and lawful use. That Masonry, or anything
which is incidental to it, is intended or contemplated to be hawked
about and used in the business pursuits and struggles of men, as
capital for making money or for the advancement of their mere
personal triumphs, is the grossest perversion of noble aims and the
most cheating of popular fallacies."
(Proceedings 1873 Page 220)
· Your Committee therefore presents the following resolution:
Resolved: That Section 127 of Ordinances be amended by adding at
the end thereof the following:
· No Lodge or member of a Lodge, without the express sanction of
Grand Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print advertising of
any kind in or for any medium or publication, which purports to be
Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for any body.
order or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to
membership.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
WRITTEN CEREMONIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
At our last annual communication a recommendation was adopted ·
that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee to examine
and report at this communication on the written ceremonies of this
grand lodge. The committee appointed for that purpose herewith pre·
sents its report.
We have examined in detail the existing ceremonies for the laying
of cornerstones, the institution of new lodges, the constitution of newly
chartered lodges, the dedication of Masonic halls and the presentation
of fifty year buttons. It was not our purpose to rewrite any of these
ceremonies, only to remove inconsistencies, inaccurate statements, correct grammar and revise such floor work as detracted from the occasion.
We attach to this report a complete copy of these ceremonies as revised
and recommend that they be adopted in the form presented herewith.
It will be immediately apparent that we have not suggested modifications which change the theme or substance of any of these cere·
monies. Only one slight addition is made to any. We are, however,
suggesting numerous al~erations and we desire that the representatives
of the constituent lodges be fully advised as to those modifications
which we recommend. They are too numerous to be detailed separately
in this report•but the committee is prepared to state its reasons for any
and every change, if desired. For the convenience of the brethren assembled at this communication and in the interest of economy of time,
we shall outline in general terms some of the modifications and point
directly to those which may be classified as being of a more pronounced
nature.
In the matter of punctuation and the use of capital letters, we have
made many revisions to conform to modern usage. The ceremonies as
printed heretofore have used punctuation and capital letters according
to standards not prevalent today.
In three instances, the laying of cornerstones, the instituting of new
lodges and the dedicating of Masonic halls, we have changed the order
of speeches opening the ceremonies. When the officers arrive at the site
of the cornerstone the ceremony as it exists today opens, without any
introduction, with.a prayer by the Grand Chaplain and after the prayer,
the Grand Master explains the reason for the gathering. We have re·
vised this portion so that the Grand Master's declaration comes first and
then the prayer, after which the ceremony continues. The ceremony for
instituting a new lodge, at present, opens with a biblical passage by the
Grand Master, then a prayer by the Grand Chaplain and then a declara·

140

141

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

tion by the Grand Master as to the reason for the gathering. We recom•
mend that the declaration come first and that after the Grand Master
has stated the reason for the assemblage, the ceremony should continue.
The ceremony for the dedication of a Masonic hall at present opens
with a speech by the Grand Master as to dedications and historical
facts and after he has spoken at some length, the Master of the lodge
invites him to dedicate the hall and the Grand Master accepts the
invitation. We recommend that the ceremony open with the invitation
and the acceptance and that then the Grand Master detail the Biblical
and historical matters. It has been our experience that due to the open·
ing of these ceremonies in the manner existing at present, Grand Masters
in past years have felt constrained to make some extemporaneous explanation of the occasion before taking up the ritualistic work. The ritualistic explanation for the assemblage in each instance is entirely adequate and logically should come before the prayers, or Biblical and
historical matters. The ceremony in each instance will then naturally
and logically be opened.
.
In several instances we have taken the expression of a thought out
of a negative form and put in into a positive form. One example will
suffice to illustrate these changes. In the ceremony for instituting a new
lodge, as it exists at the present time, the Grand Master in speaking of
the duty of a Mason says, "He must not hesitate to refuse to recom·
mend any man for the degrees of Masonry unless he has strong reasons
to believe that he will ultimately reflect honor upon our ancient institution." We recommend that this thought be stated in the positive form:
"He should refuse to recommend any man for the degrees of Masonry
unless he has strong reasons to believe that the applicant will ultimately
reflect honor on our ancient institution."
In the ceremony of dedicating a Masonic hall we have eliminated
the procession of the grand officers around the ~mblem. We recog~ize
that our ancient brethren were given to processions on many occasions
and that it is probably a relic from times past, however, it has been .our
observation that this procession usually detracts from the occasion.
There is no time for a rehearsal and it is often difficult of execution due
to the attendance and crowded condition. We strongly recommend
that the procession be deleted and have made no provision for it in the
ceremony as revised.
In the ceremonies for the dedication of a Masonic hall and the
constitution of a newly chartered lodge, all of the grand lodge officers
are formed in a square around the emblem and in the latter the brethren
of the lodge are formed in another square around the grand lodge
officers. The result has been that there is a closed square, or two squares,
around the emblem and the brethren seated on the sidelines cannot see
what is occurring within, thus the core of the entire ceremony is c~m­
pletely screened from those who came to see it. In these two ceremomes,
we have retained the square, but have formed it with only six grand

officers widely separated. The brethren who are seated on the sidelines
will be able to see the entire ceremony and the form of the square will be
preserved. In these ceremonies we have omitted the kneeling of the
officers and what the book has called the grand honors but which were
not the grand honors in this jurisdiction. ·
In most of the ceremonies, we are presenting the prayers of the
Grand Chaplain in slightly simplified forms. At present, he addresses
the Great Creator by from three to five titles or attributes. We have
reduced these to one or two. We believe that the prayers of the Grand
Chaplain, while not changed in substance, are presented in forms more
in keeping with the tempo of modem times. We have also eliminated a
few phrases which speak of God as being jealous or vengeful and instead, we ascribe to Him the attributes of love and light.
The prayer of the Chaplain in the ceremony for presenting fifty
year buttons has been entirely rewritten. The existing form in effect
tells the recipient that he has one foot in the grave and the other on sinking ground. We know of no reason why this or any other prayer need
be morbid. We also have delayed the conducting of the recipient to the
center of the lodge so that he will not be required to stand so long. We
have tried to retain the essentials but to brighten this ceremony. It
should be a happy occasion and not one concerned with the suggestion
of death. We require the Master to talk while adjusting the button, in
the hope that facetious remarks sometimes heard about the adjusting
will be avoided.
·
In the ceremony for the constitution of a lodge we have omitted the
Installation of officers. It should be remem·b ered that under the provi·
sions of our 1aw this ceremony must occur within sixty days after an
annual communication; in other words, it must occur between the middle of October and the middle of . December. Almost invariably, constitution ceremonies are scheduled prior to the election of officers at the
December stated meeting. The result is that two complete installations
of officers are made in two months or less. It has been our observation
also that when the grand lodge is called to refreshment for the purpose
of Installing the officers, many of those in attendance depart. Usually
there Is a delay for a substantial time while the lodge room is set up for
the installation. The ceremony for the institution of a new lodge has
never contained the installation service and we are at a loss to understand any necessity for the installation as a part of the constitution
ceremony if it is entirely proper for the officers to function in their
respective stations and places from the time of the institution until the
constitution without being installed. The installation is also somewhat
of an anomaly because the ceremony of constitution is in the grand
lodge. Under the present form , the grand lodge opens, constitutes the
new lodge and then calls off, the grand lodge officers vacate their sta·
tfons and places, a constituent lodge at refreshment comes into being
without having been opened, the officers thereof are installed, the con-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

142

143

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

stituent lodge is called off and labor resumed in the grand lodge. In the
form which we recommend, the entire evening will be a grand lodge
affair without the interposition of a constituent lodge. We believe time
will be saved, confusion avoided and a few speeches go undelivered.
In the ceremony for laying a cornerstone, at present, the Grand
Master declares the purpose of the assemblage by speaking to the Senior
Grand Warden and ordering him to notify the Junior Grand Warden.
who in turn is directed to notify those assembled as to the purpose of
the gathering. Within a tiled meeting we are accustomed to this method
of passing an order of the chair to the brethren, but to the profane it
must seem a peculiar custom and one for which they are unlikely to flnd
any rhyme or reason. In the form which we recommend, the Grand
Master makes the declaration directly to those assembled without pass..
ing it down through the grand wardens. It appears to us that this par..
ticular of the existing ceremony serves no purpose, unless it be to take
up time, hence we have eliminated it. In this ceremony we are recom..
mending the addition of two very short paragraphs immediately before
the corn, wine and oil are poured upon the stone. It appears to your com ..
mittee that those assembled might wonder why these three things were
poured upon the stone and we have given a brief explanation therefore.
We have also made a slight change in the procedure for testing the
stone. As it exists at the present time, the Grand Master lays the stone
and then directs the Deputy Grand Master to ascertain if it is square and
the two grand wardens to ascertain whether it is level and properly
adjusted. It appears to us that it would be more logical for the Grand
Master to ascertain whether the stone was square before he laid it. For
that reason we have him direct the Deputy Grand Master to ascertain
whether the stone is square, the Grand Master lays it and has the grand
wardens ascertain whether it has been properly laid. At the present
time when the Grand Master directs the Senior Grand Warden to ascer..
tain whether the stone is level. the Senior Grand Warden reports that ·
he finds "In that respect the craftsmen have done their duty." After his
testing of the stone. the Junior Grand Warden makes the same report.
As a matter of fact, the craftsmen have had nothing whatever to do with
making the stone level or properly adjusting it, these have been done
by the Grand Master. We recommend the modification o~ the responses
of the two grand' wardens so that they will merely report that the stone
is level and is properly adjusted without stating who is responsible.
In this ceremony we also have omitted a half dozen words applicable
only to a Masonic temple, which omissions will make the ceremony
proper for either a public building or a Masonic temple and will not
require improvision by the Grand Master, as is suggested in the book at
the present time, when he is laying the cornerstone of a public building.
In both the cornerstone and dedication ceremonies, we have made
slight modifications of the remarks made to the principal Architect. It
has been our observation that the brother designated to take the part of

the Principal Architect is seldom the actual architect of the ·building and
even may ~ave n~ actual connection with the plans or construction. On
both occasions this fact will be .known to the brethren assembled and fo
some of the profane at the public ceremony. We believe that in the form
which we are recommending the language is such that it will retaiD.· all
th.e substance of the present phraseology but will not stimulate in the
m.Ind~ of obse~ers the fact that the brother who receives or returns the
working tools is not the architect of the building. In each ceremony in
which the Master of the lodge or the Principal Architect speaks we have
made the tongue twisting phraseology more easy of expre;sion arid
slightlr shorter. This should be a boon to those who have to memorize
these Imes.

CEREMONY FOR THE LAYING OF A CORNERSTONE
Grand Master: Friends and brethren, it has been a custom among
the fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons, from time immemorial. to
assemble for the purpose of laying the foundation stones of certain
buildings, when requested so to do by those having authority. The
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California, having been invited to lay the cornerstone of this
building, we have here assembled and will now proceed with that pleas.
ing duty.
· In accordance with the teachings of our institution, it is our duty,
before entering upon any great or important undertaking, to invoke the
aid and blessing of God. We shall, therefore. reverently unite with our
Grand Chaplain in an address to the Throne of Grace.
The Grand Master calls up the brethren.
Grand Chaplain: Almighty and eternal God, who laid the foundations of the earth, we beseech Thee to look with favor on this our undertaking of laying the cornerstone of a material building. We look to Thee
for guidance and we pray that Thou wilt on all occasions give wisdoni
to guide us, strength to support us and the beauty of holiness to adorn
our labors and to render them acceptable in Thy sight. Grant Thy
blessing and watchful care to sustain and protect the workmen who are
here to be employed. So order their lives and their work that no discord
or confusion may disturb the harmony that should be theirs. And we
pray that when the structure shall be finished, it shall be devoted to all

that stands for good and the glory of Thy holy name. Also, we pray
that when our labors on earth are ~nded, we may be received in that
house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Amen.

cavity beneath the stone certain memorials of the period in which it was

foundations an enduring record may be found by succeeding generations to bear testimony to the untiring, unending industry of the Free
and Accepted Masons. Has such a deposit now been prepared?

The laying of a cornerstone of a great edifice was the occasion of a
solemn rite in ancient times. To the pagan mind it appeared as an undertaking which would provoke the jealousy of the Diety unless a blood
sacrifice was offered. Archaeology has uncovered mute evidence of this
practice.
In the advance of civilization, man's changing concept of the Diety,
from a jealous and vengeful God to a God of love and mercy, has
changed the ceremony to one of joy and thanksgiving. The fraternity of
Free and Accepted Masons, looking ever to the goodness and compassion of the Great Architect of the Universe, lays cornerstones with an
offering of corn, wine and oil.
The Grand Marshal will take the three vessels and distribute them.

With.the formation of a grand lodge in the city of London in 1717
a regulation was adopted declaring that the privilege of assembling as
Masons, theretofore possessed by all the brethren to be exercised at
their pleasure, should be vested in certain lodges convened in certain
places and that, with the exception of four old lodges then existing, no
lodge thereafter should be convened without a warrant from the Grand
Master with the consent of the Grand Lodge. From that time warrants
of constitution date their existence.
A warrant of constitution, or as we term it, a charter, in this jurisdiction emanates from the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California and no lodge may be constituted as such until it has received its charter. The Grand Master,
however, may issue a dispensation authorizing and empowering the
brethre~ therein named "to form and open a Lodge after the manner of
Free and Accepted Masons, and therein to admit to membership and
· make Freemasons, according to the ancient custom and not otherwise.''
While a lodge may not be constituted until it has received its charter
the phrase "in a just and legally constituted lodge" refers not only t~
a lodge working under a charter, but likewise to one working under a
dispensat~on from_ the Grand Master. So far as the regularity and legality of their work is concerned, lodges under dispensation and chartered
lodges have the same standing. There are, however, certain restrictions
imposed upon lodges under dispensation and they do not possess all the
powers of chartered lodges. A lodge under dispensation, for instance, is
not entitled to ·representat ion in the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California, although it may
send delegates thereto who are admitted to seats and have a voice but
no vote: furthermore, it exists subject to the will and pleasure of the
Grand Master, who may at any time revoke the authority under which
it has theretofore worked.
Our constitution requires that new lodges must' work a time under
dispensation as a test of the ability of the officers and brethren to properly perform the duties incumbent upon them and exhibit satisfactory
evidence of Masonic capability.
The authority conferred by a dispensation continues only until the
first day of the month in which the next succeeding Annual Communica tion is held. At that time, the dispensation is returned to the Grand Secretary, together with the by-laws, book of records and returns and a
petition for a charter may be presented. 1£, after an examination of its
work and proceedings, it appears to the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California that the petition
should be granted, a charter is issued and a number assigned to the
lodge and within sixty days thereafter the lodge is duly constituted.
The petition may be refused without any further order being made and

the lodge ceases to exist or a charter may be refused and the dispensation continued in force until the next Annual Communication.
Thus, whether the lodge to be opened this evening will eventually
receive a charter depends solely upon the manner in which the brethren
comprising it discharge the duties and responsibilities devolving upon
them. Not only is it required that they shall in all things conform to
certain rules and regulations, but it is likewise essential that they shall
observe the spirit no less than the letter of the law.
It is, I trust, understood that there must be no departure from the
esoteric work adopted by the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free
and Accepted Masons of the State of California and taught by the
Grand Lecturer. This duty devolves upon the officers of the lodge and
a petition would be denied if, upon examination, it should appear that
the Master and Wardens were not competent to confer the degrees of
Masonry in accordance with the ritual.
There is, however, a further responsibility. which the brethren share
with the officers of the lodge. Upon each member of the lodge devolves
the duty of guarding its portals. The members of a lodge working under
a dispensation should be particularly careful that a searching inquiry
be made into the character and standing of those who present applications.
It too frequently happens that the organization of a new lodge is
hailed as an opportunity to obtain fellowship with us ·b y some to whom it
has theretofore been denied and by others who have feared to seek it.
They presume on the perhaps natural desire of the brethren of the new
lodge to increase the membership and it is unfortunately true that the
mistaken idea that numbers indicate success sometimes causes the
brethren of a new lodge to disregard the fundamentals upon which the
membership of the fraternity is recruited.
I hope I need not remind you that Masonry solicits no man for
membership: he must come to us of his own free will and accord, soliciting the favor which we confer upon those whom we accept as members.
A member of a Masonic lodge is not justified in giving his recommendation to one who has signified a desire for the degrees of Masonry
merely ·because he knows nothing detrimental to his character. More
than this is required. He should refuse to recommend any man for the
degrees of Masonry unless he has strong reasons to believe that the
applicant will ultimately reflect honor on our ancient institution.
The Masonic capabilities of a lodge working under dispensation will
be determined no less by the character of its members than by the character of its work. As the strength of a chain is tested by its weakest link,
so the standard of a Masonic lodge is set by its least desirable member.
However excellent might have been the work performed by the
officers and however exact had been the compliance with the rules and
regulations, a charter would not issue to a lodge which had shown itself
careless of its honor and reputation, so unmindful of its obligations as

to admit one not worthy and well qualified.
It is believed that those who have been instrumental in forming this
new lo~~e are not only conversant with their duties and responsibilities, .
but willu~g and eager .to faithfully discharge them. accordingly a
dispensation has been issued to them which will now be read by

Grand Master: We read in the holy writings that when all the work
that Solomon made for the house of the Lord was finished, he assembled
the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the chiefs of the
fathers of the children of Israel and then the house which was erected to
God was dedicated to His Holy Name.
We have gathered in imitation of the children of Israel to dedicate
this buil~ing to Freemasonry. virtue and universal benevolence, thus
perpetuating the custom which has come down to us from time immemorial.
Among the ancients, every temple, altar and statue was dedicated to
some divinity. The Hebrews extended this ceremony even to their private
houses and it was a custom in Israel to dedicate a new house to God with
prayer. praise and thanksgiving. This was done in order to secure the
divine presence and blessing, for it was believed that no pious or sensible
man would expect to dwell safely in a house which was not under the
immediate protection of God. A distinction, however, was made between
consecration and dedication; for sacred things were both consecrated and

162

dedicated, while profane things such as private dwelling houses, were
only dedicated: This distinction has been observed among other nations,
many of whom consecrated their churches to the worship of God, but
dedicated them to or placed them under the especial patronage of some
particular saint.
You will remember that a similar practice prevails in our institution
and that while we consecrate our lodges to the honor and glory of God,
we dedicate them to the memory of the Holy Saints John and the building itself is dedicated to Freemasonry, virtue and universal benevolence.
You may be interested in knowing that this is the form of dedication
of the first Masonic hall of which we have authentic information. The
ceremony of that first dedication, in 1774:, was in all its essentials identical with that which will be performed tonight. To those unmindful of
its symbolism, it will be nothing but an unmeaning form but in truth
and fact the ceremony is fraught with significance.
In devoting anything to religious purposes the anointing with oil
was considered by the ancient Hebrews as a necessary part of the ceremony. The tabernacle in the wilderness and all its holy vessels were, it
is said, by God's express command, anointed with oil. Masonic halls are
dedicated to the sacred purposes to which .they were built by strewing
corn, wine and oil upon the emblem.
The corn alone is carried in a golden pitcher, the wine and oil being
contained in silver vessels. It is to remind us that the first, as a necessity
and the staff of life, is of more importance and more worthy of honor
than the others, which are but comforts.
These should also remind of our duty to share our bread with the
hungry, cheer the sorrowful and pour the healing oil of consolation into
the wounds which sickness has made in the bodies or affliction has rent
in the hearts of our fellow men.

PRESENTATION OF FIFTY-YEAR BUTTON
Over two hundred and fifty veteran buttons are presented each
year. It is therefore impractical for the Grand Master or other principal
officers of the grand lodge to make the presentations. However, the importance of the occasion to the recipient should cause care to be exercised in selecting the officer who is to make the presentation and in the
planning of the program. If, because of the infirmities of age or otherwise,
the recipient cannot attend a lodge meeting, the presentation may be
made at his home in the presence of his family and friends.
If the presentation is made at a stated or special meeting of the lodge
one or two selections of music will add greatly to the occasion.
At an appropriate junction the officer who is to make the presentation (designated herein as the Master) shall begin as follows:
Master: The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California has noted with gratification that
Brother ........................ has been a member of a regular lodge of Masons
for ............ years and at this time we shall have the pleasure and privilege
of bestowing upon him a visible token of its fraternal love and appreciation. Brother .................... was initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason
on ................ in .................... Lodge, No ......... , passed to the degree of
Fellowcraft on ............ and raised to the sublime degree of Master
Mason on ............. He is now a member of ................ Lodge, No..............
