REPoRT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
There is a new trend in Masonic activities and it is a trend toward
increased educatiOn. Just as doctors have their post-graduate courses
and lawyers their program of continuing education of the Bar, so the
Fraternity is recognizing and accepting the responsibility for a continuing education of its members.
To think that three short lessons in Masonry, representing the three
degrees, is the end of all instruction in the meaning, history and application of the valuable lessons contained therein and terminates all further
responsibility of the Lodge is becoming an out-moded notion.
Committees to advance Masonic Education have been appointed
in the past in this jurisdiction. They struggled for a time, found indifferent support and faded out. The same thing might happen to this Committee except that somewhere along the years the tide has turned and
there is now a new interest in Masonic subjects.
Nor is this interest limited to California. Your Committee has surveyed the situation elsewhere and believes the following examples
should be reported:
1. In France the degrees are given less rapidly. The minimum time
for advancing from one degree to another is eight months and is more
often one or two years. The candidate is required to study symbolism
and assimilate the teachings of each degree.

168

169

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

2. In New Zealand an excellent program of Masonic Education is
carried on. The Grand Lodge lecturers devote their time to delivering
lectures on the ethics, symbolism and history of Masonry. In addition,
a system of Research Lodges is provided whose members carry on research, hold discussions and send out speakers and papers to outlying
Lodges upon request. Such programs have proven a valuable supple·
ment to local Lodge programs.

made in California by the constituent Lodges or volunteer groups of
Masons to further the cause of education. There are many such in the
state. To take an example, Hollywood Lodge No. 355 has been conducting a round-table discussion on a monthly basis for many ·years.
The San Francisco Masonic Research group has been active for some
fifteen years. I know of individual Lodges which conduct regular programs on Masonic Law, history and symbolism.

3. In our own country, as early as I 841, the Grand Master of
Ohio, in his annual message. advised the subordinate Lodges to acquire
libraries and introduce into their meetings lectures on the various arts
and sciences connected with the Fraternity. In 1843 the Grand Jurisdiction of Kentucky adopted legislation to promote Masonic Education.

All concede that the newly raised Mason needs instruction in symbolism and history to supplement the excellent instruction booklets now
supplied each candidate in this jurisdiction. For the experienced Mason
more intriguing subjects are Masonic Law, the relationship of Masonry
to Communism, Catholicism, Religion and Politics, Negro Masonry,
Investigations, Masonic Offenses, and a myriad of others.

4. The Grand Jurisdiction of Iowa has an extremely active and
energetic educational program. Since I am a resident of Long Beach,
which is sometimes referred to as the capitol of Iowa, I acknowledge
admiration for Iowa's work but as a thoroughly indoctrinated Californian I predict that California can put on a bigger and bet(er program.

Since our last Annual Communication Iowa sponsored the midwest
conference on Masonic Education. Ten midwest and two eastern jurisdictions were represented at the conference and discussed all phases
of educational work. Iowa makes use of one Lodge of Research, a
splendid Grand Lodge library and an active Grand Lodge Committee
on Masonic Education with an office director, a field worker and a
stenographer.
· 5. The most popular method of carrying on the work of Masonic
Education in the United States is by means of Research Lodges. Seven
Grand Jurisdictions have authorized this form of organization. They
are: New York, which has had a Research Lodge since 1931; Connecticut; Iowa; Missouri, which claims the largest Research Lodge in the
world; Oregon; Washington, and. lastly. Virginia, with the newest
Lodge of Research, chartered this year. These organizations hold
charters from their Grand Jurisdictions which, ordinarily, prohibit the
conferring of degrees and limit their activities to research and discussion, the preparation of papers on Masonic subjects and the furnishing
of speakers to constituent Lodges who desire to have an address on,
or discussion of, some interesting Masonic subject as part of their own
programs.
You can see from the foregoing report that the desirability of continuing Masonic Education is generally conceded among the various
Grand Jurisdictions. It is more a question of how to accomplish the
desired end and the work of this Committee has therefore been concentrated on methods of education.
Your Committee has also investigated the present efforts now being

I dare say there is not one Master or Warden present at this communication who has not felt the need for an address or discussion of an
educational nature as a substitute for the usual degree night or a supplement to a stated meeting. A variation from the usual routine always
stimulates attendance and enriches the Masonic experience of the
members..
There are many Lodges which would welcome speeches or discussions on these subjects. There are many eminent Masons among us
well qualified to deliver speeches or lead discussions. Unfortunately,
there is no machinery to bring the two together. Your present Committee has had many calls along this line but it is obviously beyond the
capacity of any committee to supply the needs of a jurisdiction as large
in membership and as vast in area as ours. Moreover, there are drawbacks on entrusting this important work to a committee which necessarily
varies from time to time in membership, capacity and energy. Distances
in California are too great to gain the full advantage of a single central
library location as is done in Iowa.
Of the several plans considered and compared, your Committee feels
a modification of the Oregon plan is best adapted to California. This
involves the creation of a minimum of two Lodges of Research, one for
the north and one for the south, with the probability that others will be
added later. The function of these Lodges would be, not to confer degrees but to accumulate, preserve and disseminate to the constituent
Lodges Masonic information of every nature. A panel of speakers can
be built up. well qualified and willing to deliver speeches or lead discussions of an educational nature when requested to do so by other
Lodges. The advantages of the plan are these:
1. Continuity of program and the advantages of cumulative
experience since the Research Lodge would be permanent.

170

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

2. Grand Lodge is relieved of primary responsibility for what
might otherwise become a cumbersome and expensive burden.
3. Geographical distribution of the Research Lodges would
act as a magnet to the brilliant speakers and studious minds of the
Fraternity with the resulting benefit of interchange of ideas and a
directed program.
4. Proximity to Lodges would also cut travel time and inconvenience for those brethren devoting themselves to the work.
5. No expensive staff would be needed under the Research
Lodge plan.
6. A more flexible plan could be followed since each Research
Lodge can meet the peculiar needs of its own section of the state.
It is true that enabling legislation to provide for the orderly creation
and operation of Research Lodges will have to be adopted at this communication if the plan is to be put into effect. A draft of proposed legislation is attached to this report marked "Exhibit A." I will not read it
at this time but merely state that the Committee thinks f.t is sufficient
·
for the purpose.
In preparing this report I acknowledge the able assistance of ViceChairman Triggs and other members of the Committee, the inspiring
leadership of our Grand Master, the encouragement of other Grand
Officers and Past Grand Masters, all of whom are fully awake to the
desirability of Masonic Education and cognizant of the need of a workable plan to bring it to fruition.
The Grand Master has traveled extensively this year and has often
addressed the brethren on the subject of this report. Invariably he has
received an enthusiastic response. Possible points of friction have been
eliminated when the true purposes of the educational program are explained. It is not a substitute for ritualistic perfection. Instruction in the
ritual must go on as before. It is not a substitute for the so-called higher
degrees. Masonic Education is concerned with a more perfect appreciation and application of the three degrees of Blue Lodge Masonry.
Last year we closed the first hundred years of Masonry in California.
This year we have commenced another century, and I cannot think of a
more constructive, forward-looking theme on which we enter the new
century than that announced in the sincere and inspirational Annual
Message of Most Worshipful Arthur Paulsen, who is deeply interested
in Masonic Education. If we can initiate a well-planned program of
education at this Communication it will mark 1951 as one of the most
important in the history of the Grand Lodge.
In order to carry out the high aims on which I have reported your
Committee recommends:
1. That the Grand Lodge adopt a policy of encouraging Masonic
Education .through Research Lodges.

2. That legislation providing for the creation and operation of Research Lodges be adopted in the form submitted with this report.

There is a wide difference in the net worth of the respective lodges.
At the present time lodges can own cash, hank accounts. government. state and municipal bonds and investments which are legal for
California savings hanks, and Temple securities which must first he
approved by a Grand Lodge Committee set up for that purpose. Life
Membership Funds cannot he invested in Temple securities.
There is a very urgent and definite demand upon the part of many
lodges for a broader investment program. Therefore, the Committee
definitely felt that a sound investment policy should apply to every lodge.
small or large. Each lodge has its own individual problem and its own
philosophy as to investments. Each lodge should he able to make its own
decision within any investment policy set up by Grand Lodge. Neither
Grand Lodge. as such. nor any Committee thereof. should make investments for or on behalf of any lodge.
Whether or not to broaden its investments would he within the determina.tion of each lodge, as it visualizes its own problems. The rule we
are proposing would be permissive-it would not he compulsory.
Therefore. as to constituent lodges, the Prudent Man Rule investment policy which we recommend for the investment of liquid funds,
exclusive of Temple property or Temple securities, is as follows:
Section 1 ) At least 10% of the funds available for investment must
be in:
A) Cash aad/or bank accounts.
B) Obligations of the United States or those for the payment of
which the faith of the United States is pledged.
C) Obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions. provided they were issued pursuant to law and that the faith and
credit of such municipal corporation or district is pledged for their payment.
D) Such other securities as are legal investments for California savings hanks.
·
Section 2) Up to 20% may he invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will he fully listed
and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange.
B) Preferred stocks. which are or will be fully listed and registered
on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission
as a National Securities Exchange.
No such investments, however, shall be made which at the time of
purchase will result in the total market value of the securities referred
to in this section exceeding twenty percent ( 20% ) of the total market
value of all the cash. hank accounts and securities held.
Section 3) Up to forty percent ( 10% ) may he invested in:
A) Common stocks, which must he fully listed and registered on an

exchange registered with th-e Securities and Exchange Commission as a
National Securities Exchange, except that this listing requirement shall
not apply to bank and insurance company stocks.
B) Shares of Investment Trusts.
No such investments. however, shall be made which at the time of
purchase will result in the total market value of the securities referred to
in this section exceeding forty percent ( 10% ) of the total market value
of all the cash. hank accounts and securities held.
In the event a constituent lodge decides to invest in securities described in Sections 2 and 3 above. it shall confer and counsel with the
professional Investment Advisor used by Grand Lodge. whose fees will
he paid by Grand Lodge.
Presently Grand Lodge law prohibits the investment of Life Membership Funds in Temple securities and limits such investments to those
set forth in Section 1 above.
We recommend that this law be changed so as to permit the diversification of investments of Life Membership Funds in accordance with the
provisions of Sections 1, 2 and 3 above. and subject to the same restrictions, provided that the accounts of such funds are kej,t and maintained
separately and apart from all other lodge assets.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY
LIABILITY INSURANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodg.e of California:
The special committee to study the question of public liability insurance with reference to making it mandatory upon all of the constituent
lodges has completed its study and begs leave to report as follows:
For the purpose of putting into effect the voluntary plan of insurance
made available during 1950 questionaires were sent to all lodges and
constituent bodies of the jurisdiction.
Answers were returned on four hundred questionnaires which included seventy-five returned from Temple associations. Of the lodges
reporting 36% had some form of liability insurance in force. In each in-

180

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

stance the form of policy was very limited in its coverage and in most
instances too low.
It has been impossible to secure an accurate picture of the accident
history of lodges in this jurisdiction which could be completely relied
upon. The only true loss experience available is for the period March
1, 1950 to March 1, 1951 during the time the voluntary plan policy has
been in force. There were some minor claims made and small amounts
of money paid, but nothing of any consequence. We have heard rumors
of other losses in prior years but with no definite information. It is understood that there was one fatality and in another instance a serious automobile accident in Southern California.
About the time that this committee began its study of the desirability
of this type of coverage for constituent lodges the insurance carrier
handling the voluntary plan expressed a desire to cancel its policy, then
in force. It therefore became necessary for the insurance counsel to
locate a new company willing to write the coverage. This was accomplished and the policy is now placed in the Seaboard Surety Company,
which company meets all the requirements of sound insurance underwriting.
Your committee was composed of an insurance broker, an attorney,
and an executive of The Pacific Telephone & Telegraph Company.
Each one has had some experience with the problems involved in the
matter of insurance. Each member of your committee felt that the exposure of the lodges and their members to litigation was sufficient to
warrant the carrying of public liability insurance coverage as a part of
the Grand Lodge Program. Most members of lodges do not realize
that their lodges are unincorporated associations and a suit against a
lodge can individually include each and every member of the lodge. In
the absence of any ability to collect from the lodge treasury, and if they
sought to bring in the individual members of the lodge for that.purpose,
they could proceed not only against the property of the lodge itself. but
against the property of each individual member of the lodge to enforce
payment of any judgment secured.

It is the contention of your Committee that each lodge comes within
the purview of that section of the Code of Civil Procedure of the State
of California-that in the case of a suit anyone seeking damages could
name not only the lodge, but each individual member of the lodge and
thereby compel them to defend themselves against any such action
which might be filed, whether it be justified or otherwise. Some lawyer
members may cite a legal proposition to the contrary, but it is always expensive to defend a lawsuit.
In view of this, your committee feels that it is important that each
and every lodge be required to carry insurance sufficiently broad to
protect, not only the joint property of the lodge and the members composing such lodge, but also the individual liability of each member
thereof in their capacity as such member.
The policy now in force and available on a voluntary basis insures:
"The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California; and/or its constituent lodges
to whom certificates of insurance may be issued hereunder;
and/or the Masonic Homes of California, a corporation; and/or
the Masonic Boards of Relief, and/or Employment Bureaus;
and/or the Masonic Club Houses at the University of California
at Berkeley and Los Angeles, California; and/or Masonic Temple Associations to whom certificates of insurance may be issued
hereunder; and/or any other person, association, organization,
firm, or corporation to whom certificates of insurance may be
issued hereunder."
The coverages accorded by the policy are as follows :

In support of that statement see Section 388 of the Code of Civil
Procedure of the State of California, which reads as follows:
"When two or more persons associated in any business, transact
such business under a common name, whether it comprises the
names of such persons or not, the associates may be sued by such
common names, the summons in such cases being served on one
or more of the assoc~ates: and the judgment in the action shall
bind the joint property of all the associates, and the individual
property of the party or parties served with the process, in the
same manner as if all had been named defendents and had been
sued upon their joint liability."

The coverage of the policy is such that almost every conceivable
occurrence which could take place under any circumstance involving
activity of the insured lodge is covered under the policy and each member of the lodge is also protected along with the lodge. The policy goes
further to the effect that each member of the lodge, although he is in the
position of being an insured of the policy, likewise is in the position of
being a member of the public if he should at any time be injured and
make a claim against the lodge. If his claim were legitimate it would be
covered under the policy. This does not mean of course that it is an
accident and health policy.
The high limits of coverage are very important in view of the fact
that today large judgments are often given for trivial occurrences. One
might as well be without insurance as to be without enough insurance.
The limits of liability and the other clauses of the policy make it a most
desirable and acceptable form of insurance.
The annual premiums for each lodge are based upon the membership
of the lodge so that a just and proportional rate is charged to each lodge.
In support of the recommendation which your committee is making
on this case we attach copies of all the material which was used in formulating this following recommendation.
Your committee unanimously recommends that a resolution be passed
by Grand Lodge requiring that public liability and property damage
insurance be mandatory for all constituent lodges in this jurisdiction,
with the provision that the lodge shall have the option of electing to
come under the grand lodge program of insurance or provide themselves
with coverage comparable to that provided by Grand Lodge.
It is believed by the insurance counsel. who has placed the present
public liability insurance for Grand Lodge, and your Committee, that
should the lodges of this jurisdiction sign up 100% for coverage now
available the premiums can be further reduced. We might even. go
further and say that the coverage of the policy might be broadened
where possible if all lodges come in under the program.
In view of the broad coverages and excellent limits of the policy
herein referred to, it is hoped that no lodge will exercise the option of
securing a separate insurance policy comparable to the Grand Lodge
program even though they might be able to find it.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
There has been referred to the Committee on Grievances a total of
42 records. This report to Grand Lodge by your Committee will deal ·
with 30 of these records. The remaining 12 records will be covered by
separate reports due to the fact that they involve appeals, petitions for
restoration, or some other situation which, in the opinion of your Committee, require them to be separately considered.
Certain types of errors in Masonic Trial procedure seem to occur,
year after year, in spite of the fact that such errors are repeatedly called
to the attention of Grand Lodge. It seems not amiss to mention again
one of these. In doing so, we quote from our report to Grand Lodge at
its 1950 convention:
"Many Masonic trials arise out of matters which· have been the
subject of criminal court procedure, resulting in a conviction of the
accused. In such cases, in the preparation of Masonic charges,
where automatic expulsion under Section 332 is not available, the
offense committed by the accused should be charged rather than the
fact that the accused has been convicted of the offense. It is the
commission of the offense which constitutes unmasonic conduct
rather than the conviction therefor. To charge the conviction rather
than the offense itself is to plead a result rather than the cause."
Your Committee proposes to recommend to Grand Lodge the affirmance of the result reached in the following trial records:

Trial Record No. 1230
Your committee, to which was referred Trial Record No. 1230, reports as follows:
Accused, H. A. W., a member of Penrhyn Lodge No. 258, was ex.pelled by his lodge, after conviction of unmasonic conduct. There were
two specifications in the charges-first, that in June, 1945, the accused
was adjudged guilty of adultery in a divorce action brought against
him in West Virginia, and second, that on November 11, 1940, he was
arrested in San Bernardino County, California, for grand theft, which
was later reduced to petty theft, on conviction of which he served thirty
days in the county jail.
At the masonic trial a certified copy of the divorce judgment in West
Virginia was introduced in evidence. It recited that accused had been
. absent from the state and had been served with summons by publication in a newspaper and that he was guilty of adultery and the divorce
was granted on that ground.
On the second specification the following evidence was introduced:
A police report card of the Sheriff's Office of San Bernardino County
filled in with typing showing the general description of the accused, and
a statement of his name and address in West Virginia and the words
"Crime Grand Theft (reduced to P. T.) Date: 11-28.-40." Two pic.tures of the accused are attached to this card. A letter from the secre.tary of the lodge in San Bernardino stating that he had information that
accused was involved in a holdup there in 1948 which was reduced to a
charge of carrying concealed weapons, and that the police records
showed that 9e had b~en involved in purse snatching in 1940 in West
Virginia, which was reduced to petty theft for which he served a
sentence.
Service of the charges in this masonic proceeding was made personally by the tiler of Penrhyn Lodge at Auburn, thirteen days before
the date of trial. Where an accused is within the jurisdiction of the
lodge, service should be made at least ten days before the trial, while if
he is without said jurisdiction but within the state of California, the
service must be thirty days prior to trial and may be made by mail. We
assume that Auburn, being eight miles from Penrhyn, is within the jurisdiction of Penrhyn Lodge and that the ten days service in this case was
sufficient.
However, the charges do not state masonic offenses. As often pointed
out in the past, it is the commission of an offense against the law which
is a Masonic offense and not the conviction for the same in court nor
the adjudication of the facts by a state court. In this case the adultery,
if any, was the masonic offense and not the finding of adultery by a
divorce court, and the crime set out in the second specification was the
masonic offense and not the facts of being arrested, convicted and imprisoned for it.

190

Adopted

191

192

193

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The evidence on the second specification was entirely incompetent.
The letter from the lodge secretary was admittedly pure hearsay and
would be legally such even had the secretary had actual knowledge of
the events recited. The police record was also legally hearsay and not
the authenticated record required by Section 319 of the Ordinances. The
Sheriff's Office at San Bernardino had apparently used one of their own
report cards to type in the information they had about an old petty
theft conviction in West Virginia, and this even confused the accuser
in this case so that the specification recites the conviction as having
occurred in San Bernardino. The charges make no mention of the concealed weapons charge there which was referred to by the lodge secretary in San Bernardino,
As to the first specification, Sections 319, 992 and 993 Ross' Digest
authorize the use of certified copies of records of criminal convictions in
state courts as prima facie evidence of guilt, and under Section 754,
Ross' Digest. the record of a judgment in a civil action adjudicating the
fact of guilt of adultery, as here. would be like evidence. We feel. however, that the weight, if not the admissibility, of such evidence is greatly
lessened where the civil case involved is one in whi<:h judgmnt was
granted by default and particularly where the service on the defendant
was by publication. In the divorce case involved in this trial record it is
not at all certain that the accused even knew of the divorce action
brought against him in West Virginia. He was adjudged as absent from
that state with address unknown and the summons was published in a
newspaper. The judgment in the divorce case states that he was guilty of
adultery, without specifications of time, place, persons or other details.
Taken in connection with the errors as to the second specification we feel
that the proof on the first specification is far from satisfactory to establish the masonic offense aimed at. As stated before, the charges actually
set forth no masonic offenses.
As amended charges may be brought in this case and the matter
again tried, we feel that we should mention another point.
We cannot tell from the record when accused became a Mason. The
police record states his age was 23 in 1940, and he was then living in
West Virginia. The divorce action was in 1945 and the alleged adultery
necessarily occurred prior to that time.
Last year, 1950, in Trial Record No. 1191 (Grand Lodge Proceedings, page 184 ) we held and Grand Lodge approved our report that
automatic expulsion could apply only to convictions occurring after the
accused became a Mason, and we recommended that "in the event
charges may be preferred they should charge a Masonic offense occurring either after accused had become a Mason or in the course of
his application for Masonry." We feel that any old offenses such as
petty theft and the adultery in West Virginia in this case might be met
by charging the failure to divulge them to an investigating committee if
he was questioned. If the accused herein was convicted of carrying a

concealed weapon in San Bernardino in 1948, as suggested in the correspondence herein, that might be the proper basis for charges.
As the charges here do not state properly any masonic offenses, and
as the evidence taken was incompetent and insufficient to prove the
crimes and the adultery which were apparently sought to be charged,
this conviction must be reversed.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved: That the action of Penrhyn Lodge No. 258 in expe1ling H. A. W. be reversed and set aside and the matter remanded
to that lodge for such further proceedings not inconsistent with this
report as it may desire.
Adopted

Trial Record No. 1237
Your committee on grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1237, reports as follows:
Accused L. S. M. (a member of Whittier Lodge No. 323) was
charged with unmasonic conduct based upon five specifications of petty
theft.
The charge was filed by the Junior Warden by direction of the
Master of Whittier Lodge. The Master of the Lodge presided at the
trial. The accused did not appear at the trial but wrote a letter in which
he conceded t}te truth of the specifications. The Commissioners found
the accused "guilty" of each of the specifications and fixed the penalty
at expulsion, but did not vote upon the charge of unmasonic conduct.
Under Section 956 of Ross' Digest if the Master of a Lodge directs
the Junior Warden to prefer charges against one of its members such
Master cannot preside at the trial and ordinarily a violation of this section would be so prejudicial as to require reversal. However, in this case
the guilt of the accused is admitted and it is therefore clear that no
prejudice resulted to the accused from this irregularity. For the same
reason your committee is of the opinion that the failure of the Commissions to find on the charge of unmasonic conduct is a technical error and
that the Grand Lodge should supply a finding of "guilty" on the charge
of unmasonic conduct.
We, therefore, offer and move the adoption of the following resolution:
Resolved: That in Trial Record No. 1237 a finding of "guilty..
on the charge of unmasonic conduct be and it is hereby supplied and
that the action of Whittier Lodge No. 323 in expelling L. S. M. be
and it is hereby ratified, affirmed and approved.
Adopted

Your committee believes that the provision for forfeiture of all Masonic rights and privileges in such cases requires. e~pulsion: and not

and therefore offers the following resolution:

Trial Record No. 1251
To your Committee on Grievances there has been referred Trial
Record No. 1251 involving an accused, J. R. K.
An appeal has been taken from the penalty of expulsion fixed by the
Trial Commission.
By an amended complaint, the accused was charged with unmasonic
conduct, supported by three specifications, which may be summarized
as follows:
Specification 1. That the accused, knowing that he had been
convicted of felonies on two separate occasions involving forgery
and illegal sale of liquor, answered "No" to question No. 12 in the
Application for Degrees, which reads:
"Do you know of any physical, legal, or moral reason which
would prevent you from becoming a Free Mason?":
and that the accused, throughout, wilfully concealed the facts of his
former conviction and incarceration from Norwalk Lodge No. 315,
F. & A. M.: that the accused failed to register with the Sheriff of Los
Angeles County as an ex-convict, as required by the County Ordinances:
Specification 2. That on October 17, 1930, the accused was
convicted of forgery in Texas: was sentenced to two years, and
served a term of one year and twenty-seven days pursuant thereto:
and
Specification 3. That on or about March 1, 1935, the accused
was convicted of the crime of selling liquor, a felony in the State of
Texas, was sentenced to three years in prison, and served two years,
nine months, and twenty-six days pursuant thereto.
It will be noted that Specifications 2 and 3 charge that the accused
suffered convictions of two offenses--one in 1930 and one in 1935.
Neither of said Specilkations charge the commission of the offenses for
which the accused was convicted. It has been repeatedly held by _the
Grand Lodge that a charge of being convicted of a crime is not a masonic
offense. It is the commission of the crime which should be set forth in the
speciflcation and not the conviction therefor.
There is no dispute in the record concerning the fact that the accused
was convicted of forgery in Texas on October 17, 1930 and that he likewise was convicted of selling liquor on March 1, 1935. The record also
shows that in 1935, the Governor of Texas issued a conditional pardon
to the accused for the forgery crime of 1930 and that some time during
the l 930's, (the exact date not appearing) a conditional pardon was
given for the liquor selling crime committed in 1935.
Under date of December 2, 1946, the accused made
application
for degrees in Norwalk Lodge No. 315 and was thereafter elected to,

Adopted

195

his

196

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

and received, his degrees in that Lodge. It was in that application that he
answered "No" to question 12 relating to "physical, legal, or moral
reason" which would prevent him from becoming a Free Mason.
On April 1, 1951. the present Masonic charges were preferred
against the accused. The elected Commissioners held their first meeting
on May 19, 1951, at which time a continuance was granted to June 30,
1951. In the meantime, and on June 3, 1951, the Governor of Texas
granted the accused a full pardon and restoration of citizenship for bo~h
of the crimes committed by the accused--one in 1930 and the other m
1935.
Turning now to the record relative to Specification 1 ~hargin.g the
failure to disclose the criminal conviction in answer to question 12 m the
application for degrees, we find no evidence whatsoever i~. the,,record of
any concealment by the accused other than his answer of No to question 12. There is no evidence whatsoever that any of the members of the
Investigating Committee ever inquired of accused as to prior convictions.
In this connection, we may observe that on at least two former occasions,
an effort has been made to get Grand Lodge to amend the form of the
Application for degrees by including therein a specific question rela?ng
to former criminal convictions. In both instances, Grand Lodge declined
to amend the form of the Application.
Let there be no doubt that an accused may be properly disciplined
if he fails to disclose former criminal convictions in response to a direct
question which would call for such disclosure or if his failure to disclose
same during the course of his investigation amounts to a fraudulent
concealment.
This case therefore, clearly presents the question as to whether the
mere failure ~f a petitioner to disclose prior criminal conviction~ in response to question 12 of the Application, standing alone, constitutes a
Masonic offense for which discipline may be imposed after the degrees
are received. The lodges of this jurisdiction are entitled to a clea.rcut
answer to this question for their future guidance. Y ~ur Comm1tte.e
recommends that the question be answered in the negative and that 1t
be the ruling of Grand Lodge that the mere failure of ~ petitioner to
disclose prior criminal convictions in response to question 12 of the
Application, standing alone, without other facts show~ng an actual
fraudulent concealment, does not constitute a Masonic offense for
which discipline may be imposed after the degrees are received.
During the trial of the accused, proper court records showin~ the
conviction of the accused of the crimes of forgery and sale of liquor
were introduced in evidence. Under many former rulings, such records
constitute prima facie evidence of the guilt of the accused of t.he crimes
for which he was convicted. The conviction for those crimes 1s not denied by the accused. However, the accused, through his counsel, endeavored to prove, and made an offer of proof, to the general effect that,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

197

in fact, the accused was not guilty of either of said crimes. The W orshipful Master, presiding at the trial. sustained the objections and declined to permit the Trial Commission to receive the offered evidence.
Section 314 of our Ordinances gives the accused the right to make statements in justification and extenuation. Instances are not Jacking in which
accuseds have been acquitted on a Masonic trial. although previously
convicted for the same offense in the courts of the ]and. The ruling,
therefore, was clearly erroneous and that alone would require a reversal
·
of the conviction.
Your Committee, therefore, offers and moves the adoption of the following resolution:
. Be It Resolved: That the conviction of the accused, J. R. K.,
and the fixing of the penalty at expulsion, be, and the same hereby
is, reversed and the matter dismissed.
Be It Further Resolved: That the reversal and dismissal hereby
ordered shall not be a bar to the prosecution of other charges
against accused based upon facts showing an actual fraudulent
concealment of the criminal convictions prior to the application for
degrees if proof thereof be available.
Be It Further Resolved: That it is the sense of Grand Lodge that
the mere failure of a petitioner to disclose prior criminal convictions in response to question 12 of the Application for degrees,
standing alone, and without other facts showing an actual fraudulent concealment, do not constitute a Masonic offense for which
discipline may be imposed after the degrees are received.
Adopted •

Trial Record No. 1256
To your Committee on Grievances has been referred Trial Record
No. 1256 involving T. M. C., a member of Palos Verdes Lodge No. 389.
Said T. M. C. is presently a resident of Scottsbluff, Nebraska. He is
there engaged in the liquor business as an officer of Terry Carpenter,
Inc. This corporation holds a license regularly issued by the State of
Nebraska for the "off sale" of liquor-in other words, it is a liquor
store. It does not engage in the sale of liquor for consumption on the
premises.
The Grand Jurisdiction of Nebraska, in whose :jurisdiction the said
T. M. C. resides, has made it a Masonic offense for a Mason to engage
in the sale, as a beverage, of intoxicating liquor, including beer and wine.
The actions of T. M. C. are therefore a violation of the Masonic Law
of Nebraska.
Masonic charges were preferred against the said T. M. C. in Nebraska, due and proper service was made of the charges, and the said
T. M. C. declined to appear, claiming that the Grand Lodge of Ne-

199

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

braska had no jurisdiction over him. A Masonic trial was had in d11e
and proper fashion and resulted in the expulsion of T. M. C. A copy of
the record of said trial in Nebraska has been flied with the Grand Secretary and referred to your Grievance Committee.
Section 210 of our Ordinances prohibits a Mason in California from
engaging in the saloon business or as a barkeeper except in connection
with, and as a part of. the operation of a bona flde hotel or restaurant.
Under our ordinances, it is not an offense for a Mason to engage in
the so-called "off sale" of liquor, either as a wholesaler or a retailer.
Our ordinances contain no prohibition against a Mason operating a
liquor store where liquor is not consumed on the premises. This, however. is a Masonic offense in Nebraska and for it the said T. M. C. has
been duly and regularly ordered expelled by the Grand Jurisdiction of
Nebraska.
Section 331 of our Ordinances provides as follows:
"Whenever it shall appear by the record of conviction from another Masonic jurisdiction, recognized by us, that a member of one
of our Lodges, resident in such jurisdiction, has been suspended or
expelled for unmasonic conduct in such jurisdiction while a resident
thereof. it shall be the duty of the Junior Warden of the Lodge in
this jurisdiction of which he is a member to prefer charges against
him for the acts and conduct alleged in the charges preferred in the
foreign jurisdiction and of which he was there convicted, and the
same proceedings shall thereupon be had as in ordinary cases: provided that the record of conviction of the foreign jurisdiction shall
be received on the trial as prima facie evidence of the guilt of the
brother of such acts and conduct."
In the opinion of your Committee, Sec. 331 contemplates that the unmasonic conduct alleged in the foreign jurisdiction must be of an offense
which would constitute unmasonic conduct in this jurisdiction. Ordinarily, and in the absence of proof of extenuating circumstances, we
would extend full faith and credit to a foreign adjudication of unmasonic
conduct. Nebraska has an unquestioned right to deny Masonic privileges to a sojourning Mason who violates its Masonic law just as California reserves and exercises jurisdiction over Masons sojourning in
this jurisdiction.
However, since it is clear that the so-called "off sale" of liquor is not
a masonic offense under our law, it would be an idle act for Palos Verdes
Lodge No. 389 to proceed with a trial of the accused which is predicated
upon his conviction in Nebraska. If the Palos Verdes Lodge should
proceed with such a trial and it should result in disciplinary action
against the accused, your Committee would be compelled to advise
Grand Lodge that such disciplinary action should be reversed.
We therefore offer and move the adoption of the following resolution:

Resolved: That the record of the trial and expulsion of T. M. C.
by the Grand Lodge of Nebraska be received and flied by the Grand
Secretary; and
Be It Further Resolved: That such adjudication of expulsion be
declared to be without force or effect within this grand jurisdiction
only because it is based upon facts which do not constitute a ma·
sonic offense in this grand jurisdiction.
The report of the Committee on Grievances failed of adoption.
The Deputy Grand Master, presiding at the time, ordered the record
sent to Palos Verdes Lodge No. 389 for proceedings in accordance with
Section 331.

. REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CENTENNIAL
ARRANGEMEN TS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Committee submitted a progress report to the brethren of Grand
Lodge at the 1950 Annual Communication, and recommended that an
appropriate record of the Centennial be compiled under the supervision
of the Grand Secretary and published in a volume similar to that in
which were set forth the Proceedings of the Diamond Jubilee. This
recommendation was referred to the Committees on Policy and General
Purposes and on Finance (page 138). The Committee on Finance concurred in the recommendation and provided that the cost of same should
"be paid from. funds in the hands of the Centennial Committee if any
surplus remain after payment of all expenses, if not, that the cost be paid
from Grand Lodge General Fund."
The lodges of the jurisdiction per capita payments amounted to
$140,879.00, of which $81,315.92 was expended, leaving an unexpended
balance of $59,563.08. After earmarking an estimated amount for cost
of publication of the Centennial volume, the Committee recommended
that the balance be refunded to the respective lodges, pro rata, ( 33%%
each). which has been done.
Nothing was left undone which might reasonably have been done
for entertainment and hospitality. In the Centennial Appendix, Proceedings of 1950, the highlights of the celebration and official record
of special addresses which were delivered by the Grand Master and
Distinguished Guests were set forth. There was also a brief account
of the activities of the Committee and a list of Distinguished Guests.
Individual appreciations of those who participated in any capacity will
be contained in the Centennial volume. This is in keeping with the
thought of the Committee that "No matter how magnificent are the
possibilities of a project it can be marred by failure of or incomplete
discharge of those functions which seem minute or inconsequential."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON COLUMBIA TEMPLE
RESTORATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Columbia Temple Restoration is pleased to
submit herewith a report of its activities for the past year:
Pursuant to authorization of this Grand Lodge at the last Annual
Communication, the Committee proceeded to furnish and equip the
Columbia Lodge Room with furniture of design and appearance as that
used in the original Temple. By the 1st of April 1951, the Temple was
complete in this respect and ready for use. Accordingly, the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Arthur Paulsen, requested Tuolumne Lodge No.
8 of Sonora, California to confer the first Third degree in the newly
constructed and furnished Temple. As 8 o'clock on April 21,'1951, the
Lodge was opened by Worshipful Master Wallace E. Ware and his
corps of Officers, who conferred the Third degree on Brother George
Alexander Murphy. Past Grand Master, Brother Leon Whitsell was
received as a representative of the Grand Master and acted as Master
of Ceremonies for the occasion. .
The Committee wishes to express its appreciation to all the members
of Tuolumne Lodge No. 8 for their co-operation and support during the
construction of the Temple and in the assisting of the various activities
which followed.
The following is a statement of the capital expenditure for the fiscal
year ending July 31, 1951:

34.50
In accordance wtih instructions from the Grand Master, a fire proof
vault was authorized to be placed in the basement of the Temple to
store the valuable records of the Grand Lodge. Brothers Donald Beach
Kirby and Harold Engle were designated as the Architect and Engineer,
respectively. The work was awarded to George Bates, Contractor, according to the plans herewith attached, for the sum of $6,766.00. The
work was started July 26, 1951 and completed Sept. 28, 1951. No expenditures for this account were made during the fiscal year. From August 1, 1951 to date, $4,625.48 has been expended for the construction.
During the past year, a new heating system has been installed and
also an air conditioning unit which makes the Lodge Room comfortable
at all seasons of the year.
The care. operation, maintenance and use of the Temple at all times,

is subject to the direction and supervision of three members of this

by Brother Ray Irwin, who has done an excellent job, consequently, the
building is in perfect repair and is available for inspection at all times.
The property of the Temple has been accurately inventoried and a
strict method of accountability has been put into effe<;t.
Originally, this Committee recommended that the Lodge Room floor
be left uncovered, but after six months of use, it has been found to be

is attached hereto.
A letter received from the Director of Beaches and Parks of the
State of California, dated August 31, 1951, requested that the appearance of the building ·b e "toned down," that is, remove the mortar and
effiorescence caused by crystalline powder from the used brick veneer on
the exterior of the building. It is recommended that this work be done
at an estimated cost of $500.00.
It was originally intended that the first floor room b~ used as an
assembly room for Lodges using the facilities of the Temple, but is now
felt by the Committee that a better use of the room can be made by its
being converted into a Masonic Museum to store and display all of the
historic paraphernalia, which can be assembled. It is recommended that
a member be appointed to this Committee who can give his full time to
the gathering, classifying, arranging and displaying of all this material.
The above suggestion is prompted by the fact that so many have visited
the new Masonic Temple in Columbia that a permanent Museum of this
type would not only provide a safe storing place for all this paraphernalia, ·b ut would provide much of interest for those visiting the Temple.
Since the formal opening of the Temple, seven lodges have conferred
degrees in the Temple, and it is hoped that more Lodges throughout the
state, will make use of its facilities. More publicity has been planned in
order that all Lodges will be more familiar with the use of the Temple
and its facilities. It is recommended to the Grand Master that two additional members be added to the Committee from different parts of the
state to help carry out this program.
Permission was granted to the First Presbyterian Church of Columbia to use the lower hall in which to conduct services during the time
their building was being restored from damage due to fire. A letter of
appreciation was received from them for this privilege.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

.'Y.~ur Co~mittee on Lodge Financing submits herewith a report of its
activities dunng the Masonic year just ended.
Literally hundreds of communications have been received, many of
them concerning Lodge activities outside the jurisdiction of this particular Committee, which nevertheless had to be acknowledged and/or
referred to proper channels.
.
During. the current year your Committee has been called on to approve or disapprove more than sixty applications, pursuant to Sections
78 and 152 of the Constitution and Ordinances.
A complete file on every case which has been submitted to the Committee, including all the details of the request, exhibits and pertinent
d~ta required for guidance in arriving at a decision, comments by Committee members, together with a copy of written consent, is mailed to the
Grand Secretary's office as a part of the official records df this Grand
Lodge.
While severe material restrictions have been imposed on the building of certain types of structures since the Korean incident developd
more than a year ago. the Defense Production Authority of the Department of Commerce has considered it in the public interest and important
enough to the welfare and preservation of our way of life to grant priorities for the construction of nine new Masonic Temples in California,
six of which have already received your Committee's approval.
Although this report primarily concerns the work of the Committee
for the current Masonic year, it should be noted that since the end of
hostilities of World War II, thirty new Masonic Temples have been
built or are now being built in California. The great majority of them
have been built with the aid of membership donated labor, and only
three or four of the Lodges have found it necessary to resort to a small
amount of outside financing to complete their temples. All the other
Temple properties are owned free and clear. In this connection it is
worthy to report that the Boards of Directors of the thirty Temple Associations concerned have discovered that the same vision, faith, courage
and intelligence employed in the building of these Lodge homes are required in the operation of them. Most of the new Temples are going
concerns, paying their way. and in most every instance are centers of
comm.unity activities. Naturally. wherever Masons have banded together
to build a Temple with their own hands, there has been a renaissance
of fundamental Masonic spirit, welding all together in stronger ties of
brotherly love and affection.
Despite the Temple building activity of recent years, there remains
throughout California a critical lack of proper housing for Masonic
Lodges. For this reason, many lodges lacking adequate financial re-

GRAND LODGE OF CALlfORNIA

205

sources and desiring to create long range programs to acquire necessary
funds for future building i)rograms, have appealed to your Committee
for permission to purchase building sites. and to incorporate hall associations to be used as vehicles for raising funds and for handling the
building and management of Temple properties. Your Committ~e·s
attitude has been to cooperate to the fullest extent. at the same time
pointing out the pitfalls of hastily conceived and inadequately financed
building programs, and the tremendous responsibility of operating and
maintaining Temple properties after they have been completed.
Your Committee deems it a real privilege to have been able to grant
permission to commence construction on several new Masonic Temples
in California this year. It is a further pleasure to report that the financing
of all of these buildings will require no fixed debt, aside from the noninterest bearing loan made by the Lodge to its own Temple Association.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTION MONTH OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee is pleased to advise you that much interest has
been demonstrated throughout the Jurisdiction in the matter of this
Observance during the year just concluded. The Brethren throughout
the Jurisdiction have responded well to the various requests directed to
them by the Committee, and we wish to take this opportunity to thank
them for their support and interest. The Inspectors of the various districts were also of considerable assistance, and we wish to express our
thanks to them.
The reports received from the Lodges to date indicate a total of 112
open meetings, at which there was an attendance of 15,270 in addition
to 296 closed meetings which were attended by 20, l 43. This makes a
total of 408 meetings, with a reported total attendance of 35,413.
In view of the fact that Constitution Month Observance in California
has now become an accepted tradition, which is due in large part to the
efforts of this Grand Lodge, your Com1J1.ittee is of the opinion that there
should be a reorganization of the activities of the Committee in order to
permit its work to become more effective. We especially make reference
to the efforts of Grand Master Paulsen to standardize the work of
committees of this sort, and to co-ordinate their efforts in order that
the maximum results might be obtainable. We make particular reference
to this report, and request that it be given serious consideration by future
committees to whom is designated the purpose of this Committee.
Your Committee is also of the opinion that its efforts should not be
confined entirely to the month of September, but that an effort should
be made throughout the entire year to acquaint the members of the
Fraternity with its work and procedure. We suggest also that some
thought be given to the preparation of a booklet by the Grand Lodge
for distribution to the membership, which booklet should contain the
Constitution of the United States, the Declaration of Independence,
and other similar documents, together with the necessary introduction
and comments. In this way, your Committee is of the opinion that the
full import of Constitution Month Observance will be impressed upon
the Fraternity generally.
Your Committee has experienced some little difficulty in securing
sufficient speakers of ability to acquaint the membership with the Constitution and its position in our body politic, and it is our further suggestion that an effort be made to further co-ordinate the efforts of the
Committee along the lines of securing a list of capable speakers who
might be available to the various Subordinate Lodges throughout the
State. We note, however, the increased interest that is manifest through-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

213

out the State on the part of the Subordinate Lodges in observing the
birth of the Constitution. This augers well for the future, for the Constitution of the United States has been a powerful force in the lives of
all of the people of the world, and of all generations of people ever since
its adoption. Ours is ·a government of laws and not of men. With such
a system jof government and law established in the world, even though
only one nation enjoyed it and prospered under it, no aspiration for a
similar way of life in any part of the world is futile-and it is the worldwide understanding and appreciation of that fact which has given
universal importance to the Constitution of the United States ever since
its adoption.
As America faces the future let us pause to recollect that the farseeing vision of our constitutional fathers resulted in an instrument of
government which no foe of human rights has penetrated and survival
of which has met every challenge to the natural rights of man. Our
Fraterntiy is to be commended for the efforts it has heretofore expended
in acquainting the peoples of this State with the provisions of this
immortal document. Our most formidable fortress of defense in time
of stress still remains the Constitution of the United States.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM R. McKAY
JAMES T. FRASER
LEET. MULLEN
DUDLEY H. NEBECKER
WILLIAM P. SELF

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC INFORMATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Information reports as follows:
Your Committee has continued its policy of progressing slowly as
indicated in its report of 1947. the policy of observing the results of one
step before taking another. Four years have been occupied in issuing,
with the approval of Grand Lodge, the four booklets now ~eing presented to all candidates: the Address to the Candidate: the Book of the
Entered Apprentice, the Book of the Fellow Craft, and the Book of the
Master Mason. These have given general satisfaction and it is believed
that they have accomplished, in part at least, their objective of gain~ng
the interest of the Candidate and of giving him considerable information
about the Fraternity.
Last year, your Committee presented for approval a manuscript en-

214

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

titled "707 Questions and Answers about Freemasonry," which was
ref erred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, with the intention that such Committee would have a year to review that manuscript before making its recommendation to Grand Lodge at this present
Communication. It is well to repeat what was said in the last annual report of your Committee, that questions and answers are only questions
and answers; they have their shortcomings; but they do fill a want in
many quarters, because they present facts in a way which is more helpful to some than if set forth in solid expository form.

that time, it has failed to educate its members on phases which it now
thinks important, it is not likely to do so by any quick process or short
easy procedure.

The volume of this proposed publication is rather great, approximately 100 pages, and may impress some as excessive, but the thought
behind it is that such a book will serve as a permanent text-book to be
used in educational work by the lodges, for it is probable that the most
active program of instruction would not exhaust these 707 Questions and
Answers in less than two or three years, at the end of which they may be
repeated with as much value as before.
The Questions and Answers are divided into various subjects, such
as History, Masonic Literature, Rituals, the Three Degrees, Rites of
Freemasonry, Masonic Jurisprudence, Freemasonry and Religion, Freemasonry and Roman Catholicism, Freemasonry and Mormonism and
Miscellaneous. The subject of History is broken down into the subheads
of the Origin of Freemasonry, the Gothic Operative Era, the Transition into Speculative Masonry, the Foundation of the Grand Lodge of
England, European Masonry. the division into Ancients and Moderns,
arid Freemasonry in America. All of the Answers are intended to be
factual and accurate and to reflect the conclusions of the most reliable
modem authorities.

It is embarrassing to have to admit that there is not now available a
single, short, readable and reliable history of Freemasonry in print. Four
and seven volume works are likely to discourage the beginner and shorter
works have either been incomplete or have, one by one, retired to the
shelves of second hand book stores. Accordingly, the next undertaking
planned by your Committee is an Essay on Freemasonry which will give
a comprehensive view of the subject in about 150 pages. The size and
nature of the work is such, however, that its presentation to Grand
Lodge will probably be accompanied by the recommendation that it be
distributed at a _price which will return the cost of printing.
At the present day, people, including Freemasons, are disposed to
be impatient, to ask for quick, easy solutions of their problems; those who
want to buckle down to hard work and patient and sustained effort are
the exceptions. It must be remembered that Freemasonry is not a simple
subject; it is the development of several centuries and the work of many
hands. The Grand Lodge of California is now a century old, and, if in

215

Those who really want to understand the problem and to find a solution for it, should first enquire what has been the experience of this
Grand Lodge in its attempts to promote Masonic Education. It is available in Committee reports and Grand Masters' reports, appearing in
Grand Lodge proceedings over the past 36 years. If one has not the time
for such research, one may again read the 1947 report of your Committee where that experience was digested. Since 1915, no less than six
different plans have been tried. Again and again programs started with
zeal and enthusiasm came, in a few years, to complete stops. The first
of these occupied ten years; the second, seven years; the third, five years;
the fourth, three years; the fifth, eight years, and the present plan, beginning in 1947 is now completing its fourth year.
It is based on the fundamental thought that the few weeks while the
candidate is receiving his degrees and when he is in a receptive, enquiring and curious frame of mind, is the critical period when Masonic
information will be avidly absorbed; that this should be a rputine procedure like the instructions in the candidate's lectures; and that whatever
is imparted should be material previously approved by Grand Lodge.
An educational program, if it accomplishes anything, must involve much
effort on the part of the lodges. Some lodges may not care to make this
effort, but those which adopt and consistently follow a set program will
find that it provides work for more members and keeps them interested
in the lodge. lq time, but not immediately, it will provide us with a membership much better informed on the character and purposes of Freemasonry.
Your Committee wishes to express its sincere appreciation for the
helpful cooperation of the Most Worshipful Grand Secretary and his
Assistant in attending to the printing and distribution of the literature
issued by your Committee. At the last Annual Communication, the Committee on Finance, instead of appropriating funds directly for your Committee's printing, added the amount to the printing appropriation of the
Grand Secretary, thus increasing his burdens. Your Committee wishes
the Grand Secretary to know that your Committee was not accessory
before the fact, but, now that it has been done, your Committee approves
of it.
Your Committee recommends:
1. That, subject to approval by Grand Lodge of the "707 Questions
and Answers about Freemasonry," $5,000 be appropriated or added to
the Grand Secretary's printing appropriation for the publication of this
book; that copies thereof be distributed free to each lodge in number
approximating 1 % of the membership of such lodge, with a minimum of

216

3 copies to each lodge; and that additional copies be sold to lodges or
members at approximately the cost to be estimated by the Grand Secretary.
2. That your Committee be continued, and that there be appropriated, for the general expense of your Committee during the ensuing Masonic year, the sum of $500.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DE MOLAY
.To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is the 5th Annual Report of the Committee on De Molay. This
Committee has carefully followed the plan which was approved by our
Grand Lodge in 1946, namely:
"It is a plan of education and coordination rather than one of sponsorship. Our plan would create a group of men who would act as coordinators between De Molay and Masonry in our State. From time to
time they would be authorized to bring to our Lodges the message and
needs of De Molay. to enlist the aid of men who would be willing to
assist in the t11ork and to keep a watchful eye on the activities of De
Molay. Finally they would report annually to Grand Lodge the progress
of that Order in California." ·
The work of your Committee on De Malay is progressing satisfactorily, yet each member feels there is so ·much to be done to cause
Masons individually to become more interested in this excellent program for youth which the De Malay offers. The need is still great for
active advisors who are capable and interested.
The Chairman of this Committee from its inception was Charles E.
Ustenwalter of Los Angeles, under whose competent and loving leadership the group has worked in harmony.
Brother Listenwalter found it best, after many, many years of
Masonic service, not to continue such a heavy work schedule and, therefore, requested the Most Worshipful Grand Master to release him from
this committee. This was done with regret.
There have been two additions to the Committee, Brothers Edwin
R. Brooks of Richmond and Alvin E. Clark of Sacramento, whose territory is from Oakland and Sacramento to the Oregon border. They are
getting excellent results in that area.

At 4.15 P.M. Grand Lodge was called off until 10:00 A.M. Wednesday morning.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Cal.ifomia:
Your Committee on By-Laws have carefully examined the one
hundred and eleven amendments to By-Laws submitted during the past
year. It is apparent that Masters are continuing to give attention to the
By-Laws of their Lodges and the necessary amendments are presented,
adopted and sent to Grand Lodge for approval.
In 1946 our Committee called attention to the error of including the
contribution to the Masonic Homes in the amount of the fees charged for
the Degrees, or in the affiliation fee. We feel that our urging in the
Committee reports, that study be given to the By-Laws of the Lodges,
has brought about a much better condition in this respect. The Committee's work has increased considerably, but it has been worthwhile.
In 1943, thirty-eight amendments were submitted-1944 ninetyone-1945 eighty-one-1946 one hundred and ten-1947 two hundred
and forty-one-1948 two hundred and eighteen-1950 fifty-eight-and
this year as stated--one hundred and eleven.
A noted baseball manager said that if there were no errors, the game
would lose much of its interest to the spectators. In all operations
whether fraternal or business, errors occur. It has been the policy of the
Grand Secretary's office to assist in every way possible to see that the
amendments when finally submitted, were proper as to form. In reviewing the amendments we have followed this same policy. Errors that
were inadvertently overlooked by the Grand Secretary and the Grand
Master, we have in many cases, been able to correct in conference with
the Lodge representatives in attendance at the Grand Lodge. We have
never emphasized these problems. In 1947 we did report-"During the
past year one Lodge discovered that its By-Laws stated and required
a certain amount for the Three Degrees. For a number of years this
Lodge had only been charging approximately one-half this amount. A
number of other mistakes came to light this year concerning other
Lodges.
"Our Committee join with the Grand Secretary in urging a careful
reading of the By-Laws by Lodge Officers. The Installation Ceremony
instructs the Master to see that the By-Laws of his Lodge are strictly
complied with. H~ should read them carefully when he takes office."
It is further our recollection about then we learned that two Lodges
were unable to find their By-Laws as they had been missing for some
years. How they complied with the requirement that every person
Raised to the Degree of Master Mason in the Lodge, oi elected to be a
member thereof, shall sign its By-Laws, is a mystery. They promptly
adopted a new set of By-Laws.
In 1948 we worked out corrections as to the minimum amount to be
charged for the Degrees. No emphasis has been directed to By-Laws

220 .

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

sent back to a Lodge for correct action. Ross' Digest contains a form of
certificate which was prepared to assist in making the amendments to
By~Laws, and we feel that the results accomplished have been helpful
and corrected situations that needed attention.
This year we have corrected errors in amendments submitted as to
dates. errors in stating the correct amount of money where there was a
variance in the amendments. certificates not signed by the Secretary.
etc. Ross' Digest supports a ruling of Grand Master Filmer ( 1913) that
an increase of dues adopted. does not take effect until the end of that
quarter. Two amendments involve this point. One amendment had been
approved as to the prior effect of the increase. and the other held with
Ross' Digest that it could not take effect until the end of the quarter.
We have approved both amendments, but on condition that the increase
takes effect at the end of the quarter.
Two amendments read "and for affiliation the sum of Ten Dollars,
except that the affiliation fee shall be Ten Dollars if the demit accompanying the application is issued by this Lodge or a Lodge of this jurisdiction." The correspondence and our conferences clarified the fact
that the Lodge means an affiliation fee of the same amount, for all
Brothers affiliating with the Lodge whether of this jurisdiction or any
other jurisdiction. Even though strangely worded the purpose is proper
and we have approved the amendments.
The Grand Master applied common sense and good judgment and
granted a request to change the meeting place of a Lodge although all
technical by-law requirements could not be met. The question is now
mute and the proper result was accomplished. Our Committee concur in
the action followed by the Grand Master.
All the amendments are listed here as in the Grand Secretary's Report except four-San Pasquale No. 452, Charter Rock No. 410, Sisson
No. 310, and Vallee de France No. 329.
With the corrections made we now approve all the amendments to
the By-Laws submitted as being proper, certified and in accordance with
masonic law. They also have the approval of the Grand Master and the
Grand Secretary.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Special Committee on Memorial Building continued its work as
instructed by this Grand Lodge. The complexion of the Committee's
thinking of necessity is altered by economic conditions and Government
restrictions which prevent construction of buildings for Fraternal use.
We have continued to track down every lead we get and it has developed a substantial record for continued consideration. We have under
consideration at this time several parcels of land with improvements
presently on them. To thoroughly investigate these properties takes
time and much effort for we are not only faced with the possible cost of
demolition but your Committee is giving full consideration to the possi- .
bility of rebuilding an old structure for our use. While there are several
properties that could be made suitable to comply with the recommendations as stated by this Grand Lodge in 1948, 1949 and 1950, we are not
ready to recommend any single parcel. We, therefore, recommend that
the Memorial Buildin~ Committee be continued and that this Grand
Lodge, at this Session, consider the following recommendations:
1. Because of the continued growth of this Grand Lodge an
effort be made to hold the next five Annual .Communications, commencing with the year 1952, in the San Francisco Civic Auditorium, or some other suitable meeting place, subject to approval
of the Grand Master.
2. That this Grand Lodge vote a 50c per member annual per
capita tax for the purpose of establishing a Memorial Building Fund
so that when building restrictions are lifted and it is determined to
proceed with a Memorial Building sufficient funds will be on hand
to be able to adequately finance such a project.
3. That should future conditions or circumstances develop
which would make it unwise to proceed with such a project as a
result of facilities becoming available to this Grand Lodge through
some other means or program of planning that the Memorial Building Fund referred to in number 1 above revert to the general funds
of Grand Lodge, thus, in effect, increasing reserves for contingencies or reducing future per capita assessments.
Respectfully submitted,

Loms SuTTER

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
MEMORIAL SERVICE

To the.Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
· There has bee~ no change during the past year of the membership
on the Special Taxation Committee.
The Committee has continued to advise subordi~ate lodges and the
committees and various agencies of Grand Lodge respecting their taxation problems. We have given advice to the Boards of Relief and Employment with respect to their voluntarily coming under the Social Security Act, following our report of last year in which we advised that the
Act had been amended to allow charitable institutions to elect to come
under its terms. With respect to such charitable employers, the Social
Security Act is now on the same basis as the State Employment Act
which also allows voluntary acceptance of the Act.
It was expected that there would be many rules issued by the Internal Revenue Department governing and regulating the manner, method
and effect of such voluntary election, but no such rules have yet been
published.
We wish to again remind the subordinate lodges that they must
make a report of all employees (except ritualistic officers) whose wages
are more than $50.00 per calendar quarter for both the State Employment Act and the Federal Social Security Act and to pay the taxes
therefore. We make this observation because we are still r_eceiving reports from some lodges indicating they have never made such reports
and have become subject to penalties.
If there is any appreciable change made in the interpretation of the
amendments to the Social Security Act in the long expected rules and
regulations to be issued, we will make a special report to the Grand
Master.
·
Respectfully submitted,

R. p. WISECARVER
