REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
The rapidity with which time passes has been commented upon by
the sages of all ages. Yet the operation of the human mind is such that
each generation must make the discovery for itself. It is startling to us
that it has been such a little while since we last met here. The earth has
completed another revolution around the sun and another year has
passed into immeasurable time.
·
In the brief period of a year the Great Architect of the universe has
seen flt, in his infinite wisdom, to call 270 members of this Grand Lodge
to the Celestjal Lodge above. The majority of our lodges suffered no
loss and for this we are indeed grateful. But the angel of death laid a
heavy hand upon others. Alhambra Lodge No. 322 suffered the greatest
loss-losing six. Three lodges--Washington Lodge No. 20, South Gate
Lodge No. 320, and Willits Lodge No. 353, lost four each. Ten lodges
lost three each; forty-one lodges lost two each and one-hundred-forty
lodges lost one each.
The loyalty and devotion with which men serve this fraternity is
demonstrated by the number of years in which many of our deceased
brethren gave of their time and substance to further its interests. Archibald Thompson Kerr of Chico Lodge No. 111 was a Master Mason for
70 years. Andie Lester Bonham of Valley Lodge No. 135 served for 66
years. Charles Eben Flye of Washington Lodge No. 20 and LeWis
Harmon Barker of Palo Alto ·L odge No. 346 devoted 64 years each to
Masonry. Of those who have passed since our last report 174 served at
least a quarter of a century and 27 served a half century or more.
A cloud of gloom has descended upon one of our oldest and most
respected lodges-Summit Lodge No. 112 of Knights Ferry. In its long
and honorable career this lodge, chartered in 1857, has never had as
many as fifty members, and most of the time less than forty, so the loss

230

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

of even one member was keenly felt. Since the last communication of
this Grand Lodge three of its Past Masters and three of its members have
entered the last sleep, thus losing in one year approximately one-eighth
of its membership. Time does not permit us to give in detail the faithful
work that these brethren have contributed, but our sympathy and understanding go to the brethren of Summit Lodge and our sincere hope that
they will be spared a repetition of such sorrow.

BoYD B. RAKESTRAW

FRANK MACPHERSON SMITH

Death did on April 7, 1951 write the final chapter on the brilliant
career of Past Grand Master Frank M. Smith, who died at his Pasadena
home, 765 Old Mill Road, after weeks of illness.
Serving this Grand Lodge during one of the most trying periods of
its history, he made a record that it will be difficult to surpass.
Later in this Memorial Service the Most Worshipful Lloyd E. Wilson, Past Grand Master, will deliver a special eulogy to the memory of
this beloved friend and distinguished Mason.
ARTHUR EDWARD TANGEMAN

The memories of men are faulty and it may be for this reason that
heart attacks appear to be on the increase as so many of our brethren·
have been stricken. Such a fate befell Art Tangeman May 13, 1951 at his
home in San Dimas.
At the age of 31 Art petitioned San Dimas Lodge No. 428 and was
elected November 6, 1914. He was initiated on the night of his election,
passed December 4th of the same year and raised January 2, 1915. His
Masonic activities covered every phase of lodge work and he served
·w ith distinction in the Oriental chair. In 1925 he was appointed Inspector
of the 94th District and for a quarter of a century rendered excellent
service in that important office.
Brother Tangeman was born February 17, 1883 at Newton, Kansas.
He attended the public schools and coming to California at 13 years of
age completed his education here, graduating from Pomona College in
1909.
With the exception of the time he served as a soldier in World War
I, his entire adult life was given to the citrus industry. He was an important grower and was a director in several citrus packing and selling
organizations.
Arthur married Miss Ruth Pierce October 16, 1923. She survives
him. His other survivors are two brothers-Walter E. Tangeman, Past
Master of San Dimas Lodge and Ralph Tangeman of Pomona.
Arthur Tangeman was a faithful worker in the vineyard of Masonry.
His passing leaves a void in our ranks but we are better because he
passed this way.

231

Boyd B. Rakestraw passed away Saturday afternoon March 24th
following a heart attack which came upon him while working in his
garden. He was taken to the hospital where he soon seemed well enough
to be returned to his home. A few hours later he fell into the sleep from
which there is no awaking.
Boyd was born October 12, 1890 at Nebraska City. Nebraska. His
father was Supervisor of Indian Schools, and as a youngster Boyd traveled extensively with him in Oregon, Washington and California. He
entered the University of California in 1910 but was forced to leave to ·
assist his mother who had lost her sight. After working two years for
the Southern Pacific Railroad he again entered college, working his way,
and helping his widowed mother. He graduated with a Bachelor of
Science degree in 1916.
In 1919 he became Assistant Director of the University Extension
and in 1931 was appointed Assistant to the Comptroller of the University of California. In connection with the University Extension, as a
hobby, he published the Wheeler Hall Productions-mostly motion pictures-for the public. Many national activities occupied his attention,
among them the Association of Film Libraries, National University
Extension Association, Business Officers of Universities and the International Conference of Supervised Correspondence Study. In World
War II he was business manager of the Division of Statistics and Planning of the War Industries Board of Washington, D. C. Recently he
made trips to Japan where he established Extension Division Work.
He served. as Master of Henry Morse Stephens Lodge No. 541 in
1944 and was instrumental in organizing the Berkeley High Twelve
Club and was president of the National Organization. He was a trustee
of the Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley from 1944 until the time of his
death. He was an enthusiastic Mason and faithfully served his lodge
and the Grand Lodge. He endeared himself to all by his friendliness,
fine character, wise decisions and fine fellowship.
The funeral was conducted Tuesday afternoon March 27th from the
Congregational Church of Berkeley, of which he was a member. Joint
services were held by the Reverend V. Loper and the officers of the
lodge.
His wife Josie, and their three daughters, Mary, Frances, and Janice,
and the many relatives have the most sincere sympathy of this Grand
Lodge in the loss of such a wonderful husband, father and friend. The
world has lost much in his passing but his presence among us left much
of great benefit and he also left a memory that is deeply treasured.
REYNOLD EDWARD PEARCE BLIGHT

At eleven P. M. September 4, 1951, Masonry lost one of its most
ardent supporters in the passing of Reynold E. Blight. His physical

232

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OP THE

<:ondition had been deteriorating for several years yet his death came
as a severe shock to his many friends and brethren.
Reynold Blight was born May 19, 1879 in Torrington, Devonshire,
England. At an early age he moved to Toronto, Canada and received
his education in the public schools of that city. He then transferred his
activities to New York City, remaining there until 1903 when he came
to California, locating in the city of San Francisco. A year later he
decided to make Los Angeles his home and maintained his residence in
that city for the remainder of his life.
By profession an expert accountant, he held many offices of responsibility and trust in the field of accountancy not only in Los Angeles but
also in the state and in national organizations. He was Dean of the
Southwestern University School of Commerce, Accounts and Finance.
Some of the most prominent business men of Southern California were
his pupils, and it was in this activity that he probably did most to mold
the lives of young men. These men now proudly recall that in many
classes Reynold did not mention commercialism at all but spent the
entire period in lectures on philosophy, religion, history and ethics, and
they readily admit that these lectures have been a guide and an inspiration for them through life. He held executive positions in many large
corporations.
Reynold Blight was a profound student of religion and for several
years was pastor of the Church of the People. He was a lay minister of
the Episcopal Church and his services were eagerly sought by churches
and organizations for lectures on civic, social, ethical and religious
topics. He was an authority on the esoteric significance of ancient religions and wrote much on this subject. A prolific writer, he did during
his career publish several magazines, and in 1923 was called to Washington to do important work in the educational program of the Supreme
Council of the Scottish Rite, as well as to edit the New Age Magazine
and other publications of the Council.
His social responsibilities he took seriously and was a member of the
Los Angeles City Board of Education for four years. He was a member
of the Board of Library Commissioners for many years and the splendid
library system now enjoyed by the City of Los Angeles was largely due
to his efforts. He served the state of California as State Franchise Commissioner.

It was only natural that a man of his capabilities, knowledge and .
understanding should gravitate to Freemasonry. He was made a Mason
in Golden State Lodge No. 358 in 1913 and in 1930 demitted to form
Liberal Arts Lodge No. 677 in the then thinly settled community of
Westwood. He was the second Master of the lodge. His ability was

233

recognized by the Grand Lodge and for many years he served as chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Education. The articles
which he wrote during that period are now a part of the libraries of
many of us. He was Grand Orator in 1934 and for years was a member
of ·Grand Lodge Masonic Homes Endowment Board. He joined the
Scottish Rite Bodies in 1914, was given the rank and decoration of
Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in 1919, and coroneted a
33rd Degree Mason four years later.
Reynold Blight was the personification of all that Masonry holds
dear. He was a clear-thinking, right-acting, broad-minded man; an
idealist with his head in the clouds but his feet firmly on the ground.
We leave him in the loving care, goodness and mercy of our Supreme
Grand Master and thank Him that Reynold was one of us.
JAMES KENNETT FISK

Masonic and American Legion funeral rites were held Friday September 14, 1951 for James Kennett Fisk in Oakland's Scottish Rite Temple. Brother Fisk, who had suffered from a heart ailment for several
years, died at Veterans Administration Hospital in Oakland Monday
night September 10th.
Born in Helena, Montana, he came to California with his parents,
was educated in this state, graduating from the University of California
in 1905. He later became assistant recorder of the University and held
that position for ten years.
Upon the entry of the United States in World War I he entered the
armed services. becoming an aviator in the Army Signal Corps. When
the Congress of the United States granted a charter to the American
Legion in 1919, James Fisk became an active and enthusiastic member.
In 1924 he was appointed Adjutant of the ·Legion and occupied that
office until August 1945. He was a past commander of Berkeley Post
No. 7, and was Americanism Chairman of the Legion in 1922. For
many years he was chairman of the California Joint IDJmigration Committee which consisted of representatives of the Legion, the Grange,
Native Sons of the Golden West, and State Federation of Labor.
Jim, as he was affectionately known to his brethren, petitioned Perris
Lodge No. 411, was elected and received the first degree in that lodge.
The second and third degrees were conferred upon him as a courtesy by
Charter Rock Lodge No. 410. He received the third degree April 10,
1920 and shortly thereafter affiliated with Charter Rock Lodge and was
immediately appointed to the line of officers. He was elected Master
and filled that important post in 1927.
His administrative ability and his unbounded enthusiasm for the
order attracted the attention of Grand Lodge and in 1941 Grand Master

234

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Lloyd E. Wilson appointed him Grand Marshal. His work was so satisfactory that the succeeding Grand Master Frank M. Smith re-appointed
him and he served equally well in 1942. In 1946 he was Chairman of
Distinguished Guests Committee, and in 1947 and 1948 served as a
member of the same committee. In 1948-49-50 he gave exceptional
service as Chairman of the Correspondenc e Committee. He was a member of this committee at the time of his death.
We lament the passing of this distinguished man and Mason but we
know that he had a joyous reunion with his many friends who were
awaiting him in his Father's House.
ALFRED JOSEPH THIBODEAU

Alfred Joseph Thibodeau, Past Master of San Francisco Lodge No.
360 and Inspector of the 42nd Masonic District, was born July 13, 1895,
entered into rest October 30, 1950.
Our departed brother was born in Clyde, Cloud County, Kansas
and attended public schools at Crookston, Minn. and Twin Falls, Idaho.
He enlisted in the Second Idaho Infantry and served six months on the
Mexican Border in 1916. He volunteered for overseas duty in World
War I and saw action in 5 major engagements with the 9th Machine
Gun Battalion, 3rd Division, in France. He was slightly wounded at
Chateau Thierry and was later seriously wounded in the ·Argonne Forest resulting in over two years in many hospitals and an even twenty
operations. He was awarded the Silver Star and Purple Heart decorations. He received a disability discharge from Letterman General Hospital in December 1920 and attended Polytechnic College of Engineer. ing and Heald Engineering College in San Francisco and received a
Bachelor of Science degree in Mechanical Engineering. He subsequently
opened a drafting office in San Francisco specializing in the development of inventions.
During the years followipg World War I he was active in veterans
affairs; assisted in the organization of a chapter of disabled American
veterans, a post of Veterans for Foreign Wars and a chapter of Military
Order of the Purple Heart. He was also actively interested in various
youth movements; served as Associate Guardian of the International
Order of Job's Daughters for four years; was Troop Committee Chairman of Troop 54, Boy Scouts of America.
He applied for the degree of Masonry in San Francisco Lodge No.
360 and was raised on May 22, 1926; was appointed Senior Steward in
. 1936 and served as Worshipful Master in 1939. He then served as
officers coach until his outstanding ability in the ritualistic work of our
order was recognized and he was appointed Inspector of the 42nd Masonic District in 1946 by the then Grand Master Arthur W . Brouillet.

Al's principal hobby was the culture of San Francisco's official
Hower, the dahlia, and at the time of his death he had an outstanding
collection of 147 varieties. He has served as the Secretary of the Dahlia
Society of California since 1947. He was also active in religious affairs
being a member of the Board of Deacons of the 7th Ave. Presbyterian
Church of which he was a member.
. Brother Thibodeau was on June 22, 1921 united in marriage to
Mil~red Ah_r.e ns•. a native of San Francisco, who with one daughter,
Elame, survive him. Our heartfelt sympathy is theirs in the hour of their
afBiction, deprived as they are of the loving companionship and protection of the devoted husband and affectionate father.
Although Al rarely complained those of us who knew him best
realized that he suffered untold agony from his war wounds but stout of
heart and determined of purpose~ he ran with patience the race that was
s~t before him without other interest than to do the right thing at the
nght. time. And n~w that the goal has been achieved and he has gone
to jom that Celestial Lodge .we offer loving testimonial to one in whom
all proper elements united and worked together for the making of a
.
truly good man.
"May he rest his weary head on the soft bosom of endless time;
May he sleep in the comfort of eternal peace."
In the monitorial section of the Master's lecture of the first degree
we find these words : "By the exercise of Brothedy Love we are taught
to re~ard the y.rhole human species as one family, the high and the low,
the rich and the poor, who, as created by one Almighty Parent and
inhabitants of the same planet, are to aid, support and protect' each
ot~e~. On this principle Masonry unites men of every country, sect and
opmio~; and causes true friendship to exist among those who might
otherwise have remained at a perpetual distance." If our fraternity accomplished nothing more than this, this alone would justify its existence,
for the probabilities are that had it not been for our fraternal association
the paths of our deceased brethren and ours would never have crossed.
While we speak highly of the virtues of our departed brethren, we
do not assert that they were perfect men for only one perfect man ever
lived and He died upon a cross nearly two thousand years ago. But we
do assert that through the fabric of their lives there was woven a golden
thread of truth, honesty and fair dealing, brotherly love and a respect
for the rights and opinions of others. They practiced the teachings of
Freemasonry and were shining lights of the eternal verities.
Our brethren are gone. Never again in this world will we feel the
warm clasp of their hands. Never again in this world will we be met
by the cheerful smile of their greetings. But they are not forgotten, for

every wave of memory will bring fond recollections of close association.
So, in this final tribute, we do not say "goodbye" but "goodnight", for
it will not be long-and the wisest among us cannot say how longbefore we will greet them again in our Father's House, and our salutation will be-"Good Morning My Brothers!"
·
Our thoughts at this time have been beautifully expressed by the
poet Wilcox, who said:

"It seemeth such a little way to me
Across to that strange country,
The Beyond:
And yet, not strange, for it has
grown to be
The home of those of whom I am so fond.
And so for me there is no Death
It is but crossing, with abated breath
A little strip of sea,
To find one's loved ones waiting
on the shore,
More beautiful. more precious
than before."

EULOGY
FRANK MACPHERSON SMITH

.By LLOYD E. WILSON, Past Grand Master, Grand Secretary
Once more, in a Communication of the Grand Lodge, I stand in a
place not of my own choice to pay tribute to one who received the high. est honor that could be conferred by his Masonic Brethren, and one,
who by his action, earned the approbation of all who had the honor to
associate with him.
Frank MacPherson Smith was born in Rock Island, Illinois, April 1,
1894, and hence had just passed the fifty-seventh anniV'ersary of his
birth when he was summoned by the Supreme Grand Master. He received his education in the public schools of Los Angeles, later in the
preparatory school of the University of Southern California, and
finally in the University of Southern California Law Department, where
he received the degree of Bachelor of Laws. He then entered upon a
legal career which was to bring him to the judicial notice of all who are
familiar with the courts of this state. In 1931 he was appointed to the
Municipal Court of Los Angeles, and only two years later was unanimously chosen presiding judge of those courts. At the end of that year he
received an appointment to the Superior Court of Los Angeles, was
elected to that court in 1934, and re-elected in 1940,' serving until his
voluntary retirement early in 195.J. He served on the State Judicial
Council for more than ten years.
Judge Sil)ith was married in 1919 to Eunice Richards of Seattle.
Washington, and to· them was born a daughter. Barbara Jane, and a·
son. Richards.
·
At the outbreak of World War I in 1917, Brother Smith offered his
services to his country and as a Sergeant in Company B. 364th· In£antry,
in France was seriously wounded in combat, bearing the marks 0£ these
wounds throughout his life. It was perhaps his own service in behalf of
his country and his intense patriotism that caused him; at the outbreak
of World War II, to see so clearly what the position of Masons and
Masonry should be.
Freemasonry, and naturally its Lodges and the Grand Lodge in
California, claimed a large part of time and thought of Brother Frank
Smith. He became a Mason in Argonne Lodge No. 514, San Francisco,
in 1922. Later, demitting to East Gate Lodge No. 290, Los Angeles, he
served as Master in 1933. He was a member of the Los Angeles Board
of Relief from 1931 to 1938, serving as its president in 1937 and 1938,
in which latter year he was also President of the Southern California
Past Masters' Association. He served the Masonic Homes Endowment
Board as its Secretary in 1934 and 1935, and as Chairman from 1936,
until he was installed by the Grand Lodge as its Grand Master in 1941.

239

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

His othe; Masonic connections are equally well-known, and in the
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite he was honored with the degree of
Knight Commander of the Court of Honor.

The hospital visitation program throughout the state was undertaken
during his incumbency, and many other activities, of which fortunately
there is a complete record in the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge, as
well as in the comprehensive message which Grand Master Smith gave
at the end of his stewardship.
While there were, of course, many men in Grand Lodge who were
the intimate friends of Frank Smith, I am the one perhaps in the best
position to pay a tribute to him in his capacity as Grand Master, because
he was the first Grand Master with whom I had the honor to serve as
Grand Secretary. He had been Deputy Grand Master during my own
term as Grand Master. and it was, therefore, the continuation of a close
personal friendship between us as Grand Master and Grand Secretary.
It was fortunate indeed that there should be this union of friendship
between the Grand Master and Grand Secretary in that year of crisis.
We had many common interests, and I always knew that I could go
to him for guidance and advice. It was a great satisfaction to carry out a
program which I know would stand the test of time. It was this leadership--patriotic, sincere, well-planned-which led us on to the great
achievement, which was ultimately that of the Grand Lodge of California
in its war service. It was, likewise, that sort of friendship and that leadership which drew the Grand Lodge Officers about him, and which won
for him a complete commitment to every service to which he called them.
It has been said, and many times proved, that men are raised up for
a great hour; that when there is a need, the man will appear. So it was
with Frank MacPherson Smith. The need was created by the emergency,
which confronted the Nation, and, fortunately. the Grand Lodge of
California ha'd at its head the man that was needed for the hour. He
rose to the occasion; he met the requirements which were demanded of
him; he performed the service magnificently.
What a great blessing it would have been to us if, in these past few
years, we had been permitted still to draw upon that wisdom and that
leadership in all our activities and programs. It was not, however, to be,
and now we pay this last tribute to him, thankful for all that he gave,
thankful for the friendship that was ours, knowing full well that his
impact upon his time was sufficiently great that it will not be lost down
through the years.
Such was the contribution of Frank MacPherson Smith, and gratefully we acknowledge our debt to him for all that he did.

238

. It was fortunate indeed for the Grand Lodge that Brother Frank
Smith was chosen to be its Grand Master in October 1941, because,
only fifty days after he was installed as Grand Master, the United ·
States was at war. Grand Master Smith immediately, sensing the magnitude of the impending conflict and the responsibility which Masons
must undertake, took prompt action. He had served his country as an
enlisted man, had sacrificed in behalf of it, and consequently was perhaps more aware than others of what might lie ahead of this nation and
of the individuals who served it.
•
As evidence of the speed with which he acted, I should like to refer
to and quote a small portion from a proclamation issued by Grand
Master Smith on December 16, 1941, only nine days after the Pearl
Harbor disaster. This proclamation, ordered read in every Lodge in the
state, recited what had happened since 1933 by the treachery and
duplicity of the Axis powers. He said in part. "Between this day and that
certain day of the future, when the forces of democracy throw open the
gate of liberation for all mankind, much must be done. It shall be our
proud and eager duty, both as America~s and as M:aso~s. ~o don the
garments of work, of sacrifice, and of 1ro~ determination ... He t~en
gave his direction for the immediate day m thes~ ~ords. obey implicitly the orders of those in command; pursue religiously the allotted
daily tasks; cheerfully and gratefully accept the extra hours imposed by,
and dedicated to, the war effort; volunteer, whenever and wherever
possible, extra service. to the national cause: and, ·finally, contribute to
the limit of ability and fortune, to the programs re~ecting the national
will' to complete victory."
This comprehension of the problem and immediate action, looking
toward its solution, was characteristic of Grand Master Smith, and it
was 'under his direction that the Grand Lodge of California embarked
upon a great program of war time service, wh~ch b~oug~t distinct!on to
him and great credit to the Grand Lodge of California. It 1s not desirable,
at this time, to record in detail the entire war program. Suffice to say
that he planned and helped carry through the campaign for the War
Relief Fund, which was so outstandingly successful. It was he who set
up the Masonic War Activities Committee and attende? all. its _meetings, helping to determine policy and to plan programs. Likewise, 1t was
his relief plan whereby our own members in the Armed Forces could be
served throughout the .world, wherever they might present a need.
It was he, too, who planned the service for the Grand Lodge of
the Philippine Islands by which their members were kept in good standing. and recordlj smd addresses later provided for that Grand Lodge.

MORNING SESSION, THURSDAY, OCTOBER 11, 1951
Grand Lodge was called on at 10:00 A.M., the Grand Master presiding. The Very Reverend Grand Chaplain offered the morning prayer.
The minutes of Wednesday morning. October 10, were read and approved.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Charters respectfully submits the following report and recommendations.
Since the last communication of Grand Lodge, the Grand Master
issued dispensations to form n"ew lodges to be known as Los Altos,
Castro Valley, Blue Lakes and Magnolia Park.
The records of these Lodges have been examined and found to be in
order.

Los ALTOS, U. D.
Los Altos Lodge was instituted February 28, 1951, and now has a
membership of 46. Although it meets at the Palo Alto Temple, efforts are
being made to obtain quarters in Los Altos. The Lodge has able leadership and is being administered along sound and progressive lines. Its
location is in a rapidly developing community which can well support
a Masonic Lodge.
We therefore recommend that a charter be granted to Los Altos
Lodge No. 712 in the County of Santa Clara.
CASTRO VALLEY,

u. D.

Castro Valley Lodge was instituted May 19, 1951, with the legal
maximum of 50 charter members. Since then they have read or accepted
22 petitions for degrees. The Lodge is adequately financed, having a
cash ]:,alance of over $1.500.00.
Castro Valley is principally a residential community on the fringe
of the tremendous industrial area of San Leandro, Alameda and Oakland, where further substan.tial increases in population appear inevitable.
This Lodge is already taking its place in the community life and prospects for its future are bright.
Your committee therefore recommends that a charter be granted to
Castro Valley Lodge No. 713 in the County of Alameda.
BLUE LAKES,

u. D.

Blue Lakes Lodge in San Bruno, San Mateo County. is the outgrowth of a Masonic club formed in 1949 for the purpose of starting

Your committee therefore recommends that a charter be granted to
Blue Lakes Lodge No. 714 in the County .of San Mateo.
MAGNOLIA PARK,

u. D.

Magnolia Park Lodge takes its name from a rapidly growing section
of Burbank. The lodge began with 38 charter members and since its institution has received nine petitions for affiliation and ten petitions for
the degrees. The neighboring lodges are large and active. The population in the past two decades has increased six fold, yet no new lodge has
been chartered in this area in the past twenty-three years. It is our
opinion that ample opportunity exists for a successful lodge. This lodge
has over $2,000 in cash, all necessary equipment, and no outstanding
bills.
Your committee therefore recommends the granting of a charter to
Magnolia Park Lodge No. 715 in the County of Los Angeles.
Respectfully submitted,
GLENN

issued.

.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIPORNIA

Grand Lodge of Italy

Amendment of Section 245

At the opening of Grand Lodge. M. W. Brother Wilson, Grand
Secretary. called attention to unflnished business held over from the 1950
Communication of Grand Lodge, one item of which related to consideration of recognition of a Grand Lodge in Italy. M. W. Brother Hervey,
who is our outstandini:J authority on foreign Masonry, discussed this
matter at some length. There was also discussion by Brother Cogliandro
of Speranza Lodge No. 219 as a result of which action in the matter of
Italian Masonry was held over until this year.
Unfortunately for us, other fraternal duties have called Brother
Hervey to Washington, D. C., where he is at the present time. Before
his departure. he called me to his office and asked me to request that the
matter of recognition of any Grand Lodge in Italy be again held over
for another year. He advised me that he intends to go to Italy sometime
in the coming winter and make a thorough study of Italian Masonry.
He will, of course, present the results of this important investigation at
the 1952 Communication of the Grand Lodge.
Brother Hervey advised that at the present time the Masonic situation in Italy is far too confused to justify action at present, _and I
therefore submit this request for your consideration and action.

The proposed amendment to Section 245 of our Ordinances would
make it possible for a lodge to refuse to refund that portion of the fees
for the degrees, not earned by conferring the degrees, in cases where an
applicant moves to another jurisdiction and with the permission of the
lodge receives the degrees or part of them in a lodge in another jurisdiction. Generally. a man does not move to another jurisdiction except
for necessary business purposes, and your Committee feels that our
present law, which requires the refunding of the unearned fees under
these circumstances, should not be relaxed and that it would be unfair
to an applicant to require him to pay the fees twice merely because he
moves to another jurisdiction and with the consent of his lodge takes
the degrees there.
Your Committee therefore recommends that this proposed amendment to Section 245 be not adopted.
Report adopted.

254

Adopted.
Brother Antonio Cogliandro caused to be read a letter prepared by
him on the above subject and the Grand Secretary was directed to supply
the Committee on Policy and General Purposes with copies of the communication.
Amendment of Section 133
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred the resolution to amend Article IV, Section 2, of the Uniform
Code of By-Laws and Section 245 of the Ordinances, begs leave to
report as follows.
The proposed amendment to Article IV, Section 2, of the Uniform
Code of By-Laws to provide that the Lodge may forfeit the fees of an
entered apprentice or fellowcraft who does not complete his degrees
within 5 years from the da.t e of initiation removes an uncertainty and .a
problem which has bothered our lodges for many years and makes it
possible for the lodges to remove from their books a possible liability
for refunds. Your Committee therefore approves this proposed amendment, and the Committee on Jurisprudence will report as to the legislation.
Adopted concurrent with the report of the Committee on Jurispru-- ·
dence.

Amendment of Section 163
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred the proposed amendment to Section 163 of the Ordinances,
begs leave to report as follows.
The proposed amendment would permit a Past Master who joins
with others in• applying for a dispensation for a new lodge to retain his
membership in the lodge of which he is then a member. In other words,
it would permit a Past Master under these circumstances to have membership in two lodges at the same time. Membership in two or more
lodges in this jurisdiction by the same Mason would make for confusion
and would present other problems which I'll not take time to enumerate
because your Committee feels that there is a more important reason for
not adopting this proposed amendment. Your Committee feels that this
proposed legislation is class legislation which would apply only to a
very small number of the fraternity. It is not necessary that a group
applying for a dispensation to form a new lodge have a Past Master of
a lodge in this jurisdiction as one of the petitioning group. Those who
petition should concentrate their interest and attention to the affairs of
the new lodge if it is to prosper and become a reality. Plural membership
would tend to divide this interest and attention and accordingly, for the
reasons above stated, your Committee recommends that the proposed
amendment be not adopted.
The Committee on Jurisprudence concurs in this recommendation.
Report adopted.

Life Membe rship for Fifty-Y ear Membe r
Your Committee on Policy and Genera l Purpose s, to which was
referred the resolution that brethren who receive 50-year buttons should
also receive from Grand Lodge a life membership certificate, begs leave
to report as follows :
It is always difficult to pass upon a suggest ion such as this because
our generos ity and sympat hy are involved. Your Commi ttee finds that
this proposa l would not be accepta ble to many of our brethre n who
conside r the remission of dues an act of charity and, of course, it goes
without saying that the mere fact that a brother has been a member of
the fraternt y for 50 years does not necessa rily mean that he has contributed very much to the fraterni ty. Our laws now provide a method
for remitting the dues of an old member who needs this help, and your
Committee does not feel that the unneces sary remission of dues should
be encoura ged. We therefor e recommend that this resolution be not
adopted .
The Committee on Finance concurs in this recommendation.
Report adopted .

Lodge Memor ial Service
Your Committee on Policy and Genera l Purpose s, to which was
referred the resolution that a Memorial Service be authoriz ed by Grand
Lodge for constitu tent lodges to be conduc ted by them at least once a
year, begs leave to report as follows.
Your Committee wishes to make clear at the outset that it does not
disappr ove the idea of an annual Memorial Service in the constitu ent
lodges. On the contrar y, your Committee feels that it is a fine annual
tribute to our decease d brethren . Howeve r, your Committee feels that
the officers of our lodges are now required to memorize a great deal of
ritual and other ceremonies, and that it would be an unneces sary burden
upon the officers to add a Memori al Service to these requirements. We
realize that the resoluti on does not require that the Memorial Service
be memorized, but we know, as you do, that such a service should be
memorized if it is to be properl y given and that few officers of lodges
would care to memorize this service for the purpose of giving it only
once each year.
Your Committee further feels that each lodge has its own ideas as
to how and when a Memorial Service should be conduct ed and that the
officers and members of the constitu ent lodges should be encoura ged to
use their own ingenui ty to conduc t a service which will fit their particul ar
lodge and its circumstances, and that Grand Lodge should not, directly

257

or indirectly, impose upon the lodges a requirem ent that a particu lar
form of service be used.
We therefor e recommend that the resolution be not adopted .
. The Special Committee on Ceremonies reporte d their coAcurrence
m the above recommendation.
Report adopted .

AFTERNO ON SESSION -Thursday , October 11, 1951

Amendmen t of Sections 15, 16, 17 and 18

At 1 :30 P.M. Grand Lodge was called on, the Grand Master presiding.

The resolution presented by Brother Henry W. Coil a Past Master
of Ri~ers~de Lodge No. 635 to repeal sections 15, 16, 17 and 18 of our
Constitution and enact a new section to be numbered 15 has had the
thoughtful consideratio n of your Committee on Policy 'and General
Purposes.
It presents a straight and simple question of policy as to voting in an
Annual Communication.
The four sections which would be repealed by the adoption of the
proposed resolution provide first that each elected or appointed incumbent officer of the Grand Lodge who is present and each brother
who has held an elective grand office in the past shall have one vote.
It is further provided in our existing law that all the Past Masters
of a lodge shall have one vote for the group. In other words, if one Past
Master from X lodge is present he is entitled to one vote and if there
are present two, five or ten Past Masters from that lodge, they still
have only one vote among them. If they cannot agree among themselves
how .this vote is to be cast they, presumably, can cast their individual
fractions of on~ vote. This presents no problem on a written vote, although o_n a v01ce vote t~e fractio~s would. of course, not be distinguishable. This fact does not in and of itself necessitate a change in so fundam~ntal a matter ~s the system of voting. Certainty can always be obtained by a standing vote and this did happen at a Communication only
a few years ago. If a lodge does not have a Past Master present of
cours~ this one vote is lost. The Master, other officer or elected re~e­
sentative does not inherit it from the absent Past Masters. The same
would be true under the proposed legislation.
Section 17 provides that none of the members about whom I have
been speaking thus far can vote in a dual capacity.
This brings us to a consideratio n of the present section 18 where the
v?lume of voting strength is to be found. To paraphrase this section. it
~ives to each lodge represented three votes whether the representati on
is. ~y one, two or th~ee persons. If a lodge is represented by one in~ividual whether he is the Master, a warden or the elected representative_. h~ may cast three votes. If only two of these three are present, the
semor in rank may cast two votes and the junior one vote. 1£ the Master
an~ both Wardens are present, they each have one vote. No matter
which of the combinations just mentioned are in attendance there are
three votes which may be cast.
'
The resolution presented by our brother would change this entire
system and give to each member of Grand Lodge present one vote regardless of the capacity in which he is present. It will immediately be
seen that the resolution would effect a fundamenta l change.
It might appear to have appeal as being in the democratic tradition,

Amendmen t of Section 301
A resolution to amend Section 301 of the Ordinances has been presented by Brother Frank B. Belcher, a Past Master of Wilshire Lodge
No. 445 and chairman of our Committee on Grievances. It deals with
the Master who presides over a trial on charges of unmasonic conduct.
It presents this question of policy: Shall every Masonic trial be
presided over by the incumbent Master of the lodge, if he is not disqualified because of partiality or because he will be a witness called to
testify, or should it be possible for the Grand Master to appoint a qualified Past Master to preside over the trial?
~t- the present time the Master of a lodge must preside over every
trial in his lodge unless he is disqualified because he cannot fairly try
the matter or because he will testify at the trial. This is true regardless
of the nature of the training and' experience of the Master.
Presiding over a trial is not the easiest of . tasks. The Master who
presides over a Masonic trial is in much the same position as a judge
presiding over a jury criminal trial. except that he does not decide what
punishment shall be inflicted. He must decide whether offered evidence
will be admitted and pass upon questions of procedure.
It should be agreed by all that a lodge in which a trial is held should
have the benefit of the services as the presiding officer of one qualified by
experience or training to occupy that important post.
The legislation set out in the resolution provides that when the copy
of the charges is forwarded to the Grand Secretary, a step required by
our present law, the Grand Master, or if he has delegated this power,
the Deputy Grand Master or a Grand Warden, shall appoint either the
Master of the lodge or a qualified Past Master of our jurisdiction to preside at the trial. The legislation does not affect procedures as to the
election of commissioners and the other preliminary steps. Likewise it
does not change the present section as to the disqualification of a Master
who cannot try the matter fairly or who is to testify.
The adoption of the resolution should result in an improvement in
the administrati on of Masonic justice, reduce the number of reversals
and the cost of retrials.
Your committee unanimously recommends the adoption of the policy
expressed by the proposed legislation.
Adopted concurrent with the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence.

a premium on proximity of a lodge to the meeting place of the Annual
Communication, since it is logical to assume that lodges near to the meeting place would have more Past Masters present than those at a distance.
Whether near or far, the incumbent Master and Wardens could be

Research Lodges
This Committee has considered the report of the Special Committee
on Masonic Education relative to warranting lodges for Masonic research and which report submits comprehensive legislation to that end.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered all
of the details set out in the plan. We approve all parts of the plan which
involve questions of policy and the general purposes of the Grand Lodge.
We have but three minor recommendations to make. First, we
recommend that provision be made in the legislation that in the event of
the dissolution of a research lodge its funds and assets shall revert to
the Grand Lodge as the funds and assets of other lodges revert upon
dissolution.
The second recommendation is that the policy reJative to the status
of officers and Past Masters as to non-membership in the Grand Lodge
be clearly stated in the legislation. The legislation proposed by the Special Committee provides that a research lodge "shall not be entitled to
representation or vote in Grand Lodge." From this one would conclude
that the intention was against membership in Grand Lodge as an attribute of office in a research lodge but it might leave debatable the status
of a Past Master of a research lodge who was not also a Past Master
of a lodge which confers degrees. The Special Committee states that it
intended that membership in Grand Lodge would not be acquired by
becoming a Past Master of a research lodge and we recommend that
provision be made in the legislation that the officers and Past Masters
of a research lodge, as such, shall not be members of the Grand Lodge.
The third recommendation is that the Masonic information which the lodges are authorized to disseminate shall be subject to approval by a
committee of the Grand Lodge designated by the Grand Master before
it is disseminated. The special committee concurs in this safeguard.

These three recommendations, as should readily be seen, do not
alter or impair the proposed research lodges. In all other particulars we
approve the policy expressed and recommend the adoption of legislation to that end.
See report of the Committee on Jurisprudence for disposition of this
matter.

Decision No. 4
The recommendation of the Grand Master relative to the report of
the Committee on Jurisprudence adopted at the 1875 communication
(Ross Digest, 875) that a petition for the degrees could not be received
from one who had served a term in a state prison was referred to t!ie
Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The recommendation presents the question: Shall the policy established by the adoption of the report in f875 now be reversed?
Seven of the eight members of this committee recommend that you
do not reverse. Past Grand Master Warlow does not agree with the
majority. He then suggested a partial reversal, but the seven other members do not concur in the suggestion.
The · issue raised by the recommendation is of such importance to
the craft, in our opinion, that not to speak in plain terms or to leave unexplored any phase of the question would be a disservice. Therefore, if
it seems to any that the question could be discussed in fewer words or
with less exploration, the failure to do so must be attributed solely to
our concern for the welfare of the fraternity.
The question is one that easily lends itself to an emotional appeal
upon· behalf of one who, it is claimed, has rehabilitated himself and is
leading an exemplary life. But if it may be said that close c~ses sometimes make bad law, it may also be said that sympathy sometimes leads
to bad decisions.
We are presented squarely with the question whet~e~ all men ~ho
have served terms in a state prison shall now be made eligible to petition
for the degrees in our lodges. That is ~tating it bluntly, but that is the
effect of the recommendation. It is not the case of one man or two men,
but of all who are in that class.
Those who are not familiar with the administration of criminal
justice may not understand what class of persons are ineligible ~y virtue of the 1875 action and if it takes a few moments to explam and
clarify, it is hoped your time will not be wasted.
Two specific cases are mentioned in the message of the Grand
Master and it is stated that their convictions occurred in their early
youth. Your committee is as sympathetic toward youthful transgressions
as the average person, but let us not lose sight of the larger issue because
these two may have served prison terms in what is described in the

267

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

general term "early youth." It is not stated whether they were over or
under twenty-one years of age at the time, but unless they are now well
along in years, they must have been over twenty-one, as will presently
appear. It really makes no difference though because we are determining
the question of eligibility from this time forward. Let us therefore look
at the present situation.
Anyone who commits an act which otherwise would be a crime but
who at the time is under the age of eighteen years is not prosecuted in
the regular courts but comes within the exclusive jurisdiction of the
Juvenile Court. Under the act creating that court no complaint is flied
against him and he is not charged with the commission of a crime. Rather
a petition is flied on his behalf alleging the occurrence and praying that
he be declared a ward of the Juvenile Court. If the allegations are "sustained" he is so declared and may be released to his parents or detained.
Detention may be in a juvenile hall, camp or one of the facilities of the
Youth Authority. The latter is the maximum penalty and as a practical
matter does not happen except after several declaration$ of wardship
by the court. The relationship of the court and the youth is that of
guardian and ward and even in the extreme instance, certification to the
Youth Authority, the juvenile is not sent to a state prison, but to the
Youth Authority who may parole him home or detain him in the Preston
School of Industry at lone, the Nelles School at Whittier or its facilities
at Lancaster, Deuel or elsewhere. In any event no one who commits a
transgression before he is is over eighteen is barred from presenting a
petition to a lodge because of detention growing out of that act or acts.
. The situation is the same if the perpetrator is over eighteen but under
twenty-one at the time of the act. In such a case the jurisdiction of the
Juvenile Court is optional and it may accept jurisdiction or refuse it. As
a practical matter the refusal generally occurs only when the court deems
the minor unfit for treatment by the court because of numerous previous
handlings, but even then he does not fall within the class of those ineligible under the 1875 action of this body. If he is over eighteen and
under twenty-one years of age at the time the act is committed, the
courts are without power to sentence him for more than ninety days in
jail, which is not a term in a prison. Otherwise the judge must certify the
defendant to the Youth Authority. As has been seen, this latter sentence
does not make him ineligible thereafter.
Now we come to those who have committec_l criminal acts after they
have passed their twenty-first birthday. It is stated in the message of the
Grand Master that at the time this body adopted the rule of ineligibility
in 1875 the law exacted an "eye for an eye" and small children were
sent to prison for long periods of confinement. (I told the Grand Master
yesterday that I could not speak authoritatively about the courts in
1875 because I wasn't even in existence then and it now occurs to me
that he wasn't either, so we . speak with equal authority.) Whatever

may have been the situation in 1875, the fact that things have changed
is an argument for not changing the rule now.
None will contend that criminal justice as administered in the courts
today exacts an eye for an eye and we have just seen that children and
persons under twenty-one, are not confined in our state prisons today.
Rather than arguing that the rule should be changed because it was
adopted at a time when criminal justice was more stern than at present,
should we not consider the fact that those who now are sentenced to
state prison may be less worthy than some who might have been so
sentenced in 1875?
As suggested in the Grand Master's message, criminal courts now
are authorized to grant probation and under that power nearly all first
offenders and many repeaters receive some probationary sentence. This
may entail no detention whatever, a fine or a period in the county jail.
If the sentence is to the county jail, the conviction is not even of a felony,
but of'a misdemeanor. The man sentenced to a state prison is one whom
the trial judge considers unworthy of probation, usually because he is
before the court with a record of other criminal convictions. It is this
class whom it is now proposed to make eligible to petition our lodges.
It would not be fair to presume to speak of other counties on this
short notice, but from personal observation it may be said that ap~
proximately nine-tenths of those convicted in Los Angeles County are
not barred by the present rule of ineligibility. Whether they should re~
ceive the degrees now rests with the lodges they may petition.
Not knowing that this issue would be before us, it has not been possible to check statutes and regulations, as would have been done, but it is
believed that one who has served a term in a state prison cannot enlist
in the army, navy or marine corps. Shall he now be made eligible to
receive our degrees? One who has served a term in a state prison cannot
obtain a real estate or insurance brokers' license. Shall he nevertheless
now be made eligible in Masonry? It is believed that he would be ineligible to practice medicine, dentistry or law, but it is now proposed
that he shall be made eligible for Masonry.
One who has served a term in a state prison (or been convicted of a
felony without receiving a prison term) who testifies in any court, in a
civil or criminal matter, may be asked whether he has been so convicted
and it is the duty of the judge to instruct the jury, if there be one, that
such a conviction impeaches the witness under our law. It is up to the
jury to decide the effect of this or any other impeachment, but at least
the law infers that perhaps such a witness is not to be trusted even under
oath in court. Shall he now become eligible to petition for our degrees?
When the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence was adopted in
1875 the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California consisted of 198 constituent lodges and
11,463 members. While this rule has been in effect it has grown to over

six hundred lodges and attained a membership in excess of two hundred
thousand. Is it necessary or desirable now to open a door that has been
·
closed for seventy-six years?

agreement with that committee of which I am now a member, and I file
this minority report which is my right.
Brethren, I believe in redemption, but if a man cannot redeem himself then a lot of you fellows down there, and a lot of us fellows up here,
are going to fry for a long time.
Let us be practical about this matter, and also be specific. We have
had a full discussion, both now and in 1918. I believe that there is a
middle ground between the old law of 1875 and the Grand Master's
present recommendation, and that this middle ground should be acceptable to all. It will not indiscriminately open our doors, but it will allow
one who has been guilty of a serious offense, and who has redeemed
himself by positive living, to submit his whole life to determine if he is
presently worthy and presently under the tongue of good report.
I propose:
1. That the decision of 1875 be repealed.
2. That one who has been convicted of a felony, served time and
been officially pardoned, may apply for and receive the degrees of Masonry under the following conditions:
(a) His offense must have been one not involving moral turpitude.
( b) For 10 years or more since the date of his pardon, he must
have lived within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge.
( c) The report of the investigating committee must be in writing, be full and favorable, and be submitted to the Grand
l\1aster for his consideration prior to balloting.
( d ) The Grand Master may, in his discre~ grant per~ission
to the Lodge to ballot on the application, but sucn shall be
permissive only and not constitute a recommendation, or,
the Grand Master may refuse such permission and this
shall constitute a rejection of the application.
( e) If the permission is granted then the application shall be
voted upon in a regular manner.
As a part of my proposal one other matter should be taken into consideration. The form of the application for the degrees of Masonry
should include the question,
"Have you ever been convicted of a crime other than a minor
traffic violation? It so, state the nature of the offense, the date and
place of the trial and the penalty imposed.''
Brethren, we regard our fraternity as a great Charitable Institution
but true charity ministers to the minds and souls of men as well as to
their bodies. Mere largess is not enough. If a man, after a mistake, has
for many years "worked diligently, lived creditably and acted honorably
by all men," if he has affirmatively promoted "the general good of

Your committee majority are not men who would hunt down a man
who has been convicted of a felony and thereafter served a term in a
state prison, we do not advocate the old Chinese practice of putting a ·
board collar around their necks so that all may read thereon the details
of their offense, but we do not feel that the right to petition for membership in our order is one of the inalienable rights granted to men. If there
be one or two, or even more, who have served prison terms and thereafter so lived that they would otherwise be worthy of our regard, we are
pleased. However, we deem it would be a disservice to Masonry out of
emotion for these, now to reverse this long established policy and make
eligible the thousands confined in San Quentin, Folsom, Chino and
the other penal institutions of this and other states.
Past Grand Master John R. Moore, for the Committee on Jurisprudence, reported the concurrence Qf that Committee in the majority report

Past Grand Master Warlow presented a minority report as follows:
I stand before you in an unusual position, one which, if the subject
of our discussion was not so serious, would probably be considered
amusing.
I am a member of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
which has just rendered its report relative to the decision of 1875
(Ross Digest, Section 875), and the present Grand Master's recommendation that that decision be now repudiated.
In 1918, in delivering a message to Grand Lodge, I reported my
formal decision that one convicted of a felony was not eligible to apply
for the degrees of Masonry. The Committee on Jurisprudence and the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes after a conference, indicated informally that they would refuse to approve that decision and
it was withdrawn. Thereafter I introduced an amendment to Section 208
of our Ordinances which would have made such an individual clearly
ineligible to apply for the degrees of Masonry. This amendment was
rejected.
Our present Grand Master has reported these facts to you in his
Decision No. IV, but he did not disclose my connection with the matter.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes, with four of its
regular nine members absent, has just rendered its report which reverses
its 1918 position. The amusing part, if it is amusing. is that in these same
three years I too have revised my opinion. I am, therefore, still in dis-

Brethren, this fraternity of ours is big enough, sound enough and

That is simple justice and we need not fear justice.
I move the adoption of this minority report as a substitute motion

There are already two decisions on this subject in the Edicts and

Spanish Language Lodges
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes after considerable
discussion regarding the resolution of Robert F. Shippee, Past Master of
Henry S. Orme Lodge No. 458, that the incoming Grand Master appoint
a special committee for the purpose of considering and reporting upon
the advisability of dispensating and chartering a Lodge or Lodges to
work in the Spanish language are of the opinion that this resolution
should be disapproved.
We find no real demand or need for such Lodges and the other
foreign language Lodges exist for historical reasons. We see no reason
to expand foreign language Lodges in this jurisdiction.
We therefore recommend this Resolution be not adopted.
The report of the Committee was not adopted.
The following Resolution was submitted for consideration:
Resolved: That the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee for the purpose of considering and reporting upon the advisability
of dispensating and chartering a lodge or lodges to work in the Spanish
language.
Resolution adopted.

Special Committee on Ceremonies
The motion introduced requesting the Grand Master to appoint a
special committee on the revision of Grand Lodge ceremonies has come
before the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The purpose of the motion is to permit the special committee appointed last year to complete its undertaking.
The Grand Lodge Ceremony of Installation is in need of substantial
revision. The special committee which reported on October 9th as to
other ceremonial revisions did not have time to complete their work on
the installation service of Grand Lodge Officers. They or their successors
should be given the opportunity to complete this revision.
We recommend the adoption of the motion.
Adopted.
Amendment of Sections 210 and 332%
Brother Alfred F. Ross, Past Master of Reading Lodge No. 254 and
a member of the Grand Lodge Committee on Grievances, has offered
two separate resolutions dealing with barkeepers and those engaged in
the saloon business. The first resolution, our number No. 11, proposes the
enactment of a new section of the Ordinances to l;>e numbered 332~.
It provides for expulsion without trial under certain circumstances of one
so engaged and sets forth a special procedure which includes sixty days'
notice to the offending brother.
The other resolution, our number No. 34, apparently is offered as an
alternate and proposes the repeal of Section 210 of the Ordinances. This

272

273

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

latter resolution, if adopted, would reverse the long-time policy of the
Grand Lodge and permit our membership to engage in the saloon business and keep bar.
Over the years, Grand Lodge has frequently expressed its opinion
upon the subject of the liquor business and while its present laws on that
subject might be somewhat clarified by additional legislation, the general intent of a medium ground between the two extremes.of th~ issue
is apparently the continuing expressed desire of Grand Lodge.
We see no desirability in departing from the present law of our
fraternity, nor do we feel that the proposed summary proceedings of
Resolution No. 11 should be adopted.
There is in resolution No. 11 a proposal in relation to the proceedings where the accused, in substance, is to plead guilty. It presents an
interesting point, but it is our view that if it is to be adopted, it should
be adapted and applied to all trials. We therefore offer the following
resolution:
· Resolved: That Resolutions Policy and General Purpose Committee No. 11 and No. 34 presented at this Communication of the
Grand Lodge be not adopted and that the incoming Grand Master
be requested to appoint a special committee to study and recommend, if it would seem desirable to them, amendments to our present
general trial law, looking to the simplifkation of proceedings where
a plea of guilty to the .charge is to be offered.
We move the adoption of this resolution.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported their concurrence in the
above recommendations.
Report.adopted.

Amendment of Section 301

Your Committee has given serious and extended consideration to
the recommendation of the Grand Master respecting the creation of Research Lodges and while we are in accord with the general idea of the
Grand Master, we cannot recommend the adoption of the legislation
which has been submitted by the Special Committee on Research Lodges.

tested, we recommend the following:

Resolved: That Section 301 of the Ordinances be amended to read
as follows:
Sec. 301. Upon receipt of a copy of the charges by the Grand Secretary, the Grand Master, or the Deputy Grand Master, Senior Grand
Warden, or Junior Grand Warden, if designated by the Grand Master
so to do, shall appoint the Master of the Lodge in which said charges
are pending, or any Past Master of this jurisdiction, in good standing
and skilled in Masonic Law, to preside at the trial. The person so appointed, if other than the Master of the Lodge, shall be known as the
Trial Master and shall have all the powers and duties of the Master of
the Lodge as prescribed by Article IV of Part II of these Ordinances;
provided, however, that nothing herein shall be deemed to prevent the
Master of the Lodge from receiving the charges, calling and presiding
at the meeting for the election of Commissioners, fixing the time and
place for the first meeting of the Commissioners, directing the giving of
notice to the accuser, the accused, and the Trial Commissioners, and the
announcing of the result of the trial in the Lodge, as prescribed in said
.
Article IV of Part III.
A Master or Past Master who cannot fairly try the matter or who is
a witness, is disqualified to preside at the trial.
Adopted.
Decision No. 3
With reference to the Grand Master's Decision No. III your committee reports:
King Soldmon's Lodge No. 260 asked approval of its resolution declaring in effect that no officer or member of the Lodge will have authority to incur any indebtedness of more than $200.00 against the Lodge
for any single activity excepting relief, unless approved by a majority
vote of the membership prior to such activity, and that the resolution be
not changed unless the membership have 30 days' notice thereof.
We concur in the Grand Master's opinion that because the resolution
referred to, by implication authorizes the incurring of indebtedness
amounting to $200.00 or less without lodge authority, it violates our law
which forbids any expenditure of lodge funds, other than relief, not
authorized by the lodge.
Adopted.

and experience and your committee recommends:

MORNING SESSION, FRIDAY, OCTOBER 12,

Decision No. 5
Your Committee reports on the Grand Master's Decision No.Vas
follows:
Upon the question of physical qualification the Grand Master held:
That there is a distinction between a mere applicant and a candidate
who has received one or more degrees and that Masonry owes a greater
duty to a brother than to the uninitiated: that physical disability suffered
by a candidate after he has received one or more degrees is no bar to his
advancement and that despite such physical disability by such candidate
he is entitled to receive the remaining degree or degrees unless his
rights thereto have been foreclosed in some other manner.
This decision is sound and fraternal and is in accord with Masonic
•
law.
A motion to disapprove Decision No. 5 and to rescind Section 515 of
the Edicts and Resolutions was ruled out of order by the Deputy Grand
Master, presiding at the time, because the motion involved two .s eparate
questions.
The report of the Committee was adopted.

SoTOYOME LooGE No. 123

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Since the last Annual Communication, your Finance Committee has
made a thorough survey as respects the financial arrangements between
the late Brother Ely Bush and his wife, Alice Bush, and Sotoyome Lodge
No. 123. This special survey was contemplated following the last Annual Communication and was made more important as the result of the
death of Mrs. Bush. widow of Brother Ely Bush.
Members of your Finance Committee spent some time in Healdsburg
with officers and a special committee for the Lodge who, in turn, have
appeared before the Finance Committee at this Communication. While
there are a number of matters still to be determined in connection with
the B.nal closing as a result of this escrow agreement, it is the considered
judgment of the officers of the Lodge that they would like to continue
paying monthly on the obligation to Grand Lodge at a minimum payment of $75.00 per month. They have indicated to the Committee their
desire to continue the $100 monthly payments but felt that because of
certain uncertainties, they ask to have the minimum fixed at $75.00.
Under the circumstances, your Finance Committee concurs that this is a
reasonable request and offer the following resolution:
Resolved: That the advances made by this Grand Lodge to
Sotoyome Lodge No. 123, balance due as of October 1, $4,850.00,
shall be repaid at the rate of (a minimum of) $75.00 per month, it
being understood that larger payments will be accepted when, as

PALOS VERDES LoooE No. 389
We are informed by the Grand Secretary that Palos Verdes Lodge
No. 389 has been made the defendant in an action concerning the title
to certain stocks owned by that Lodge and that the Grand Lodge has
also been named in the suit. While Grand Lodge does not appear to be
involved financially in the matter, the Grand Master has ordered counsel engaged to represent the Grand Lodge in the matter. The attorneys
are unable to give an estimate of the attorneys' fees or costs involved
and therefore we are unable to recommend any appropriation at this
Communication. We feel, however, that authority should be given to
the Grand Master to order payment of such fees and expenses as he
deems necessary.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:

GEORGE WASHINGTON MASONIC NATIONAL MEMORIAL ASSOCIATION

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the report of the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial Association and also that of
Past Grand Master John R. Moore, State Chairman, setting forth the
progress made by the Association and the amounts remaining to be paid.
After a careful study of the existing situation, they have strong reason
to believe that in view of the changes which have been made in the plans
for completing the project, this Grand Lodge may not be called upon for
any further contributions. However, in view of the uncertainties which
exist, we recommend that the assessment of l 5c per member be continued this year but the funds so raised not be paid over to the George
Washington Masonic Memorial Association but held by this Grand
Lodge to be disposed of only when approved by the Grand Master and
the Chairman of the Finance Committee.
In the event these funds are not paid over to the George Washington
Masonic National Memorial Association within three (3) years, such
funds are to be transferred to General Funds of this Grand Lodge.
MASONIC HOMES

INVESTMENTS FOR CONSTITUENT LoDGES

As a result of the adoption of the report of the Special Committee on
Investments for Constituent Lodges, those Lodges may now make investments in accordance with the Prudent Man Rule, subject to the restrictions in the legislation, provided that the officers or representatives
of the Lodges have consulted with Investment Counsel, whose fees shall
be paid by Grand Lodge.
The Assistant Grand Treasurer advises us that the Investment Counsel now servicing the investments under jurisdiction of the Investment
Committee, is willing to preform the same services for the Lodges of the
jurisdiction for an annual fee of not less than $3,000.00.
In the discussion of the proposed legislation with members of the
Committee on Investments for Constituent Lodges, some suggestions
have been made concerning the actual legislation, as well as plans for its
operation. As the Committee has agreed in principle with the suggestions
which have been made, we feel that it is not necessary to detail them here,
except to state that the Committee on Finance is in accord with the proposed legislation and recommends its adoption.
The fact that the plan is new handicaps us in providing the necessary
finances, but we believe that until more experience has been had that an
allowance in our budget of $3,000.00 will be sufficient, and this has been
provided.

Subsequent to the presentation to the Grand Lodge of the report of
the Trustees of the Masonic Homes in which a per capita tax of $1.00
was recommended, your Committee on Finance has carefully reviewed
the anticipated revenues and expenditures of the Homes for the coming
fiscal year. As a result, the Trustees have agreed with this Committee
that this per capita tax be reduced to seventy-6.ve cents ( 75c).
Your Committee therefore offers the following resolution and moves
its adoption:
RESOLVED, that a per capita tax of seventy-6.ve cents ( 75c) be
levied for the operation of the Masonic Homes.
MEMORIAL BUILDING COMMITI'EE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on 'Finance has considered very carefully the report of the Committee on a Memorial Building and its recommendations.
It is well to consider the activities of this Committee. It was appointed
6.rst in 1948 by Grand Master Warlow following the recommendation
of Grand Master Moore at the Annual Communication in 1947 for the
purpose of considering various sites and plans for the erection of a
building to serve as a dignified meeting place for the Grand Lodge and a
suitable location for its offices. There was made available to the Committee the amount remaining in the War Relief Fund raised during

292

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

293

World War II and now amounting to $158,507.44, subject to the prior
approval of the Grand Master, the· Deputy Grand Master, and the
Chairman of the Committee on Finance.
·
~his Committee has labored diligently but to date has not been able
to submit a proposal worthy of consideration by this Grand Lodge. In
its current report, the Committee states that due to building restrictions,
it now has under consideration several improved properties which might
be suitably remodeled for our purpose but that it is not in a position to
make a definite recommendation at this Communication. However, it
does recommend that the Committee be continued, and we concur in this.
The Committee also recognizes that we are experiencing great difficulty in accommodating the members of Grand Lodge at the Annual
Communications, hence the recommendation to hold the Annual Communications in the San Francisco Civic Auditorium for five years beginning in 1952, subject to the approval of the Grand Master. The
Committee also recognizes that moving to the Civic Center cannot be a
permanent arrangement but that eventually some provision must be made
for a permanent Grand Lodge headquarters and meeting place. However, no provision has been made for the financing of such a project,
and before any material progress can be made some attention must be
given to this important phase. Therefore, it proposes the levying of a
fifty-cent per capita tax for the purpose of creating a building fund.
Your Committee on Finance concurs in both of these recommenda. tions. Every member of the Grand Lodge has a right to attend all of its
sessions, particularly the opening session, and those who desire to do
so should be accorded by that right the provision of more commodious
quarters. The proposal to create a building fund with the assessment of
a per capita tax of 50c is sound. Our capital funds are not sufficient to
enable us to engage in a building enterprise. Outside of the War Relief
Fund, capital funds of this Grand Lodge have increased at the rate of
approximately $26,000 .a year for the past ten years. A fifty-cent per
capita tax would yield approximately $100,000.00 per annum, and if
carried over for a number of years, would create a very substantial
b~g fund.
~t should be pointed out that your Committee on Finance is not
recommending any particular type of building and that so far as we
know, no ddl!)ite proposal is under consideration. Our sole concern is
to build up the funds of Grand Lodge so that when the time comes, we •
shall be more adequately prepared to accept any proposal which may
seem sound. While we understand that it is not possible to rent the San
Francisco Civic Auditorium for two years, we believe that the Grand
Master should have the authority to engage such quarters as may seem
suitable for the next Communication and any subsequent Annual Com~on and thus relieve the crowded conditions which we find here.
~e th~fore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption,

and we are advised by the Committee on Policy and General Purpose
that it concurs in this resolution:
RESOLVED, that the amount of $158,507.44 now standing
in the War Memorial Building Fund be again made available
to the Memprial Building Committee for the purpose of acquiring
options, having plans drawn, or such other purposes as may be
deemed advisable in connection with the acquiring of a suitable
site for Grand Lodge headquarters, any such expenditures being
subject to the prior approval oE the Grand Master, the Deputy
Grand Master and the Chairman of the Committee on Finance,
with the understanding that no permanent decision shall be made
with reference to any proposed Grand Lodge headquarters or
meeting place without the approval of this Grand Lodge; ·and
BE IT RESOLVED FURTHER. that a per capita tax of
fifty cents ( 50c) be levied for the year 1951-1952, the proceeds
of which shall be paid into a building fund and to remain in such
building fund until otherwise ordered by the Grand Lodge; and
BE IT RESOLVED FURTHER. that the Grand Master be
authorized to enter into such commitments as may seem desirable
for the use of the San Francisco Civic Auditorium or such other
meeting place as may appear to be suitable for the next Annual
Communication and succeeding Annual Communications, but not
for a period exceeding five years.

GRAND LODGE AUDIT

counts of the Grand Treasurer. Disbursements were made by checks and
supported by properly approved vouchers. The disbursements made by the
Grand Secretary were from his Operating Fund bank account. Reimbursements to the Operating Fund by the Grand Treasurer were not made until
we had audited and approved the bills, which was done monthly. During
the year we found that no bills were paid by the Grand Secretary unless the
expense was provided for in the budget and the appropriation had not been
exceeded, except when prior approval had been obtained from the Grand
Master.
Bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries. A
certified list of the securities was received from the Anglo-California National
Bank, which holds the securities for safekeeping. All interest and dividends
due were received.
Sotoyome Lodge No. 123 has fulfilled its agreement during the year;
$150.00 monthly was paid by Grand Lodge and $100.00 monthly was received
by Grand Lodge from Sotoyome Lodge. No further payment from Grand
Lodge will be required as the annuitant died before the August payment was
made.
In our opinion, the attached statements present fairly the financial position of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California as at July 31, 1951, and the
result of its activities for the fiscal year 1950-51 in accordance with generally
accepted accounting principles.

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT FUND AUDIT

25.00

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
San Francisco, California
Gentlemen:
We have audited the accounts and records of the MASONIC ENDOW·
MENT FUND for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1951 and submit herewith the
following statements:
Exhibit A: Statement of Assets, July 31, 1951.
Exhibit B: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, August 1,
1950 to July 31, 1951.
Exhibit C: Statement of John and Lena Luckenbach Fund, July 31, 1951.
Exhibit D: Statement of Income and Capital Accounts for the fiscal year
ended July 31, 1951.
Schedule 1: Securities on hand, July 31, 1951.
Schedule 2: Securities redeemed and ·sold during the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1951.
