COMMENTS

$443,444.00

Cash:
The bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
All interest and dividends due from investments and saving bank accounts
were received ,b y the Grand Treasurer and deposited in the bank accounts
of the Masonic Homes. The total income received by the Homes from the
Endowment Funds amounted to $106,106,09.
Securities:
Securities on hand that were acquired in prior years, and securities
received through contributions and bequests and those purchased during
the current year are listed on Schedule 1. Securities redeemed and sold
during the current year are listed on Schedule 2.
Bonds purchased are listed at actual cost. Donated securities are listed
at market value when received, or at a nominal value of $1.00 if the actual
value is unknown.
Certified lists of securities held for the account of the Endowment Fund
were received from the Anglo California National Bank. The records were
checked to these lists and the securities not listed were inspected by us at
the office of the Grand Secretary.
During the month of June a check for $518.70 was received from Triangle
Lodge No. 548 without any notation as to what it was for. The check was
assumed to be for Endowment Fund contributions and so deposited. In
August the Lodge claimed the check was an advance payment on its 1951
annual return therefore, the Endowment Fund owes the Lodge $518. 70
which we hav~ shown as a liability on the Endowment Fund's Statement of
Assets, Exhibit A.
Increase in Fund:
The combined assets of the Endowment Fund and the Luckenbach Fund
show the following increase for the current year:

GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT-ENDOWMENT FUND

Other Endowment Assets:
The books of the Masonic Homes carry the record of the Harriet C. Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund. After the death of the beneficiaries of this
fund, the remainder will be transferred to the Endowment Fund. Schedule
2 of the Masonic Homes report shows that this fund had a balance of
$20,974.70 as at July 31, 1951.
The Masonic Homes also hold several pieces of real estate for the account
of the Endowment Fund. Whenever a sale is made, the proceeds will be
deposited to the account of the Endowment Fund.
Certificate:
In our opinion, the accompanying statements present fairly the financial
position of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund at July 31, 1951 in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles.

Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS & PARKER
Certified Public Accountants
Walter A Parker

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

MASONIC HOMES AUDIT

Investments:
At the request of the Board of Trustees, the securities held by the Homes
General Fund and those held by the various trust and special funds were
consolidated for the purposes of this report and are so listed on Schedule 1.
The trust funds' securities are still carried in separate portfolios and separate
bank accounts are maintained in order to account for each and every trust
fund in accordance with its agreement.
Bonds and stocks purchased are listed at cost; donated securities are
listed at market value when received, or at a nominal value of $1.00 if the
actual value is unknown. Life insurance policies are recorded at the amol.\Ilt
due at the death of the insured, if determinable and the premiums are fully
paid up; otherwise, at a value of $1.00.
The notes and contracts receivable were received from the sale of property and are listed at the unpaid balance as at July 31, 1951. Monthly payments of principal and interest have been received.
All bonds, stocks and notes are held by the Anglo California National
Bank and the life insurance policies and deeds for the real estate are in the
office of the Grand Secretary. Those held by the bank were verified by a
certified list from the bank and those in the Grand Secretary's office were
inspected.
Properties:
The value of the properties as shown on the Balance Sheet, Exhibit A,
is the cost of the two homes at Decoto and Covina. During the current year
$16,819.56 was disbursed as part payment on the construction of employees
cottages at Covina.

Masonic Homes of California
San Francisco, California

Funds Held in Trust:
With the exception of the Residents' Deposits, these funds were created
by donation or by bequest to the Homes for a particular purpose. The activities of each fund during the current year are shown on our Schedule 2.
All income due on the investments of these funds was received and credited
to the proper fund. Annuity payments were made as called for by the
contracts carried by the Flint Annuity and Wadleigh Endowment Funds.
Payments from the other trust funds are in accordance with the agreements.
The Residents' Deposits are personal money of the Decoto residents and the
Covina children being held in bank accounts by the superintendents for
safe-keeping. The Wadleigh Endowment Fund is to be transferred to the
Masonic Homes Endowment Fund after the death of the annuitants.
Funds Held for Special Purposes:
The Lee R. Talbert Fund was created by bequest for the benefit of the
children at Covina, therefore, this fund has been transferred to the Covina
Special Fund. The Verbarg Fund was created by bequest for the benefit
of the Decoto residents; therefore, this fund has been transferred to the
Decoto Special Fund. This was done in order to decrease the number of
separate funds carried by the Homes.
The remaining funds were created by the Board of Trustees to set aside
money that is to be used only for the purpose indicated by the title of the
fund. The Unappropriated Reserve account (formerly named ''Decoto
Monthly Grant Fund") was built up mainly from contributions of money
and property from the Decoto residents and is to be used to pay the monthly
allowance to the Decoto residents and for any other purpose except for
direct operating expenses of the Homes.
The activities of these special funds during the current year are shown
on our Schedule 3.

Revenue and Expenses:
A detailed audit was made of the revenue and expense accounts and we
satisfied ourselves as to the general correctness of the accounting records.
The Endowment Fund income received is in agreement with the Endowi;rient
Fund audit. Interest and dividends due on the investments were received.
All records of the contributions received through Lodges were examined
and the amounts received appear to be all that can be collected. All disbursements were made by checks and supported by proper vouchers.
The 1950 annual returns from the Lodges were audited and the $25.00
contributions thereon, plus the contributions received up to July 31, 1951,
agree with the amount turned over to the Treasurer by the Grand Secretary.
The per capita on 194,294 members at $1.00, in amount $194,294.00, was also
received by the Treasurer from the Grand Secretary.
The operations of the Masonic Homes resulted in an excess of revenue
over expense amounting to $113,622.63, as shown in Exhibit C.
Certificate:
In our opinion, the accompanying statements present fairly the financial
position of the Masonic Homes of California at July 31, 1951 and the res~lt
of its operations for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1951, in accordance with
generally accepted accounting principles.

Visitations to Lodges
By Mr. Henry, Mrs. Henry and/or Children
November 11, 1950: Mr. Henry was
guest at the dinner meeting of The
Edison Masonic Club.
March 22, 1951: Mr. and Mrs.
Henry were guests of The Westerners Masonic Club at a dinner in celebration of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the founding of the club.
April 2, 1951: At the stated meeting of All States Lodge No. 593, Mr.
Henry and children from the Masonic Home were special guests.
Linda Allison, Bill Angel, Ellis Ashurst, Larry Ashurst, Billy Edwards,
Bill Joy, Judy Johnson and Kathleen
Johnson participated in the program.
May 3, 1951: Bill Angel (Intermediate Boy) was the guest of East

Gate Lodge No. 290, at their stated
meeting.
May 6, 1951: Each group in the
Home was represented in a program
presented by the children of the Los
Angeles Masonic Board of Relief. A
feature of this program was the Masonic Home Choral Group. Mr.
Henry accompanied the children.
May 7, 1951: Mrs. Henry and Laura
Allison, '52, were guests at the dinner
meeting of Damascus Lodge No.
648. Mr. Henry, Bill Angel, Ellis
Ashurst, Earl Harris and Bill Joy
were guests at the stated meeting of
Anchor Lodge No. 273.
May 16, 1951: Mr. Henry was guest
speaker at a special meeting of San
Pedro Lodge No. 332.

Show'' at the Home. Presented by

Hills Lodge.

at the Home for children and staff.

and Mr. D. F. Dingman were hosts to

dinner before returning to the Home.

Annual Christmas Party given for

Lodge No. 607, at the Monrovia Masonic Temple.

Now one hundred years later our Committee is pleased to present
herewith the reviews of the proceedings of all the Grand Jurisdictions
that have come to us since the last Grand Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California. Has Masonry changed in 100 years? How many of
these problems of 100 years ago are still with us? Our Committee studied
and examined the Communications of 60 Foreign and Domestic Grand
Lodge Communications to find out.

.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
FOREWORD
It has been said, "Nothing is quite as dead as yesterday's news,"
yet I feel we may look back with some profit to the review of Masonic
thought of one hundred years ago and compare it with Masonic problems and happenings of today.
The first Committee on Foreign Correspondence in California was
composed of a group of four very distinguished Masons. Levi Stowell,
the chairman, was the first Grand Treasurer. Benjamin D. Hyam was the
first Senior Grand Deacon. J. D. Stevenson was the first Most Worshipful Grand Master of Masons in California. The fourth member was the
renowned Past Grand Master of Maryland, Charles Gilman. who was
the presiding officer when three Lodges met on the morning of April 17,
1850, for the purpose of considering the propriety of establishing a
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons for the State of California.
This first Correspondence Committee presented their report one
hundred years ago on November 5, 1851, and stated that they had
reviewed the published proceedings of sixteen Grand Lodges, Maine,
Vermont, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, New York, Maryland, District of Columbia, Virginia, North Carolina, Indiana, Michigan, Wisconsin, Missouri, Mississippi, Arkansas, and Florida. Accident, they
said, had probably prevented the reception of others.
The Committee stated that among the various subjects of greater or
less importance which had engaged the attention of their Sister Grand
Lodges during the past two years might be mentioned the following:
.1. The difficulties in the Grand Lodge of New York.
2. The propriety of organizing a Supreme or General Grand Lodge
of the United States.
3. The encroachment upon the territorial jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of New York by the Grand Lodge of Hamburg.
i. The prerogatives of a Grand Master in and out of Grand Lodge.
5. Whether Master Masons, not members of Grand Lodge, should
.be permitted to be present during the transaction of certain business
therein.
6. Whether it is competent for a Master of a Lodge, or even for the
Lodge itself, to demand of a member his reasons for voting against an
applicant for degrees, or for membership.
7. Whether the ballot ·should be taken prior to the conferring of
each degree.

481

In order to clarify the issues and present them in their current application we have grouped these topics into fourteen s4bject headings.
The first seven deal with the issues just mentioned, the remainder relate
to recent problems which are a part of Masonic thought today.
Regarding the split in the New York Grand Lodge and the troubles
over territorial jurisdiction, these questions have been settled long ago.
They are just memories of the past.
On the question of balloting, I think today that we will all agree that
a Mason is responsible to no human power for the vote that he casts on
the petition of a candidate. To his own conscience alone is he to answer
for the motives that have led to the act itself. The whole object of the
secret ballot would otherwise be defeated.
On the question of whether or not a separate ballot should be taken
prior to the conferring of each degree, it seems to be the concensus of
opinion today that only one ballot is necessary and not three.
The question or propriety of organizing a Supreme Grand Lodge of
the United States had many adherents one hundred years ago. California
seemed to be strongly in favor of it. One difficulty seemed to be the lack
of agreement upon the provisions of a general constitution. Increased
interest in the next few years led to the calling of a convention of delegates from several of the Grand Lodges at Lexington, Kentucky, on
September 17, 1853, and later a general meeting of delegates of all
Grand Lodges at Washington, D. C., on January 3, 1855.
Yet today after reviewing sixty Domestic and Foreign Grand Lodge
Communications we find only one reference to a World Organization or
to a United or General Grand Lodge, and that was in the writings of
our Missouri correspondent who, as he says, has been preaching unification these many, many years.
Regarding Masoni~ thought of a century ago. the question of
Masonic Charity would probably be most predominant. We in California saw the influx of thousands of people in a mad stampede to the
gold fields. Hundreds of these newcomers were Masons. Soon came disillusionment. sickness, and destitution. It therefore happened in the fall
of 1849 and the following winter that large numbers of Masons as well

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

as others left the mines for Sacrame nto for medtcal advice and nursing
care. Immediately a group of Masons came to the rescue and started a
hospital to take care of the influx. This was real Masonic Charity with
no thought of recompense. This group of Masons raised and paid out
over $32,000, and soon were in arrears about $14,000. That was v.r_hen
a Circular was sent to all Grand Lodges appealin g for help.

On the physical qualifications of candidat es for the honors of
Masonry the Correspo ndence Committee of 1851 expresse d surprise that
there should have been a difference of opinion on this subject. "Let a
Mason ask himself," they said, "Wheth er the candidat e who is blinnl.
or deaf, or who has lost a leg or an arm is capable of acquiring a knowledge of Masonry , so as to impart the same to another? Whethe r he is
capable of making himself known as a Mason, under all circumstances
in the dark as well as ~he light? His answer to these simple questions:
as answer them he can in but one way, will supersed e all argumen t upon
this subject."
Today there is a wide divergence .of opinion on this question. The
trend seems to be towards relaxatio n of strict physical requirements for
petitioners, especially since World War II.
New problems confronting Masonic Lodges at the present time such
as the Blood Bank, Public Schools Week, the Liquor Question , Youth
Organiza tions, and Communism will be taken up in detail in our report.
As Cor~espondence Chairma n, I offer my "Apolog ia." The topical
form of review seemed to me to present the possibility of greater unification and simpliflcation of the ideas of Masonry througho ut the world
today. This Correspo ndence Committee wanted their report to be of
sufficient interest to be read •b y thinking Masons in all parts of our
country. It was with this end in view that hours of reading, research,
editing, writing and re-writing were spent on this report.
It is the hope of this Committee that reports of Correspo ndence
Committees be read in the individual Lodges in order that all Masons
may know atid appreciate, and become better acquaint ed with the prob..
lems and achievements of Masonry in this world of ours today.

482

Today, I think, we would agree that our greatest Masonic charity
is the money that all of us contribu te to our Masonic homes. Millions of
dollars annually are given cheedull y by three and one-half million
Masons in the United States to support directly our Masonic homes and
hospitals, and indirectly through the granting of relief to help care for
our needy elderly brethren , their wives, and orphan children.
Naturall y costs are rising. Many Grand Lodges are raising the per
capita tax. Some Jurisdictions are substitut ing direct relief rather than
giving institutional care.
Do crises occur now as they did in Californ ia in 18507 Yes, brethren ,
they may occur any time and any place. Today's papers (July 15, 1951)
tell us of the devastat ing floods which are wrecking and destroyin g
Kansas City, Missouri.
Last year an appeal went out by the Most Worship ful Harry Coddington, Grand Master of Manitob a, asking for aid to help his stricken
Grand Lodge caused by tremendous floods in his province. Not long
before a heart rending appeal for aid came from the Grand Lodge of
Ecuador . You probably remember the disastrou s and terrifyin g earthquake which struck that country.
In 1851, the Grand Master said, "I would recommend that steps be
at once taken in regard to the educating of the children of Masons. I
notice other sister Grand Lodges, as well as Lodges in Europe are
engaged with much attention in this very importan t subject, and I trust
we will by judicious action be enabled to imitate them."
This question of educatin g the youth of our country seemed then
uppermost in the minds of many Grand Lodge officers. Many Europea n
jurisdictions taxed their respective members to aid in supporti ng their
schools. Here in the United States, Missouri, Kentucky, Texas, Alabama
and others had Masonic Colleges and Primary Schools.
Our Grand Masters in Californ ia at every Communication emphasized our duty to provide for the education of children of Masonic parents who needed help and for the educatio n of orphans of deceased
Masons.
Masonic Educatio n today has shifted towards the support and sponsoring of "Youth Organiza tions," the support and backi~g of the Pu~lic
School System, and more and more towards the instructing or educating
of the initiate and candidat e in the three degrees of Masonry .

The Ballot
A weapon that comes down as still
As snowflakes fall upon the sod,
But executes a freeman's will
As lightning does the will of God.
By John Pierpont
WYOMING, 1950, Committee on Jurisprudence

( 1 ) As to the proposed amendment to Sec. 537 of the Code relating
to balloting and petitions, your Committee feels that a revision of the
entire section would be preferable to the addition of a sub-section to the
present section and we therefore recommend as a substitute to the proposed amendment, the following, and recommend its adoption, to-wit:
"Sec;. 537. When more than one candidate is ready to be balloted
upon, the Master may in his discretion order the ballot to be spread upo:i
all such candidates collectively or upon each candidate separately in
such order as he may elect. If a collective ballot is ordered and it appears
clear then all of said candidates shall be deemed and declared elected to
membership. If one or more black cubes appear in such collective ballot
then such ballot shall be declared void, and a separate ballot ordered
upon each candidate in such order as the Master may elect. A clear
ballot elects each candidate to the three degrees or affiliation. Should
there appear one negative vote or black cube in the ballot box on any
individual ballot the Master SHALL order a second trial of the ballot,
but the result of the second trial shall in all cases be final and conclusive
and shall then and there ·be so declared by the ~faster and such declaration can not be set aside by the Master, the lodge, the Grand Master, or
the Grand Lodge." Adopted.
NEW YORK, 1949, Committee Report
Another proposal that was defeate~ after considerable discussion
was one that would permit each Lodge to provide in its by-laws that the
ballot on a candidate who has received an unanimous favorable report of
the Investigating Committee should require two black ballots to reject.
PENNSYLVANIA, 1950, Grand Master

Election
During recent years it has become customary to admit as guests to
the Communications of the Grand Lodge Master Masons who were not
members thereof. Inasmuch as Grand Lodge Hall at times will not conveniently accommodate all of the members of the Grand Lodge who

488

489

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

desire to attend and since in voting it is impossible to distinguish between
the members and these guests, but more especially as there is no provision in the Ahiman Rezon granting them this privilege, I have directed
that the Grand Tyler admit to subsequent Communications, only members of the Grand Lodge, i.e.• Past Masters by service and those Brethren
who at present are serving Lodges as Masters and Wardens.
I have further directed that after the Grand Lodge has been opened,
elections conducted and business, on which a vote be required, transacted, Master Masons, not members of the Grand Lodge, be admitted
as guests: provided a resolution to that effect is adopted by vote of a
majority of the members present at that Communication. However, such
guests may be required to retire if a vote becomes necessary after their
admission.

rivalry of certain competitive Masonic groups fearing that one or the
other might gain undue advantage. And so Symbolic Freemasonry
suffers.
Here in these United States we have some forty-nine Grand Lodges.
each with its Grand Master. We all must know that all Grand Masters
are not leaders: some are the products of a vicious cycle in which some
Grand Master appoints a personal friend to the foot of the line, and the
brethren, year after year, continue to advance the appointee until 6nally
he wears the purple of the fraternity. This good brother may have the
best intentions in the world: he may know all of the details of the lodges
of the l 37th District, or the working of the lodge in Podunkville, but he
lacks, not through his own fault, that necessary training which should
be required of each Grand Officer to make him realize that "Freemasonry
is an organization which unites men of every race, country and creed"
into a brotherhood of man.
The world today stands at the cross-roads of civilization. The next
decade will prove whether we are to have a peaceful world or a maelstrom of war. To our way of thinking, the section known as Western
Europe holds the key to the picture.
What are Freemasons doing about it?
Are we to follow the lead of a Grand Lodge which insists that Freemasonry must not have any spoken ideas as to what the future of this
world is to be? Are we, as an organization, to sit supinely by and permit
the Hitlers and the Mussolinis to continue their nefarious processes of
dividing the world? Adolf Hitler is dead: Benito Mussolini is dead. But
the world is ye,t full of potential Hitlers and Mussolinis eager to take up
where both laid down. That hideous ideology taught the children of
Europe is not dead. nor will it expire until that whole generation born
from 1922-40 shall have passed out of the international picture.

SOUTH DAKOTA, 1950, Grand Master
Experience is the greatest of all teachers. We recognize this fundamental fact and then fail to avail ourselves in our Grand Lodge deliberations of the greatest fund of experience, that which our Past Masters
have gathered through their Masonic careers.
We honor them, they come to Grand Lodge as Junior Warden,
Senior Warden, and 6nally as Master of their respective Lodge, and
participate in our Grand Lodge activities. And then when they should
be of greatest value to us, we relegate them to the sidelines. That ought
not to be so. Every Past Master should continue to be a member of the
Grand Lodge and have a vote and voice in its deliberations, and give us
the benefit of their experience and mature judgment.

Recommendation No. 5
I. therefore, recommend that a study be given to the feasibility of
amending our By-Laws so as to retain all Past Masters as members of
the Grand Lodge, without right to mileage, or other remuneration for
expense of attendance upon the Grand Lodge, with voting powers when
present in person, but to have no right to vote by proxy.

MASONIC HOMES
In 1949 Grand Master Paul B. Habans of the state of Louisiana
appointed a committee of three who in conjunction with a similar committee from the Eastern Star were to discuss the advisability of founding
a joint Home or separate Homes for aged and infirm members of both
of the fraternal organizations. This committee recommended that a similar committee be appointed to make a thorough study of Masonic and
Eastern Star Homes, their cost, cost of operation, service and eligibility
of membership. They further recommended that questionnaires be sent
out to constituent Lodges and Eastern Star Chapters asking for such
information as the committee felt necessary before making any definite
recommendations. The recommendations of the committee were adopted.
Brother Gayle in his Correspondence Report of last year ( 1950)
under the title, "Benevolent Activities--Masonic Homes," (pages 126
to 143 of the 1950 Proceedings of Grand Lodge) with a view of inform-

ing the Craft as to such matters, covered the operation, cost and maintenance of Masonic Homes and Benevolent activities of Grand Lodges in

Iowa, Georgia, Nebraska, Oregon, South Carolina, New York, New

During the current year, 1951, the co,mmittee made further study
of Homes and Benevolent activities in other Jurisdictions and reports
of committees of other states engaged in similar investigations. The following states are covered in the 1951 Correspondence Report: Missouri,
Arkansas, Montana, North Dakota, Colorado, District of Columbia,
Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, Illinois and Oklahoma. In this
two-year study of Masonic Homes and Benevolent Activities the committee's report covered thirty-six states.
After studying the report very carefully the committee came to the
conclusion that the erection of "A Home for Aged" is undesirable and
recommends no action be taken at this time with reference to building or
operation of "A Home for Aged."
The committee recommended instead that Grand Lodge should set
up agencies in both Grand Lodge and in the constituent Lodges of the
State, for the administration of relief to aged or indigent Masons and
·the widows of Masons in need of assistance. A resolution was introduced covering their recommendations, and was adopted as amended
by the Joint Committees of Masonic Law and Jurisprudence and Audit
and Accounts.
·
We may conclude from this careful two-year survey that the present
time is not propitious for building "Homes for the Aged." Social welfare by the Federal Government, State aid, government restrictions on
new building, rising costs, refusal of some Grand Lodges to raise the
per capita tax for home care and building are some of the reasons given
for the trend towards direct relief rather than institutional care. It is
also said that the cost per patient in a home is exorbitant, and that more
can be done at less cost under the Field Aid System.
Arkansas found it expedient to close the Masonic Home (for children) at Batesville, tran sferring the property to Arkansas College for a
cash consideration plus 40 scholarships which the Grand Lodge will
award to deserving boys and girls. Thus the work of caring for boys
and girls needing the Grand Lodge help is taken care of without the
burden of running a Masonic Home.
In 1949 funds were raised in Indiana to build a new wing to the
Administration Building of the Masonic Home. In spite of this expansion there are serious problems as to the future maintenance of the Hom'e
and a committee was appointed to study these -problems under the fol-

IOWA, 1949 (Grand Master)
•
Received a report from the Grand Master relative to a circular letter
sent to many of the Lodges suggesting the establishment of a Masonic
Home. "I may as well state in the beginning that I am against such a
project," the Grand Master declared. "During the last twelve months
it has been my privilege to visit several other jurisdictions at the time of
Grand Lodge sessions. In each of these, where they have a Masonic
Home, there has been discussion and trouble. The cost per patient in a
Home is exorbitant. We are doing more for our less fortunate members
by our Field Work than that which is being done in those jurisdictions
that have Homes."

MISSOURI, 1950

VERMONT, 1949

The committee recommended that, without discontinuing the
Masonic Home of Missouri, it be the policy to take care of future
applicants as far as practical in their own homes or in such homes as
they are living at the time of application. It was found that the cost
of such relief is less, and the morale of the recipients is much better
under the plan of outside relief. Lodges are to be required to pay a portion of such outside relief. to ease the load on the Grand Lodge and at
the same time bring home to the lodges their responsibility to their
indigent brethren.

The Grand Lodge spent for charity and relief the sum of $9,000.
There is no Masonic Home. Under the Vermont rules, after a Lodge
spends for charity in a year a sum equal to $1.00 per capita it looks to
the Grand Lodge for assistance. In many instances the Grand Lodge
gave Lodges permission to exceed the $1.00 limit and gave additional
aid from the Lodge funds. The Grand Master believes that:
"The individual. personal application of relief locally rather than
collective application in a Masonic Home is the best system."

TENNESSEE, 1950
Tennessee has no Masonic Home. In 1926, after operating a Home
for 26 years, they gave it to the State and since then have .given relief
through a fund which grants outside relief, permitting applicants to live
among their friends and relatives or, when necessary, assuming their
care in a hospital or convalescent home. $70,000.00 was appropriated
for the purpose.
For a complete and thorough discussion of the Tennessee Plan see
pages 143-145 of the Proceedings of the 1951 Grand Lodge of the State
of Louisiana. The committee stated that this plan is worthy of emulation,
since it appears to be most efficient and satisfactory to both the recipient
of the relief and to the Grand Lodge.
One interesting paragraph taken from the report is as follows :
"When a widow made application for assistance, or for admission to
the Home for herself and children, she was given the choice of coming
into the Home, or receiving assistance in her own home and community,
and, with two exceptions in six years, every applicant elected to stay
in her own home, except two, and the two families that came into the
Home remained only two months. The system worked so well with the
widows and children, that they tried it with the old people. In every
instance it was found that they, too, preferred to remain in their own
communities. In each case a budget was worked out and a definite grant
made. The old people were, of course, in some kind of a home when
they made application. After an investigation, if the home were found
to be all right, even though humble, and the people worthy, their home
was maintained for them, and a budget worked out for them that would
suit their condition and surroundings. It was found that these old people
were a definite part of the community. where they had friends and relatives, and it was hard to move them into new surroundings and among
total strangers. The budget worked out was always liberal and flexible,
and one that would raise their standard of living."

KANSAS, 1950 (Grand Master)
A sixteen-page brochure entitled "Your Kansas Masonic Home,"
liberally illustrated with pictures of the buildings and scenes of the
interior of the Home, was prepared and has been presented to the membership. This action, apparently, has met with favor as many complimentary remarks have been heard, and, in most cases, surprise expressed
as to the scope of the endeavor and the successful results attained.
We have a changing picture at our Home, which presents problems
that must be met and must be solved. We no longer have an appreciable
number of children as members of our Home family. In 1936, we provided a home and care for seventy-six boys and girls. In 1939, this number had been reduced to thirty-five youngsters, while in 1950 we have
nine on our rolls, with but five children actually residents of the Home.
From the time our Home was opened on September 10, 1896, until
1943, the number of Masons living at the Home exceeded the number
of ladies who had gained admission either as wives or widows of Master
Masons or members of the Eastern Star. In that year, for the first time,
the ladies outnumbered the men 138 to 113. Today we have 92 Masons
living at the Home, while the number of lady residents is listed at 166.
Approximately one-half of this number has been admitted through
Eastern Star affiliation.

ILLINOIS, 1950
There were 233 members on September 30, 1950, of which 141 were
men and 92 women. There were, at that time, 91 members in the hospital
of which 56 were men and 35 women. During the year there were 56
admitted and 42 deaths.
Our hospital has been full to capacity at all times and you, as a
member of the Grand Lodge of Illinois, are facing a problem which must
be solved. We must have more hospital rooms. In some of the applications for admission, which we receive, we find that we must reject the
applicant because he or she is a hospital case. In our present capacity
our hospital facilities only take care of the guests in the Home. To accept
an applicant who is financially unable to care for himself and reject one
who is physically and financially down and out is not in any way discharging our obligations to those who need our help. We have been
able, during the year, to admit four hospital cases but we have accepted
several more and have been forced to notify the Lodge that we could not
take care of the applicant until we have more room in our hospital.
Twelve new guests have gone permanently to the hospital within a few

496

days of their arrival. Brethren, this is our problem a11d one to which you
must find the answer for us.

CONNECTICUT, 1950
The work of The Masonic Charity Foundation of Connecticut is
carried on at the Masonic Home located in Wallingford, and elsewhere
about the state as occasion requires. In Wallingford, the Foundation
owns a large tract of land on which the buildings of the Home have been
erected. The buildings now include a substantial administration building,
a large fireproof dormitory erected in 1919, and a modem fireproof one
hundred bed hospital completed in 1926. These buildings with their
splendid equipment, were made possible by funds raised among the
Masons of Connecticut, ably assisted by members of the Eastern Star,
The Order of the Amaranth and The White Shrine, and represent an
investment of over Eight Hundred Thousand Dollars. The Foundation
is now caring for 340 members, of whom 226 are women and girls, and
114 men and boys. The expenses of maintenance amounted to $390,254 .68 in 1949 and were raised in part by per capita tax laid by the
Grand Lodge on the members of the Subordinate Lodges throughout the
state. By vote of the Grand Lodge, passed at its annual communication
on April 7, 1949, the per capita tax was set at 75 cents per year. The
individual Lodges are thus required to support the Grand Lodge to the
extent of 75 cents per member only. A special assessment of $20 (effective since January 1, 1931 ) was laid on all initiates and affiliates from
sister Grand Jurisdictions for the Endowment Fund. A special assessment of $6 per year (or $2 if the Mason was raised prior to January 1,
1900) was made in 1948 on all members of the Craft, effective in 1949,
to aid in carrying on the work of the Foundation.

WISCONSIN, 1950
The vision and generosity of Brother Willard A. Van Brunt, who
presented the 319 acre farm and buildings, and an endowment fund of
$200,000.00 to provide a haven for the indigent, inaugurated this great
charitable undertaking. The present Home building was erected in 1923
at a cost of $375,000.00. The hospital was built by the Order of the
Eastern Star in 1924, at a cost exceeding $78,000.00. I have had the
privilege of attending nine meetings of the Board at the Home during
the past year. I have been impressed by the spirit of contentment that
prevails. The Home is beautiful and comfortable. The food 'is plentiful
and wholesome. The care is painstaking and sympathetic. It is Masonry
in action. The Home Board is conscientiously striving to make the Home
a real haven for the needy aged.
The population during the year has averaged about 120 and there
have been only a few occasions when we had much of a waiting list.
At present there are 42 men and 77 women. There were 19 deaths during
the year and 28 admissions. The hospital has been crowded all year
and the need for larger capacity is very evident.

MISSISSIPPI, 1950
Relief Fund
This fund was created to aid our Lodges in caring for those whose
burdens have become greater than they can carry. The Board of Managers has granted all just appeals for relief received from our Lodges.
I have often wondered if all worthy cases of distress have come to the
attention of our Lodges and, through them, to the Grand Lodge. RELIEF is one of our principal Tenets and merita; our best thought in order
to dispense it in a practical manner. What a wonderful thing it is to
grant assistance to the needy so that he or she may continue to live
among friends and relatives and not be taken te strange surroundings
to suffer, and perhaps die, of homesickness. By our present system,
many a widow has ·been enabled to maintain a home and many an aged
and infirm brother has ended his days in comfort amid familiar scenes,
and surrounded by friends and loved ones. I feel that, "We builded
better than we knew." Our budget in this regard has not been exceeded
during the past year.

VERMONT, 1950 (Special Committee Report)
Masonic Charity and Relief (Current)
The charity income at the present time . comes from_two sources.
( 1 ) Income of the Permanent Charity Fund, approximately $3,000 per
year and ( 2) 25c per capita assessment, approximately $4.500 per year
making our total income for current charity or relief about $7,500 per
year. This has proved ample to cover expenses up until the year 1948.
For the past two years, however, we have shown a deficit of approximately $7.000 with a further deficit anticipated this year. If the current
trend continues one of two things must be done: The individual Lodges
must pay a greater proportion of their own charity expense or else our
Grand Lodge income for current charity must be increased.
The Grand Lodge has been paying for the last five years a pension
of $960.00 to a most worthy employee who had served this Grand Lodge
faithfully for forty years. We will no longer have this expense.
Your Committee is concerned with the increase in recent years of the
amount of refunds to suberdinate Lodges for charity and relief. While
your Committee does not in any way wish to give the impression that
these payments are not entirely deserving, we are struck, however, with
the fact that the trend on the part of many people today is to shun, not
only their public, but also their personal responsibilities.

The following telegram was read to the Craft:
Washington, D. C., June 13; 1950
Don Carpenter
Memorial Hall
Burlington, Iowa
Most Worshipful Harry Coddington, Grand Master, Manitoba,
appeals for aid to all United States Grand Lodges through this Association to help his stricken Grand Lodge relieve the great suffering caused
by tremendous floods in his province. Not setting any quota. Suggest
that if in your wisdom your Grand Lodge could contribute one cent per

M.S.A. appealing for help. Floods that ravaged the Red River Valley
caused much property damage and many Masonic families were made

Grand Lodges in Canada and the United States immediately responded to the appeal of the Grand Master Harry Coddington. The
Grand Lodge of Arkansas sent $1,000. British Columbia sent $5,000.

Grand Lodge session voted another $10,000. Idaho gave $127 through
the M.S.A. Iowa sent $900, Louisiana gave $400, and Nova Scotia
contributed $1,000. The Grand Lodge of Scotland was ready to contribute £1,000, but was notified that it was not needed.
A Special Committee acknowledged donations of more than $61,000.
Some $18,000 was contributed through the Masonic Service Association.
When the heart-rending appeal was sent qut to the World by
Grand Master Jorge Ripalda of Ecuador after the earthquake calamity
which struck that country, Grand Lodges in the United States gave
immediate assistance. The Grand Lodge of Arizona sent $200, Connecticut contributed $1,200, Kansas . sent $500, Massachusetts gave
$1,000, New Jersey gave $1,800, New Mexico $346, Oregon $250,
Rhode Island $1,242, and West Virginia gave $250. These are only a
few of the Grand Lodges that gave immediate financial assistance. This
Brethren, is Masonic Charity in action.

MASONIC EDUCATION
This subject seemed to be an important one, Many Grand Masters
spoke at length emphasizing what should be done. Committee reports
were lengthy and most of them optimistic. Some Educational Committees were made permanent, and a few new research lodges were formed.
The important question facing all Masonic Lodges. according to one
Committeeman is "How can we best teach Masonry. not only to our
initiates. but to those who are already members. and maintain the keen
interest which motivated each of them to become members?"
When and if this question can be answered satisfactorily then and
then only will we get more than the ten per cent average membership
into our Lodge Rooms. Our Grand Master Arthur Paulsen of California
said, "The mere recitation of ritual is not enough. Masonry goes further
than just ritual. What every Mason does after taking the degrees of
Masonry is to interpret the meaning for himself. What is lacking is a
system of Masonic education to further the rit_u al and symbolic work."

01-llO, 1950 (Correspondence Committee)
Educational Programs
We believe it is encouraging to note the emphasis being placed on
Masonic education. There is no universal system used. Perhaps none
could be devised to fit the needs of all Lodges. The mere fact that constructive thought is being given to this matter is what counts. The application of any plan of education is largely a local matter. Grand Lodges

can and in many instances are serving as material supply sources. A well
planned educational program will do much to prevent membership trends
going in the wrong direction.

NEW HAMPSl-llRE, 1950 (Committee Report)
The Committee on Masonic Education. after careful consideration
of the subject, is of the opinion that steps should be taken by the Grand
Lodge to provide our candidates with educational and explanatory
material to supplement the work of the several degrees.
We recommend that the Grand Lodge authorize the Committee on
Masonic Education to prepare and have published four booklets to be
entitled "On The Threshold," " Entered Apprentice," "Fellow Craft"
and " Master Mason" for distribution to the subordinate Lodges free of
cost to said Lodges, and that the Secretaries of the several Lodges be
instructed to forward a copy of the booklet "On The Threshold" to
each candidate when he is notified to appear for the conferring of the
Entered Apprentice Degree and to present to each candidate a copy of
the booklets entitled "Entered Apprentice," "Fellow Craft" and "Master
Mason" at the conclusion of the conferring of the respective degrees.

IOWA, 1950 (Special Committee on Lodges of Research)
A committee was appointed by the incoming Grand Master to make
a careful study and submit recommendations to the Grand Lodge at the
present session, giving in detail the necessary corrections of the law to
carry out such a project.
Your committee has made such a study and find and recommend
that the law should be amended to permit the formation of such Lodges
of Research in Iowa, and, especially because Iowa has always been a seat
of Masonic learning and with its many activities in that particular, that
this jurisdiction is especially fitted to aid and assist any such Lodge of
Research or the members thereof.
We have contacted all of the Grand Lodges of the United States
- with reference to their attitude about Masonic Research Lodges and
find that several have permitted the organization of such Lodges in their
jurisdictions. Probably the original Research Lodge was in New York,

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

505

and since then the Grand Lodges that have had such Research Lodges
for several years include North Carolina, Oregon, Missouri, as well as
·New York, and we learn that ten Grand Lodges of the United States
now have authorized such research organizations.
Iowa Grand Lodge Rules and Regulations for Lodges of Research
(a) "Fifteen or more Master Masons, members in good standing
of any Iowa lodge or lodges, may petition the Grand Master for, and
he may in his discretion issue, without fees and without compliance
with the usual requirements, prescribed for the issuance of a Dispensation under the present requirement of Chapter 17, of the 1949 Code, a
Dispensation to such members to form a Lodge of Research. And a
Charter may be issued, without a fee, to such a Lodge of Research upon
approval by the Grand Lodge at an annual communication: also, without
compliance with the usual requirements prescribed for the issuance of a
Charter. '
The territorial jurisdiction of such Lodge of Research when formed
shall be co-extensive with the territorial jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge.
The membership shall consist of the Charter Members thereof and
those members of Iowa lodges who are later admitted by affiliation,
which affiliation may be had without a dimit from a subordinate or regular lodge or a certificate of payment of dues.
Lodges of Research shall be designated and numbered separately
and consecutively with "Research Lodge No. 1."
A lodge formed hereunder may elect to honorary, contributing, or
subscribing membership Master Masons or lodges of Master Masons
in good stand\flg in this or any other Grand Jurisdiction in Masonic
affiliation with this Grand Lodge under such conditions as by its by-laws
may be prescribed, which by-laws shall limit the power to vote to members belonging to Iowa lodges only.
( b) A Lodge of Research shall be a lodge of research only and have
the right, power, and authority only:
( 1) To promote within its own membership Masonic study and
historical research.
( 2) The present findings and conclusions to be the lodge for discussion and interchange of judgment:
( 3) To publish at convenient intervals proceedings or transactions
containing such portions of the addresses and discussions in lodges as
may be desirable to print:
( 4) To publish new Masonic books of outstanding merit:
( 5) To reproduce or print Masonic documents of historical importance:
( 6) To reprint scarce Masonic books and pamphlets;
( 7) To open and close its lodge on the Third Degree:
( 8) To have such rights and authority as may be necessary to
carry out such work.

506

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Any publications shall be without expense to the Grand Lodge.
For the purpose of carrying out such rights, powers and authority
it may make by-laws providing for the election of its officers: for the
establishment, control. and limitations of its membership for the time and
place and nature of its meetings: for the payment of dues and to effectuate the purposes of its organization.
Neither its designation as a lodge or its organization as such, nor the
issuance of a Dispensation or a Charter shall constitute. or be construed
as giving to it, or any of its officers or members, any of the Masonic
honors, rights, powers, privileges, or authority possessed by a Masonic
lodge or by any of its officers or members, except such as are herein
specifically granted by the Grand Lodge. Nor shall it or any of its members be subject to any additional duties or obligations of a Masonic
lodge or a member thereof because it is a Masonic lodge, except under
specific regulations or orders of the Grand Lodge or its own by-laws
passed within the scope of the rights, powers, and authority granted to
it by the Grand Lodge.
( c) No person shall continue to be an active member of a Lodge of
Research unless he is a regular member in good standing in a subordinate
lodge of Masons. And such a lodge shall at all times have at least ten
members in good standing in Iowa in their subordinate lodges, or its
Charter must be revoked by the Grand Master.

MISSOURI, 1950
Chartered only 9 years ago the Missouri Lodge of Research is now
the largest institution of its kind in this country. The heartening growth
in membership is evidence of the increasing interest of the Craft in
Missouri in Masonic history and particularly in Missouri Masonic
history.
And few states have as interesting Masonic history as does Missouri,
for in no other state has Freemasonry been so woven into the fabric of
the civil, political and religious life of the state.
Within the past several years the Lodge of Research has placed in
the hands of its members numerous books and pamphlets of interest to
members of the fraternity, including the biographies of prominent Missouri Masons. Membership will mean eventually an invaluable Masonic
library.
The Grand Master said:
While there has been a fine increase in our membership in the past
year, we feel that a membership of 603 is infinitesimal when we consider
that this Grand Lodge represents almost 115,000 Master Masons. What
a man gets out of Masonry depends to a very great extent on what that
man has to put into Masonry. It is my firm conviction that membership
in the Missouri Lodge of Research and availaing ones-self of all of its
benefits will direct one, Masonically, on the surest path to the Way, the
Truth and the Light.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIO NS
Th~s subject was discussed pro and con by many Grand Masters,
Committeemen, and others. The trend in many Grand Lodges seems to
be a more liberal interpretation of this Ancient Landmark. M any Grand
Masters however, are asking that the individual Lodges assume most of
the responsibility in making the final decisions. Emphasis seems to be
on the internal rather than the external qualifications of a candidate.
Are we slowly but surely tearing down what we always have considered
one of our Ancient Landmarks? One might ask,
"What is a Landmark?" and "Who made Landmarks?" The first
question is readily answered. The Landmarks are those fundamental
principles of Freemasonry which have subsisted from time immemorial
which are not subject to repeal or change, and without which Free~
masonry would lose its distinctive character as such. This definition automatically answers the second question. If the Landmarks have existed

DELAWARE, 1950 (Foreign Correspondent)
Physical qualifications: This is one subject where there is a wide
difference of opinion as to what course to pursue. W hile quite a number
of Jurisdictions have adopted varying types of regulations as to physical
fitness in candidates, others have refused to consider any changes whatever. Some Grand Lodges leave the matter entirely up to the Grand
Masters for decision. In most cases of this kind, Grand Masters do not
relish the duty, and only under the most extreme conditions will they
grant dispensations setting aside the doctrine of "the perfect youth."
Many Grand Masters report that they refer the matter back to the Lodge
for its decision as to what constitutes ability to receive and transmit the
mysteries of Masonry. Typical of this attitude is the solution used by
Grand Master Jackson of Texas who reported:
"During the war I received numerous requests for waiver of physical
disability, which were referred back to the Lodge for their own decisions.
In my opinion, such weaknesses as asthma, nervousness, heart trouble,
stomach ulcers, hernia, arthritis, varicose veins, could not be classified
as physical disabilities under Article 430. In each instance, the Lodge
was cautioned to consider the possibility of such petitioner becoming
a charge on the Lodge. I received nine requests for my ruling on physical
disabilities who had not yet petitioned a Lodge, but had expressed a
desire to do so. In each case, I replied that this was not a question for
me to rule upon, since he had not yet petitioned the Lodge."
This question is one that this reviewer feels should be settled by
action of GRAND LODGES, not Grand Masters. All too often, as
Grand Masters come and go, rulings are changed to conform to the
ideas of the individual holding the office, and in such cases, Masters and
Lodges never know where they stand about accepting petitions from
handicapped candidates. In this connection, we found a Jurisdiction,
which shall be nameless here, where a Grand Master granted dispensations permitting reception of petitions from .m en with almost every type
of disability except total blindness and total deafness. At the other
extreme, we find several Grand Masters refusing to waive in any case
any types of disability. It would seem necessary to this writer that
Grand Lodges adopt regulations in unmistakable terms as to what is
and what is not a disqualifying disability. Delaware's law that a man
must be " sufficiently sound" in his natural or artificial mempers to conform to our ceremonies seems to be worlcing very well for us here. Very

OREGON, 1950 (Grand Master)

Dispensations Waiving Physical Qualifications
There are eleven lodges that made such requests for special dispensations and in each instance my policy was to request three letters
from brothers of the lodge who knew the petitioner, these letters to substantiate the spiritual and moral character and sobriety of the individual
in question and his non likelihood of becoming a charge upon the lodge.
In all cases where it was possible a personal interview was held and
in several instances I conferred the M.M. degree.
Though there may be many divergencies of opinion, I assure you
that it was my sense of responsibility and the exercise of weighed judgment that actuated me in these decisions. We are taught that it is the
internal and not the external quali.6cations that recommend a man for
Masonry and therefore I feel that our fraternity is greatly enriched hy
the character of those whom we have thus admitted.

SOUTH CAROLINA, 1950 (Case No. 6 Grand Lodge)
Jackson Lodge No. 53 has a petition from a man who was born without a right hand. His arm is normal to about half way between the elbow
and wrist. It is understood that he does not have an artificial hand now
but anticipates getting one.
Question:
Can the Lodge vote on his petition before he gets an artificial ha~d?
Answer:
·~
No. He could not legally file a petition because he has to state therein
that he is not deformed in person. While the law permits that deformity
to be cured by an artificial limb he is not cured until he actually has the
artificial hand. When the applicant has been fitted with an artificial
hand he may apply, and under the law it will be up to the Master to
decide whether this enables him to sufficiently comply with the regulations. (See section 100 of the Code, Article III of the Constitution. )

NEBRASKA, 1950 (Grand Lodge)
Nebraska has finally come out boldly and bravely in adherence to
the doctrine that a landmark cannot be changed. As one of the wise
Past Grand Masters of Nebraska has said: "A landmark cannot be
repealed, but it can be violated."
In a fine report in which full recognition is given to the understandable sentiment for lowering the bars for wounded veterans, and with
complete acquiescence in the principle that it is the internal, not the
external, qualifications of a man that we regard in Masonry, it has
reached the following conclusions:
"To the extent that candidates are admitted who cannot, or are not
required to perform our ancient rites (which in themselves are Landmarks) to that extent we are violating these Landmarks. To the extent
that any Landmark is violated or abandoned, our Order loses the peculiar characteristics that make it Masonry.
"No man is admitted to Masonry as a matter of right. It is a privilege ~hich we grant. If we demand of candidates that they not only
meet our intellectual, moral and spiritual standards but certain physical
standards, we are not violating any obligation that we owe them, nor
are we violating any humanitarian or Christian principles. We are only
recognizing a principle laid down by the founders of our Grand Lodge
in the preamble of the Constitution they adopted at their first communication on September 23, 1857. ' That the ancient landmarks of the Order
be held Inviolate.' "

during initiation.
(A resolution providing for modification as recommended by the
. Grand Master was rejected by Grand Lodge.)

Now that five years have passed since the end of the war, it appears
that the agitation in favor of further relaxation of traditional Masonic
physical standards is beginning to subside. Idaho voted down two resolutions which would have relaxed its requirements. Manitoba amended its
law for purposes of clarification only, with no change in its traditional
position. Nebraska reaffirmed its law, then, after two resolutions had
been introduced, referred the question again to a special committee for
study. Minnesota has a special committee studying the question, but the
committee recommended no action and further study was directed.
In 1948 the Grand Lodge of Nevada decided to relax its standards
by providing that "physical qualiftcation under Landmark XI be interpreted to mean one who can substantially conform to the ceremonies
of initiation." This, however only served to introduce other problems.
It made necessary a "standard" by which the Grand Master might, at
his discretion, issue dispensations to receive petitions from those who
have physical ·handicaps. Following is the standard for guidance of the
Grand Master: "Must possess the physical ability to conform substantially to, and receive and give instructions in, the arts and mysteries

516

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of Freemasonry; provided, the Grand Master may in his discretion issue
a dispensation to a Lodge, without charge, to receive and consider in the
usual Masonic manner the petition of a person physically deficient but
otherwise qualified; and further provided, the Master of a Lodge must
advise all members present of the physical deficiency prior to balloting
on a petition received under such dispensation.''

In California, our prese.nt law seems to be working satisfactorily.
Under Section 208, entitled "Moral and Physical Qualifications,"
we read: An applicant for the degrees of Masonry must be a man; no
woman nor eunuch; free born, being neither a slave nor the son of a
bond woman: a believer in God and a future existence; of moral conduct; capable of reading and writing; having no maim or defect in his
body that may render him incapable of learning the art, and physically
able to conform substantially to what the several degrees respectively
require of him.
Sec. 209. The question as to the physical sufficiency of the applicant
shall be left to the sound discretion of the Lodge. When the applicant
is unable to comply literally with the physical requirements the Master
shall state the nature and extent of his disabilities to the Lodge before
ballot is taken.

POWERS OF THE GRAND MASTER
One hundred years ago it seemed almost universally true that Grand
Masters enjoyed the high prerogative of Making Masons at sight, without any preliminaries, and at any suitable time and place, they alone
being the judges of the propriety, the time and the place. For so doing,
no earthly power could call them to account.
This question of implied powers caused some dissension in the
Grand Lodge of California during its second year so that immediately
the Powers of the Grand Master were questioned, and to clarify them,
Grand Lodge passed and adopted the following resolutions:
1. Resolved, That it is the sense of this Grand Lodge that the
Grand Master is but the creature of the Grand Lodge, with no implied
powers, inherent or divine.
2. Resolved, That this Grand Lodge does not acknowledge the
doctrine that a Grand Master may make Masons at sight or at will
except in a regular Lodge, by the unanimous consent of the members
there present, and that, in its opinion, Grand Masters possess no powers
except those contained in the Constitutions of Masonry and those
clearly and expressly delegated to them by their brethren.
Today many Grand Lodges have definite restrictions regarding the
powers of the Grand Master, however, a number of Jurisdictions still
allow the Grand Master the privilege and right to make a Mason at sight.

SOUTH CAROLINA, 1950 (GrandMaster)
Occasional Lodge
On July 28th I convened an Occasional Lodge for the purpose of
making Major General George H. Decker, Commanding General at
Fort Jackson, a Mason at Sight. General Decker by his enthusiastic and
consistent support was largely instrumental in the establishment of the
Masonic Lodge at Fort Jackson. He provided every facility that he
possibly could for the convenience and comfort of this Masonic body.
Not only that but General Decker is an outstanding officer and soldier
who has spent most of his life in the service of his country. He is an
efficient leader, and my action in making him a Mason, brought joy to
those Masons serving under his command. General Decker often
expressed his desire to become a Mason and I felt after due inquiry, that
he was worthy of this honor.

SOUTH CAROLINA, 1950 (Grand Master)
Every Grand Master has to make rulings on various Masonic questions which are clearly answered in the law. I requested that all such
matters be first referred to the District Deputies and if they could not
give the answer they were to come to me. This action is strictly in
accordance with Masonic law which is often ignored. This year it has
worked wonderfully well The District Deputies have been efficient and
diligent and as a result most problems have been solved in the district
where they arose.
I venture the assertion that no Grand Master has been called on to
make fewer rulings during a Masonic year.

PENNSYLVANIA, 1950 {Correspondence Committee)
The Grand Master reported that he had made five "Masons at
Sight," two of them at the same time in one of the Lodges. While he had
a perfect right to do this, it has always seemed a bit out of place since
"Masonry regards no man for his worldly wealth or honors.'' Also we
have always rather liked the phrase: "As all brothers and fellows have
done before.'' When we read of cases like this we feel just as we do
while being herded before the gate at the railroad station and see some
few extra special folks slip through by a side gate to enable them to get
good seats on the train before us hoi polloi are permitted to pass.

MASONIC BLOOD BANK
DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA, 1950 (Grand Master)
It is with much pleasure that I report on this important activity of
Masonry. The General Chairman of the Grand Lodge Blood Donor

518

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Committee has a complete report at this Communication, and I will not
repeat the information he has given you. I must, however, express my
sincere appreciation for the manner in which the Masons of the jurisdiction have responded to the appeal for blood.
Through the Masonic Blood Bank, we are able to provide blood for
all the Masons in the jurisdiction and their families. A substantial part
of our contribution has been made available to our Armed Forces in
Korea. This is truly Masonry in action, and our record this year is one
of which we can be proud.
W. Brother L. Malcolm Graham, General Chairman of the Blood
Donors Committee, made a report expressing gratification at the
splendid showing made by the Lodges and stressing the urgent need
for continued interest in this project.
He said: "Notwithstanding the fact that your Committee did not
officially begin to function until the middle of February, the final results
for the period ending December 15, 1950, reveal that the Lodges of t~is
jurisdiction have exceeded the original quota of 1,233 pints. The final
tabulation of donations made during the year discloses that a total of
1,610 pints were donated by members of the constituent Lodges and
their families, or 377 pints over the quota for a percentage of 130.58.
Our activities this year have become a subject of conversation in
every Red Cross Regional Center. The fact that we are one of the largest
organizations in the program and the manner in which we have
responded, has caused the Red Cross to publicize our efforts throughout
the country. Several requests have been received from other cities regarding our successful operation and detailed information has been furnished
by your Chairman to assist these groups in their organization.
Your Chairman feels that the Masonic Blood Bank has become firmly
established during _this second year of operation. It is one of the finest
forms of protection for our membership anyone could desire and with.
the number of donors available, should become one of the largest and
strongest programs organized. This year every Lodge in the jurisdiction
participated in and contributed to the Blood Bank, some more than
others, but sufficiently to indicate complete cooperation and accord. As
a matter of record it should be noted that twenty-four Lodges exceeded
their quotas this year as compared to ten in 1949."

MARYLAND, 1950 (Committee Report}
Blood donations during the six months ending October 31, 1950
have again reached an all-time high. The Temple donor file was called
upon to furnish 410 pints of blood as compared with 352 pints of blood
for comparable period in 1949, and 304 pints in 1948.
It is imperative that ways and means be found to increase the number
of prospective donors in the very near future in order to meet the ever
increasing demand for donations. In order to accomplish this, we recommend that the Committee be reorganized and enlarged, and through this
committee an extensive campaign be made for prospective donors in the
various Lodges.

ARKANSAS, 1950 (Grand Master)

LOUISIANA, 1951 (Grand Master)
Greater New Orleans Masonic Blood Bank-Approved
In April, 1950 I was approached with the request that I consider
sanctioning the organization of a Greater New Orleans Masonic Blood
Bank.
Brother Tom Willson, Past Master, Square and Compass Lodge
No. 417, was enthusiastic over the possibilities of such a Bank, and had
already sounded out the authorities at the Baptist Hospital, had been
promised the services of a doctor and nurse regularly, and had secured
a standard contract and copies of application blanks in use in other
Blood Banks. Under the proposed arrangement Grand Lodge would be
required to furnish without charge one of the refreshment rooms between
the hours of 5: 30 and 7: 30 two evenings a month, set up the beds and
equipment and have them ready for use before each drawing period,
dismantle them and store them after each drawing period, and leave the
social rooms clean and in usable condition. I was assured that if Grand
Lodge would provide the facilities a Blood Bank group would do the
work, and, more important, would undertake to procure the necessary
donors.

Many of you will recall the establishment of the Blood Bank at the
University Hospital here in Little Rock, as well as smaller Blood Banks
in various counties in the state, that has resulted in saving many lives
by having blood or plasma available when needed. Your Grand Lodge
financed the collection and distribution of this plasma until the State of
Arkansas made that service a part of the regular routine at the hospital.

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
ARIZONA, 1950 {Committee Report)
In 1949, a resolution was adopted to establish a Public Schools Week
celebration and requiring all Lodges to participate.
The week of January 16, 1950, was designated by the committee in
charge, as Public School Week, at which time the Masons of Arizona
were urged to encourage Community interest in the welfare of the Public Schools.
We have learned from the first Observance that the matter of the
proper time to hold it is important. Some have suggested that we hold
it in November and at the same time as the Arizona Education Association holds its annual meeting, but that would, in our opinion, mean that
our Fraternity and its primary object would be submerged. California
has found from long experience that a week in April is the best time to
hold it, and we are inclined to that view now. However, we will be glad
to abide by the wishes and decisions of the Grand Lodge.
We are certain that the need for the Observance is urgent. We know
as citizens and as Masons that there is a constant and continuous effort
being made to undermine the value and influence of the free public
school. It is our duty as Masons, charged by tradition and history, to
protect and defend and strengthen the free public school. To that end we
recommend that the Observance be continued each year at a time to be
fixed by the Grand Lodge, or the Committee appointed for that purpose,
and that ample funds be budgeted so that such expenses as may be
necessary may be provided for.

un-Masonic conduct, and shall, upon due trial and conviction of said
offense, forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges, including membership in any Lodge."
Irving E. Clark, Masonic Correspondent for Wyoming has written
a very interesting and complete report on this question. He presents both
sides, and gives many examples of how the different jurisdictions feel
about it.
Before writing his report he sent a questionnaire to every Grand
Lodge in the United States, and received replies from all but two Grand
Lodges. He asked two questions:
1. "Do the laws of your Grand Lodge permit the constituent Lodges
to accept a petition for the degrees from one who is engaged in the manufacture or sale of intoxicating liquor?"
2. "Do the laws of your Grand Lodge permit a member to engage
in the manufacture or sale of intoxicating liquor and retain membership
in the Lodge?"
Answers to the first question showed 23 no and 24 yes. Answers
to the second question showed 19 no and 28 yes.
There seems to be the same lack of agreement among the different
Grand Lodges on this question as there is on the question of the
Physical Qualifications of a candidate. The trend again seems to be
towards liberalization. Here, however, more opposition seems to be
appearing. Those jurisdictions that are holding fast or deferring action
until next year are the following: Arkansas, Arizona, Georgia, Kansas,
Kentucky, Colorado, Montana, Nebraska, Oregon, Ohio, South Dakota,
Tennessee, Washington, and Wisconsin. Those who favor liberalization
and who have repealed the above sections are Connecticut, Idaho, Minnesota, and Wyoming.
It is said that 18 Grand Jurisdictions have never had this restrictive
legislation and that a poll of these Jurisdictions by the Grand Master
from Minnesota disclosed that not one of them had experienced any
difficulties because of their leaving the matter to the discretion of their
Lodges.

barkeeper: and any Mason who may hereafter enter upon and engage

CONNECTICUT, 1950 (Special Committee)
The Proceedings include a comprehensive report by The Special
Committee on Intoxicating Liquors. The Committee, after a detailed
report, recommends that the Grand Lodge Constitution be amended,
which in effect removes the restrictions governing the management of the
business of selling or manufacturing intoxicating liquors. This resolution
was approved by the necessary two-thirds vote and final action will be
taken at the 1950 Communication.

In Idaho they seem to have simplified the question of eligibility of
petitioners in the liquor business, judging from several decisions by
Grand Master A. Edward Prince. Asked if the petition of a man working as bartender in a licensed saloon was eligible, he replied: "Yes.

barrier to the acceptance of his petition."

The only law we have regarding liquor is found in Sections 341 and
684 of the Code. Section 341 reads: "A Lodge shall not on any pretense, introduce intoxicating liquors, or permit the use of same as a beverage in any of its premises." Section 684 pertains to the use of intoxi..
eating liquor, and reads thus: "It shall be and is hereby made the impera..

as possible, the intemperate use of intoxicating liquors or beverages of
every kind and character by any of its members, and each Lodge shall
be held accountable to the Grand Lodge for the faithful performance of
this duty."

ARIZONA, 1949 (Grand Master)
The Grand Master took a fling at Masons engaging in the liquor
business and recommended legislation to correct the evil, observing:
"The manufacture, sale and distribution of intoxicating liquors is
being so abused as to become a great evil in the social life of our State
and Nation. The members of the Fraternity are becoming engaged in
such manufacture, sale and distribution in increasing numbers. The
prosecution of such business by a Master Mason being inconsistent with
his profession and his membership in the Masonic Fraternity. and being
calculated to bring the Fraternity into public disrepute, I believe that
this Grand Lodge should disapprove the conduct of such business and
condemn the engagement therein by a Master Mason as a Masonic
offense."

525

The Committee on General Policy heartily approved the recommendtion, but the jurisprudence committee couldn't agree on the matter and
action was postponed.

ARKANSAS, 1950 (Grand Master)
Anent the Masonic Liquor laws, the Grand Master remarked:
"The greatest inconsistency, in the opinion of your Grand Master,
comes in the very rigid laws we have on the sale of intoxicating liquors
and the very lax laws we have on the use of it. We, in our law, specifically say that it is not a Masonic crime to drink intoxicating liquor
and further that a Lodge should not exercise its discretion to punish for
intemperance beyond that admonition, unless the offense is habitual and
further, that if the Brother gets drunk, repents, confesses and asks forgiveness the Lodge shall not punish him.
"If our Masonic Law could prevent the sale of a single bottle of liquor
it would be different, bu.t as long as it is legally sold, a Mason, if he
wants to buy liquor will do so regardless of any Masonic Law. After all,
it is not the sale of liquor that brings the Masonic Fraternity into disrepute, but it is the purchase and use of liquor by members of the
Fraternity, and their acts in the presence of others, who know them to
be Masons, that is harmful to the reputation of the Craft as a whole."
Arkansas voted down a proposal to repeal the present Liquor Law
and another resolution to modify the present law.

GEORGIA, 1950 (CorrespondenceCommittee)
This state seems to be having more than ordinary trouble with the
liquor problem judging from the resolutions that came before the Grand
Lodge at its last communication. One resolution would make it a
Masonic offense to drink any spirituous malt, vinous, intoxicating liquor,
or to belong to a club, fraternity or society which possesses and serves
such potables, and the punishment would be summary expulsion by t~e
Grand Master, presumably without a trial or hearing. Of course this
resolution was promptly rejected and one suspects it was introduced to
becloud the whole matter. Of course, when we look the matter squarely
in the face, it is a henious crime, Masonically, to make or sell or have
anything to do with the liquor traffic, there is a certain element of culpability in the practice of drinking, imbibing, and consuming the vile stuff
either privately cir in public. Rejected all proposals.

KANSAS, 1950 (Grand Master)
Prohibition in Kansas having been repealed in the November, 1948,
election, the following by-law was enacted by the Grand Lodge at the
1949 communication: "The manufacture or sale of intoxicating liquor by

526

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

any Mason shall be deemed an offense against the Body of Masonry."
A number of inquiries were received by the Grand Master for interpre·
tation of the new law, and he was prompted to comment as follows:
"In the judgment of your Grand Master, this by-law does not represent any new policy in Kansas Masonry, but does amount to a declaration that the attitude of the Grand Lodge toward the liquor traffic
remains unchanged, notwithstanding changes in the State laws. For
more than 68 years, the manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquor,
except for medical, scientific and mechanical purposes were prohibited
by the laws of Kansas. Any Mason who violated these laws was guilty
of a Masonic offense. Under the new law, any manufacture or sale that
would have been a Masonic offense under prohibition, will still be a
Masonic offense. Any act that was sanctioned by the Masonic Institution under prohibition will continue to be sanctioned.
"A number of Kansas Masons are engaged in selling cereal malt
beverages, under state laws which define intoxicating liquors as containing more than 3.2% of alcohol by weight. If they conduct orderly,
decent places of business, and the commodity they sell is not intoxicating,
the new law does not affect them."

KENTUCKY, 1950 (Grand Master's Decision)
Opinion No. 14
Bro. James L. McNeely, secretary of Monticello Lodge No. 431
desired an opinion on the following:
Question: Give me an opinion on the eligibility of a man who has
petitioned our Lodge whose occupation is a bottler in a brewery. We
believe according to Regulation 240 of the Book of Constitution that this
party comes under the classification of la1borer.
Answer: I notice you refer to Regulation 240. I shall refer you to
Section 108 reading as follows:
Section 108. Manufacture or sale of liquors. No Lodge shall receive
the petition of anyone who is engaged in the manufacture or sale of
spirituous, vinous or malt liquors as a beverage. Any Lodge guilty of
violating this provision shall be dealt with.
It is my opinion this man referred to above would come under this
section, as being engaged in the manufacture and not entitled to a
petition.
