NORTH DAKOTA, 1950 (Grand Master)
One official decision was rendered, during the year, and this was in
regard to the liquor traffic. Several communities in North Dakota, are
organizing non-profit corporations, for the purpose of handling all liquor
sold in the community, and they work in co-operation with the municipal
authorities in the community. All earnings are used for civic improvements and no stockholder, or director receives pay for his services.
The question has arisen as to whether a Master Mason could act as
a stockholder, or director of such non-profit corporation, and, in order to
clear up the record and to encourage the orderly handling of the liquor
traffic in these communities, I have rendered the following decision:
"It is iny opinion that the serving of a Master Mason as a stockholder, or director of a non-profit corporation, engaged in the purchase
and sale of intoxicating liquor, does not constitute a Masonic offense,
provided no Master Mason actually engages in the dispensing of intoxicating liquor and derives no profit or other emolument therefrom."

WISCONSIN, 1950 (Grand Master)
Question: .(Lodge S )-May we accept petition of the production
manager of a brewery? This man's work is entirely in connection with
production and the brewery has a sales manager in charge of sales.
Decision: Petition cannot be received. While this man does not personally and directly promote the sales, indirectly he does. The success
of his job depends on his production of quality goods that will sell, and
the success of the sales manager and the entire establishment is depend·
ent on his production services. Not approved.

WASHINGTON, 1950 (Grand Master)
A man working in a brewery as a welder wanted to petition, but the

OHIO, 1949 (Committee Report)

NEVAD A, 1950 (Grand Master)

A committee studying the question of DeMolay bodies being permitted to meet in Masonic Temples asked for more time. The principal
question is apparentl y whether favorable action in this ~nstan~e would
open the way for similar requests by other non-Masonic bodies.

The. training of youth has been recognized as a most important
factor in any long-rang e movement, whether religious or political,
whether for a good purpose or for evil. It is well said "Our Youth Is Our
Life." We, as Masons in Nevada, have an obligation to support the
leaders of the Order of the DeMolay and the Order of Rainbow for
Girls, otherwise our Fraternity will remain static or deteriorate.

OKLAH OMA, 1950 (Grand Master)
In commenting on the Order of the Rainbow for Girls, and the Order
of DeMolay for Boys, the Grand Master states that the best and wisest
investment we can make today is in our American youth. Especially. he
tells us, that we should be interested in supporting and encouraging
such splendid organizations as those which are sponsored by the Eastern
Star and Masonry.

MISSOU RI, 1950 (Grand Master)
One of the finest of all youth organizations is the DeMolay. Organized some 30 years ago the growth of the Order has been little short of
phenomenal. Today the membership is over one million and is international in scope.
In over a thousand Chapters Masonic teachings are inculcated
through the medium of an impressive ritual. From the DeMolay Chapters
come the citizens and in many instances the Freemasons of tomorrow.
At a time when Masonry and Masonic influence are so essential to
the welfare of our nation it is my opinion that this organization of trained
young men deserves some recognition from Masonry. I do not recommend or even suggest sponsorship of DeMolay Chapters by Masonic
Lodges but I do believe that moral support at least is in order. .
Certainly Masons as individuals should welcome the opportunity to
encourage the boys of the DeMolay to attain a true understanding of the
·basic principles of our fraternity, thus preparing them for future
Masonic membership.

OREGO N, 1950 (Grand Master)
The Grand Master urged "moral support" of work of Youth Organizations, i.e.. DeMolay, Rainbow for Girls, Job's Daughters , which he
deemed constructive.

NEW YORK, 1949 (Grand Master)
He had a splendid report on progress of the DeMolay. The 1948
Masters of the Second Manhatta n District raised $1,200.00 to pay for
uniforms, rent, etc. Twelve Districts were working with Boy Scout
troops. All youth movements such as these should be encouraged for .
they offer the hope for the future, he said.

RHODE ISLAND , 1950 (Grand Master)
My sincere thanks to the many brethren throughout this Grand
Jurisdiction who are serving as "Dads" and in other ways contributing
to the welfare of our boys in DeMolay. One of the finest services we
~an rende.r to Freemaso nry and our Great Nation in the days to come
is by helping our boys and girls to hold fast to the ideals that have made
our. Fraternity and our Nation great in an age when they are surrounde d
by influences that are hard to combat. It is gratifying to see the increased
activity in both DeMolay and Rainbow for Girls, and I hope that many
more Chapters of each will be established in this Grand Jurisdiction.

MICHIG AN, 1950 (Board of Control Report)
During the current year, the Order of DeMolay in Michigan has
shown a very healthy growth, the direct result of the splendid work done
by the State and District Deputies. Few members of the Masonic Fraternity realize how many hours these brothers devote to this important
matter dealing directly with the young men of the State in the fourteen
to twenty-one year bracket.
The. current Grand. Council of DeMolay Annual report lists fiftytwo active Chapters, with 3, 109 members. In addition to this, there are
at present ten additional new Chapters operating under Letters Temporary, or re-established, in Wayne. Tawas, Fenton, Dimondale, Mt.
Pleasant, Muskegon, Port Huron, Northville, Commerce, and Architect
(Detroit). These have additional memberships of approximately three
hundred.

receive the backing of many Grand Lodges.

year for four $500 scholarships.

MASONRY vs. COMMUNISM
The only true solution of our political and social problems lies in
cultivating everywhere the spirit of brotherhood, of fellow feeling and
understanding between man and man, and the willingness to treat a
man as a man.-Theodore Roosevelt.
No solution has been offered regarding this problem. Many Grand
Lodges have adopted resolutions condemning it in the strongest language
possible. Many Grand Masters. Grand Orators and other Grand Lodge
Officers have condemned Communism as abhorrent to Masons and
repugnant to the concepts of Freemasonry. Some jurisdictions have gone
so far as to ban Communists from becoming members of the Fraternity.

53i

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

An exception to this trend is found in the Grand Lodge of England.
.The Grand Lodge of England has gone on record as refusing to
permit its Lodges to join in expressions of condemnation of Communism. This Grand Lodge is trying to be consistent and believes that
Masonic aloofness from all governmental philosophies, including those
that are inimical to human freedom, is the only attitude for organized
Masonry to take. This seems like a wise decision to the Dominie.
Masonry and Communism have nothing in common, neither does
Masonry and certain religious philosophies have anything in common,
but we know better than to denounce any religious sect in a Masonic
gathering or anywhere else lest it be assumed to be the official position
of Masonry. Some Masonic orators denounce Communism because they
lack a soundly positive Masonic message. If we practice our Masonry
we will find ample opportunity to resist Communism without involving
our Lodges. The process of condemnation is a progressive one and there
will be no l?nd to the things some Masons will want Masonry to condemn, after we have made a start on Communism.

ing members of the Fraternity. While we are in hearty accord with all
the sentiments expressed, yet we do not understand why the issue, if
it may so be called, of Communism should be injected into Freemasonry.
We demand of our candidates a belief in a Supreme Being and a promise
to be loyal and obedient to the laws of the country in which they live.
To this Communists cannot subscribe. If candidates or members were to
so affirm they would be guilty of perjury, which would be unmasonic
conduct. Why denounce Communism, detestable and repugnant as it
is, alone? If Modern Masonry intends to engage in public affairs let it
also take cognizance of the insidious and subversive propaganda of
other organizations which do not have the welfare of our Country at
heart. We realize the danger of Communism and all subversive movements but in our humble opinion if we continue the course we appear to
have embarked upon we will sooner or later enter a field far removed
from the fundamental concepts of the Institution.

INDIANA, 1950 (Committee on Jurisprudence)
The Committee on Jurisprudence, having considered the Grand
Master's General Recommendation No. 1, recommends that this Grand
Lodge reaffirm its unswerving opposition to Communism and to all communistic and subversive activities.

By far the subject claiming most attention and causing greatest concern is the advance of Communism and the possibility even of its infiltration into our own ranks. Indeed proof is at hand that in some instances
this has ·b een true already. To prevent the further spread of this insidious
evil, many Grand Lodges are changing their form of petitions to include
questions which will require definite statements of loyalty and declaration of principles, and some are requiring the submission of a birth certificate to accompany every petition for the Degrees or affiliation. Nearly
every Grand Lodge has adopted some form of condemnation of Communism, and many are including various other "isms" prevalent in our
own country, in their denunciations. Our own state, through the courageous leadership of Grand Master E. Carl Coleman, has taken a leading
part in this fight. M.W. Bro. Coleman has brought a very forceful message at each of the thirty District meetings held throughout our state,
which were attended by thousands of Tennessee Masons. In each of
these messages he has outlined the methods of these subversive elements
and urged the Brethren to combat them with their vote, their influence
and their unceasing vigilance. His addresses have been quoted widely by
the press throughout the state, thus making Masonry's influence felt outside its own circles.

The brethren are keenly aware of the problems facing the Fraternity and are awake to their responsibility in seeing that no person
enters our portals who is a member of an organization that has for its
purpose the destruction of our Democratic form of government, our
Fraternity and other American institutions. They were practically
unanimous in their opinion that Freemasonry should take a more active
and a more aggressive stand against any such organization, whether it
be called "Communism" or any other "ism."

MONTANA, 1950 (Grand Chaplain)
FLORIDA, 1950 (Grand Lodge)

Somewhere in America there are men who can even break down
Joe Stalin and his Politburo. Certainly we cannot see any results from
getting tough with Russia. Since the policy of getting tough with Russia
was announced there has been an increasing acceleration of the deterioration in the relations between the two countries. You don't get people
to do something for you by getting tough. In the training of the child
it has some place but adults do not react to such a policy in a favorable
manner. The opposite is true. Ask yourselves what you would do, what
your attitude would be, if someone announced he was going to get tough
with you. The developments since that policy was announced have been
disastrous. Where can we find the man who can win Joe Stalin? He is in
America now. Is he among the 3,000,000 Masons? Is he among the
Masons of Montana? Could be! Let's find him.

Resolved, By the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the Grand Jurisdiction of Florida, that Florida
Masonry denounces and condemns Communism in all its forms as
atheistic and un-American ideology, and that no true Mason or American citizen, loyal to his country, will give comfort, encouragement, help
or support thereto in even the slightest degree, or any tolerance therefor
by conduct or association; that any American and Mason so doing
would be guilty of most traitorous disloyalty to his country and to every
principle of Free Masonry; and that all Free Masons, both as Masons
and as American citizens, are hereby called upon to be unceasing in their
resolute and determined opposition to this enemy of all that we hold
precious to o~r very existence. Resolution adopted.

VERMONT, 1950 (Grand Master)

MISSISSIPPI, 1951 (Grand Lecturer)

On the subject of Socialism and the Welfare State, he speaks as
follows:
"We are funny people, aren't we? Socialism! How we dislike that
word. The spirit of 1776 still lingers. Welfare State! If someone should
tell us that this country is becoming a welfare state we would protest
in horror. The term reeks of Communism. But on the other hand, we
are not too hesitant about accepting the benefits to he obtained from a
liberal government. We will accept welfare if it is sugar coated. There
is an internal conflict, of course, but in the end we will take it. Why
not? we say. If we don't someone else will. So it goes. Social security,
socialized medicine, unemployment compensation, old age pensions, they
are all acceptable. Even now many of our cities and towns are figuring
on how to get a school from the new Federal education program. It's a
match money proposition. The citizens of the town pay for only half a
school. The other half comes from everyone else in the country. It's the
old highway program in a new costume. Oh! We detest socialism, but,
believe it or not, we are willingly becoming socialistic! The liberalistic

A laxity in balloting has allowed Communism to become a menace
in America: to infiltrate through and through our schools, government,
churches, and even ·our homes. This hydra-headed monster could not
have existed in the early days of America. It exists today because the
voters have put into the chambers of Congress through the years men
who have failed by their votes to keep the power of government in the
hands of the law-making body and curb centralized government.
Too many men, including Masons, vociferously condemn Communism, totalitarianism, dictatorship, and regimentation in foreign lands
and then, complacently, accept regimentation and socialism at home,
especially if it brings pecuniary benefits to himself or his community.
If these ideologies are obnoxious and hurtful to people abroad so much
that we are willing for our boys to die to crush them, surely, it is not
asking too much to ask that we crush all these ideologies and unAmericanisms with our ballots. Let us, henceforward, live in accord with
our denudation of every form of regimentation and infringement of the
individual's right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Talking

about it does very little, if any, good, unless words are followed by
deeds. And those deeds in the form of the ballot for true Americans for
local, state, and national offices are the deeds that can avail.

We learn from history that in the "Gold Rush" of 1849 it was only
natural that many of the newcomers to California were Masons. Fifteen
Grand Lodges, from Connecticut to Florida, issued charters or dispensations for the formation of new Lodges under their jurisdiction in California. It is of interest to our Tennessee brethren to know that two of
our "missing" Lodge numbers were assigned to California. In 1849 we
issued a dispensation to a group of our brethren to form San Juan Lodge
No. 171 at Caledonia, California, and in 1850 a dispensation was issued
to a similar group at Havilah, California, to form Havilah Mining Lodge
No. 196. We have no further record of either Lodge, nor has the Grand
Lodge of California. We have no way of knowing what Tennessee
members had a part in the organization of the new Grand Lodge. We
do know, however, that Townsend A'. Thomas of Clarksville was elected
Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge of California in 1851, and also
served as Deputy Grand Master in 1853 and 1855. He was Grand Secretary of the Grand Royal Arch Chapter of California in 1858, returned
to Tennessee and served as Grand High Priest of our Grand Royal Arch
Chapter in 1867. Undoubtedly many other Tennesseans have had a
prominent part in California Masonry, but we have the record of only
one other, John B. Moore, who made an outstanding record as Grand
Master in 1946. He is a native of Hustburg, in Humphreys County,
and resided in that county until young manhood. We are proud of his
record in California.

SOUTH CAROLINA, 1950 (Grand Master)
If liberty is to survive in the world, American men must begin to
think. They must recognize Socialistic tendencies in all forms. They
must be willing to admit that, while conditions in capitalistic America
are not ideal, there are underprivileged people, there is racial prejudice,
and there are slums that exist in many cities. They must remember also
that the humblest descendant of those, from whose hands the shackles of
siavery have recently been broken, has more dignity attached to his
personality and ·enjoys e better standard of living than any class of
people in those countries which have embraced Socialism or Communism.
To say that, because ideal conditions do not exist in America, free
enterprise should be destroyed, is just as sensible as to say that, because
we still have ignorant people and atheists, we should burn our schoolhouses and churches.

TENNESSEE, 1951 (Grand Master)
One of the greatest gatherings of Masons in America took place
in San Francisco on October 9-13, 1950, when the Grand Lodge of
California met to celebrate its lOOth anniversary. It was estimated that
10,000 Master Masons were in attendance at Civic Auditorium when
the Grand Lodge opened at 10:00 A.M. on October 9. Included in this
group were 36 Grand Masters, 23 Grand Secretaries, 3 Deputy Grand
Masters, one Grand Treasurer and 7 Past Grand Masters. Eight of the
Grand Secretaries (including Tennessee) also represented their Grand
Masters. Those in attendance were from Canadian jurisdictions from
New Brunswick to British Columbia, Costa Rica, Mexico, El Salvador,
Philippine Islands, China, and the United States from Maine to South
Carolina on the East Coast (including all of the New England States),
Central. West and Western States, North Carolina, South Carolina,
Virginia, Maryland, District of Columbia, Louisiana, Tennessee and
Texas.
One of the great disappointments of my year was not being able to
attend the California celebration. However, we were glad that our
Grand Secretary, M.W. Brother "Ted," could attend and represent us.
We shall always be grateful to the California brethren for their wonderful hospitality and the many courtesies extended to Ted and Mrs.
Doss and their lovely daughter, Jane, on the occasion of their visit to
California. Every Grand Master and Grand Secretary was given a most

NEW MEXICO, 1951 (Grand Master)
Early in my Masonic year, I received a most gracious invitation
from the Grand Lodge of California to be present and assist them in
celebrating the centenary celebration of the founding of their Grand
Lodge. I hastened to accept and, accompanied by my wife, was graciously received and entertained during the week, October 7 to 14, in
San Francisco. I marvel at their accomplishments and the manner in
which they organized and handled such an outpouring of Masons as
were present. The Grand Lodge and its officers were graciousness and
hospitality personified and the whole occasion was one of such brilliance
and achievement that it will be long remembered wherever Masons congregate. Ellsworth Meyer was every inch a Grand Master.

MAINE, 1951 (Grand Master)
Grand Lodge of California-Centennial Celebration
In accordance with the vote of Grand Lodge at the Annual Communication fn 1950, I attended the Centennial Anniversary of the Grand
Lodge of California which was held in San Francisco, October 9-13,

541

1950. Among the guests were thirty-three Grand Masters, four Deputy

These represented thirty-six Grand Lodges in the United States, five
Provinces from Canada and three foreign countries.
It is impossible in a limited space of time to go into detail as to the

their wonderful hospitality will long remain with all the guests who
were present.

the Grand Lodge, to the pleasure of all present. The Grand Lodge of
Maine was honored by having its Grand Master requested to present a
Testimonial, in behalf of all the visiting guests, in appreciation for the
unbounded hospitality and sincere friendship evinced by the Grand
Lodge of California, its officers and members.
I wish to express by sincere appreciation to the brethren of the
Grand Lodge of Maine for making it possible for me to attend this
Celebration. It is difficult to measure the good derived from such
contacts.

THE OLDEST MASONIC LODGE
We are often asked what is the oldest Masonic Lodge in the world?
It is the Lodge of Edinburgh No. 1, sometimes known as Mary's
Chapel, and in July last year, it observed the 350th anniversary of its
establishment, at which time Masonic dignitaries from far and near
journeyed to Edinburgh, Scotland, where the Lodge continues to
carry on.
And it has records to prove its long time existence for its first five
pages of minutes incorporate the Schaw Statutes which are dated
December 28, 1598: six months later, July 31, 1599, are to be found the
minutes which confirm the Lodge's claim to the oldest existing Masonic
minutes.
ANNIVERSARIES IN RHODE ISLAND
Two interesting events of the year were celebrations of anniversaries: St. John's Lodge No. 1 at Newport, being two hundred years
old: Friendship No. 7, one hundred and fifty years old.
ANY OLDER MASON?
The oldest Mason in Illinois, Brother W. B. Decker of Fairbury,
was present and accorded honors his due. Brother Decker was at that
time ninety-four years old and had been a Mason for seventy-three
years.
JOHN HANCOCK IN THE NEWS
John Hancock, illustrious signer (in large type) of the Declaration
of Independence, although an American citizen, was made a Freemason
in a Quebec, Ontario, Lodge, Merchant's Lodge No. 1, in 1760. Later on
he affiliated with St. Andrew's Lodge in Boston.

The scarcity of comments is due to the fact that we have only received three of the 1951 Communications. Further comments will probably appear in next year's report.

MASONIC "TEA" PARTY
29 of the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence were
Masons, the Boston Tea Party was a called off Master Mason's Lodge.
Every one of the officers of the Revolution from the rank of Major to
the Commander-in-chief was a Mason, except Benedict Arnold.

GOLD DIGGINGS

PAST GRAND MASTER TRUMAN
Missouri witnessed the installation of Grand Lodge officers for
·1949-50 by a Past Grand Master who also is President of the United
States, Harry S. Truman. The President flew 1,000 miles to induct into
the office of Grand Master the brother who he had appointed in line
ten years before.

The fact that this report was written in Grass Valley. the heart of
the Mother Lode Country, where gold quartz was discovered in 1851,
and where Madison Lodge No. 23 will celebrate its one hundredth
anniversary in May, 1952, suggested this subject heading, "Gold
Diggings."

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

NEW ORGANIZATION IN NEW YORK
Something new. The Masonic War Veterans of New York have
been incorporated. A Master Mason who is a veteran of the Spanish
American War or World Wars I and II are eligible for membership.
M.': W.' .Brother Charles W. Froessel, P.G.M., is the first president.

An interesting paragraph of the report reads:
"The Library's unique gift of the year was an oil painting received
fro~ Carl H. Claudy, who in turn, and in a round,about way, had
r~c~1ved it from the artist, a Mason in Czechoslovakia. It represents in a
V1V1d style the three degrees as practiced in the artist's own country.''
By legislation at this meeting of the Grand Lodge there will soon be
erected a new home for the Library in a $400,000 building designed for
use as a Masonic Library, Museum, Memorial Hall and Administrative
Offices which is shown by an architect's sketch in the current volume
of proceedings.

CALIFORNIA CENTENNIAL
M.'.W.'.Brother Ellsworth Meyer, Grand Master of California, led
off with a masterful address on "Freemasonry's Obligation to Maintain
True Americanism.'' He placed stress on holding fast to those funda~
mental principles and ideals which have made America the Land of
the Free.
GOVERNOR OF MICHIGAN
Gov. G. Mennen Williams of Michigan was made a Master Mason
recently in Lotus Lodge No. 549, in the presence of 1,600 brethren.

SON TO FATHER
Presentation of 50 Year Button
The Grand Master, M.'.W.'.Lynn B. Brodrick of Kansas, directed
M.'.W.'.Samuel G. Wiles to present his father, Brother Harry Max,
well Brodrick, at the Altar.

A CRIPPLED CHILDREN'S CLINIC
At Tucson the Grand Master participated in ceremonies of ground
breaking for a "Square and Compass Crippled Children's Clinic" to be
erected at a cost of $70,000, contributed by Masonic bodies, churches,
civic organizations, including $35,000 by the Labor Unions. Although
not exclusively a Masoinc enterprise, its Board of Directors is com~
prised of 24 Masons and some pre on a mixed Advisory Board.

WHERE ARE THE YOUNGER MASONS?
The Grand Secretary of Colorado gave a very interesting analysis
of the ages of Colorado Masons. The average age is above 50 and the
average at death is above 67. Only 21 % are under 40. He then rightly
asks: "Where are the younger men?"

REALLY DESTITUTE
Under Alabama we note their rule that their Masonic Home cannot
admit "a blind brother or sister" nor a "diseased or disabled person" nor
one with "means to pay for their keep," "neither can one with sufficient
income to pay part of their keep be entered."

several Lodges in this Jurisdiction as the Masonic birthday of George
Washington, and that the M.'.W.'.Grand Master shall, each year, at
a reasonable time prior to that date, issue and circulate a proclamation
directing the said celebration with appropriate exercises to be carried
out by the several Lodges, whereupon. it shall be the duty of the proper
officers of each Lodge in the Jurisdiction to arrange for and comply with
the proclamation, and thereafter make due report to the Grand Master
of the proceedings of the Lodge in that respect; Provided, that if such
date should fall upon Sunday or some other date deemed inconvenient
by the Grand Master, then in that event, he may, if considered advisable,
fix another date in his proclamation for such celebration.
Adopted August 22, 1923-Wyoming.

544

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Paul Blanshard's "AMERICAN FREEDOM AND
CATHOLIC POWER"

WHAT WILL RESEARCH WORKERS FIND?

Mention should be made of an outstanding book of the year which
has been added to the Grand Lodge Library, and which should appeal
to all free-thinking Masons, although it does not deal with any Masonic
subject. It is Paul Blanshard's "American Freedom and Catholic
Power," a scholarly, thought-provoking work in which the author contends that our fundamental ideals of democracy are being threatened
by the Catholic hierarchy. In the book he reminds the American people
of the great importance of religious freedom, which is an heritage belonging to American Catholics and American Protestants alike.

WILL THIS EVER HAPPEN AGAIN?
A request received by the Grand Master of Maine to confer the
Master Mason degree on six candidates on November 14, 1950, at a
special communication of said Lodge. the six candidates being own
brothers.
A search of the records indicates that this is the first time that this
situation has ever arisen in this jurisdiction, and, in all probability. it
never will happen again, when six blood brothers will apply to a Lodge
at the same time for the degrees of Masonry.
After serious consideration of this matter, feeling it to be for the best
interests of Masonry in that District, and believing that no precedent
would be established. I issued a dispensation to Marsh River Lodge for
the purpose requested.

ARE WE BETTER THAN AVERAGE?
We. as Freemasons, are supposed to be better than average in our
respective communities. As individuals we should watch the trend of
affairs and of our government - Local. State and National - and we
should think when we vote. We should support the church of our faith.
our school systems and our youth organizations. We should stand foursquare behind those projects which make for a better community. Never
should we leave our Light under a bushel-there to remain dormant and
inactive.
By John W. Hall, Gr. M. of New Mexico.

HOW TRUE - Gr. M. Lander of Maine Says:
We should guard against assembly line methods and adhere to the
principle which I have so often advocated during the past year, that our
primary object should be to put more Masonry into men, rather than
more men into Masonry.

545

President Truman is now the Senior Warden of the Missouri Lodge
of Research and, at the coming election, undoubtedly will be chosen
Worshipful Master.
·
In conversation with the President in Washington February last he
assured the Missouri delegation that if elected he would accept. He
further announced his intention to open the Library of Congress for the
photostating of records dealing with Masonry and by so doing would
render what he considered his outstanding service to the Craft.
Thus the Missouri Lodge of Research would have recourse to a rich
field of Masonic material not available elsewhere or at any other time.

POSTSCRIPT TO GOLD-Nova Scotia, 1950
"The crest and crowning of all good,
Life's final star, is Brotherhood;
And it will bring again to earth
Her long lost Poesy and Mirth;
Will send new light on every face,
A Kingly power upon the race.
An' till it comes. we, men. are slaves,
And travel downward to the dust of graves.
"Come then, clear the way, clear the way;
Blind creeds and Kings have had their day;
Break the dead branches from the path;
Our hopes are in the aftermathOur hopes are in heroic men,
Star-led to build the world again.
To this event the ages ran,
Make way for Brotherhood-Make way for Man."
-

EDWIN MARKHAM
